title: Introduction to Flight
description_handout: This course introduces the fundamental principles governing aircraft flight, including basic aerodynamics, atmospheric properties, aircraft performance, stability and control, propulsion systems, and Hypersonic vehicles. Students explore the forces acting on an aircraft and the engineering concepts that enable safe and efficient flight. The course provides a foundational understanding of flight mechanics and aircraft systems, preparing students for advanced studies in aerospace engineering.
scope_objective: Following are the scope and objective of this course: a. Understand the fundamentals of flight: Introduce the basic principles of aerodynamics, the four forces of flight, and the physical concepts governing aircraft motion. b. Study aircraft systems and performance: Develop an understanding of aircraft structures, propulsion systems, stability, control, and performance under various operating conditions. c. Apply engineering principles: Use fundamental concepts of mathematics, physics, and engineering to analyse and solve introductory flight-related problems. d. Build a foundation for advanced aerospace studies: Prepare students for higher-level courses in flight mechanics, aircraft design, aerospace propulsion, and aviation engineering.
learning_outcomes: Upon successful completion of this course, the students will have the following learning outcomes: a. Explain the principles of flight by describing the four fundamental forces (lift, weight, thrust, and drag) and their interactions during flight. b. Analyse atmospheric effects on flight by interpreting how atmospheric properties influence aircraft performance and operations. c. Apply basic aerodynamic concepts to evaluate the performance of airfoil, wings, and aircraft under various flight conditions. Birla Institute of Technology & Science, Pilani Pilani Campus ACADEMIC - UNDER GRADUATE STUDIES DIVISION Page 2 of 5 d. Evaluate aircraft performance by estimating take-off, climb, cruise, descent, landing, range, and endurance characteristics using fundamental engineering principles. e. Describe aircraft stability and control and explain how control surfaces affect aircraft motion and manoeuvrability. f. Compare aircraft propulsion systems, including propeller- and jet-powered engines, and explain their operating principles and performance characteristics. g. Learn Hypersonic flight, concepts of Newtonian theory and its application to Hypersonic vehicles. h. Solve introductory flight-related engineering problems using mathematics, physics, and computational tools where appropriate. i. Interpret the relationship between aircraft design and flight performance, recognizing how design choices affect efficiency, safety, and operational capability. j. Communicate technical concepts related to flight through written reports, calculations, and engineering discussions

title: INTRODUCTION TO BIOLOGICAL SCIENCES
description_handout: Properties of living systems, Biological macromolecules, Basic physiological processes, Genetics, Photosynthesis, Metabolism and Cellular systems. Experiments including but not limited to Microscopy, Quantification of Biomolecules, Chlorophyll extraction, Water potential in plant tissues and Cell cycle analysis.
scope_objective: The course is aimed to provide a broad introduction to the major principles and topics in biology. The relationship of the living organism with its environment at the molecular level is highlighted in line with modern research in biological sciences. By the end of the course, the student would have gained an overall understanding of the essential aspects of biology – both as a basic science and as a branch with wide-ranging applications in industry, medicine and human health. It is also expected that using the acquired knowledge, he/she would be able to devise/suggest strategies to solve some of the imminent problems faced by mankind and the world at large through technological solutions. Students shall also get hands-on experience on fundamental aspects of practical biology. 3. Text Book: TB: Simon, E.J. et al. Campbell Essential Biology with Physiology (5th Edition). title: Biological Chemistry

The course deals with the structure, properties, and significance of the major groups of biochemical compounds (amino acids, proteins, carbohydrates, nucleic acids, and lipids), the bioenergetics, enzyme mechanisms and regulation of the central metabolic pathways. Efforts will be made to include the recent advances and methodologies related to biochemistry. title: Microbiology
description_handout: Introduction and classification of microbes; isolation, cultivation, physiological and biochemical characterization of microbes; structure, physiology and genetics of microbial cell; synthetic microbiology; host parasite relationship; physical chemical methods of controlling microbes; antimicrobial drugs; clinical microbiology; microbiology of soil, water and food; and related lab components.
scope_objective: This course deals with the structure, physiology, genetics and growth of various microorganisms as well as their control. Emphasis will be given on microbes and their role in human health, environment and industry. 3. Text Book: Tortora, G.J., Funke, B.R. and Case, C.L. 2020. Microbiology: An Introduction, 12th Ed., Pearson India Education Services Pvt. Ltd. India 4. Reference books: Willey, J.M., Sherwood, L.M. and Woolverton, C.J. 2017. title: CELL BIOLOGY
scope_objective: A fundamental branch in biological sciences, cell biology exposes the learner to the structural and functional organization and working of the cell, the basic unit of life. The field is dynamic and constantly evolving. This course will give an introduction to this branch of biology, by providing experimental data wherever possible. Some of the major topics covered include the working of the cell at microscopic and molecular levels, their physiological properties, structure, intracellular organelles, interactions with microenvironments, division, regulatory mechanisms and related experimental procedures. The topics learned in this course will also be foundational for advanced courses in cell and molecular biology, as well as genetics and developmental biology. 3. Text Book (TB): Sheeler, P. and Bianchi, DE. (2009). Cell and Molecular Biology (3/E). New Delhi: Wiley. 4. Reference Books (RB): RB1: Alberts, B., et al. (2014). Essential Cell Biology (4/E). New York: Garland Science. RB2: Cooper, G.M. and Hausman, R.E. (2015). The Cell: A Molecular Approach (7/E). United States: Sinauer Associates Inc. RB3: Lodish, H., Berk, A., Kaiser, C.A., Kreiger, M. and Bretscher, A. (2016) Molecular Cell Biology (8/E). United States: W H Freeman & Co. RB4: Hardin, J., Bertoni, G. and Kleinsmith, L.J. (2016). title: RECOMBINANT DNA TECHNOLOGY
description_handout: The course deals with theoretical aspects and selected experiments of recombinant DNA manipulation. Emphasis will be placed on procedures to create chimeric molecules using examples from actual experimental work. Vector designing, PCR, DNA sequencing, in vitro mutagenesis, cloning in prokaryotic and eukaryotic systems and whole genome approaches will be covered.
scope_objective: Almost every field of modern experimental biology relies heavily on DNA manipulation techniques. This course will expose the student to the foundations and principles underlying such molecular biology methods and give a brief yet broad overview of the recent trends and applications of recombinant DNA technology. 3. Text Book (TB): Howe, Christopher J. Gene Cloning and Manipulation (2nd edition). New Delhi: Cambridge University Press India Pvt. Ltd., 2015. 4. Reference Books (RB): • RBa: Brown, Terence A. Gene Cloning and DNA Analysis: An Introduction (8th edition). United Kingdom: Wiley-Blackwell, 2010. • RBb: Primrose, Sandy B. and Richard Twyman. Principles of Gene Manipulation and Genomics (7th edition). New York: Blackwell Science, 2006. 5. Course Plan: MODULE LECTURE TOPICS TB/ RB CHAP# LEARNING OUTCOMES I Orientation to the course. Tools and techniques of recombinant DNA technology: DNA manipulation Enzymes and techniques L1: Defining the scope and context of the course. Introduction to Recombinant DNA Techniques and workflow summary. TB 1-2 TB 5-6 Understanding of basic tools/ techniques of Recombinant DNA Technology; Restriction endonucleases; Understanding of Polymerase chain reaction with variants. L2-5: Enzymes for manipulating DNA; Restriction mapping and analysis L6-12: Understanding PCR; different types of PCR – inverse PCR, multiplex PCR, quantitative real time PCR, DD PCR Genomic, cDNA & specialized libraries BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division Please Do Not Print Unless Necessary II Techniques for Cloning and Recombinant DNA Analysis Cloning vectors, Electrophoresis Protein expression L13-19: Vectors for cloning - Plasmids, DNA isolation procedure; bacterial host and its transformation; High- capacity cloning vectors (BAC, PAC, etc.); bacteriophages (including molecular aspects of phages pertinent to vector design); Viral vectors, Expression vectors, fusion tags TB 1 TB 3-6 Class Notes Understanding of how proteins are expressed in E. coli. Expression and detection of recombinant proteins. L20-22: Electrophoresis of nucleic acids; Various methods used for screening and selection of the clones; L23-25: Protein expression, SDS PAGE, Western Blotting, Immunofluorescence imaging L26-29: Nucleic acid hybridization techniques- Southern, Northern blotting, FISH III Techniques for Mutagenesis & Genome editing L30-34: Methods for site-directed mutagenesis, Genome editing by CRISPR-Cas and related gene modification techniques. TB 7 Class Notes Knowledge to base specific gene sequence modification and genome editing IV DNA sequencing L35-40: Sanger’s chemistry; NGS automated sequencing; latest advances TB 1 RBa 10 Class Notes Understanding of gene sequencing and the concepts behind making of NGS libraries. V Applications of recombinant DNA technology L41-43: Selected applications of recombinant methodologies in medicine, agriculture & biomedical science, e.g., gene therapy, RNAi, etc. TB 8 TB 9 Some latest advances in this area (assignments) 6. title: Plant Physiology
description_handout: Basic functional processes in plants; Plant tissue system, Plant-water relations, Gaseous exchange, Stomatal regulations, Mineral nutrition and absorption, Transport of material, Growth and development, Hormones and Plant Growth Regulators, Photoperiodism, Vernalization, Stress Physiology and related lab components.
scope_objective: This course attempts to make the students aware of the major features of physiological aspects of plant system. Emphasis will be given to understand the plant tissue systems, water and mineral nutrient uptake and their distribution, mechanism of transpiration and photosynthate transport, the role of hormones in plant growth & developmental and mechanism of flowering. 3. Text Book: Taiz, L. and Zeiger, E., 2003. Plant Physiology, 3rd Ed., Panima Publishing Corporation, Indian Reprint. 4. Reference books: Taiz, L. and Zeiger, E., Plant Physiology, 5th Ed., 2010, Sinauer Associate, Sunderland, USA. Web Topics: https://learninglink.oup.com/access/taiz7e 5. Course Plan Module No. Lecture/ Tutorial Session Reference Learning Outcome 1. Introduction to the subject and course layout L 1. Orientation of the course, Introduction to plant physiology Lecture slides Familiarization with the plant physiology and diversity 2. Overview of Plant Structure L 2-4. Plant tissue system (meristematic and permanent); Simple (Parenchyma, Collenchyma, Sclerenchyma) and Complex (xylem, phloem) tissues Class Notes/ Web topic 1.4 In-depth understanding of various tissue systems, their composition and functions in plants 3. Learning water and its interaction with plant body L 5-6. Water potential TB-3, RB-3 Knowledge about the water transport processes and the ascent of sap in plant system 4. How plants obtain water from the soil? L 7-10. Water movement in soil, absorption by roots and transport through xylem TB-4, RB-4 5. The transpiration / photosynthesis paradox L 11-13. Transpiration and its compromise with photosynthesis, Stomatal regulations, Transpiration ratio TB-4, RB-4 BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 2 6. Mineral requirements for plant growth L 14. Mineral Nutrition: Essential elements and their function TB-5, RB-5 Knowledge about nutrient elements required for plant growth and their deficiency symptoms 7. How are nutrients absorbed and distributed in tissues L 15-17. Mineral Nutrition: Absorption of minerals, CEC of soils, Mycorrhizal fungi TB-5, RB-5 Processes involved in nutrient absorption in plants 8. How are nutrients absorbed and distributed in tissues L 18-20. Transport of solutes and ions, Membrane transport processes, Co-transport and counter transport, Ion trafficking in roots TB-6, RB-6 Passive and active transport mechanism 9. How are metabolic products distributed in plants? L 21-23. Transport of material in phloem TB-10, RB-10 Understanding of pattern and mechanism of phloem translocation, phloem loading and unloading 10. How do plants grow? L 24-27. Growth and development: Primary & secondary meristem, SAM & RAM, Phyllotaxy TB-16, RB-16 Understanding of the growth & development of plant shoot, root and leaves 11. What controls plant growth? L 28-32. Hormones and Growth regulators: Auxins and Gibberellins TB-19, 20 RB-19, 20 Knowledge about the physiological & developmental effects of PGRs 12. What controls plant growth? L 33-36. Cytokinins, Abscisic acid, Other important growth regulators TB-21, 23 RB-21, 23 13. How plants control the timing of flowering? L 37-40. Photoreceptors, Photoperiodism, Vernalization, Floral development TB-17, 24 RB-17, 24 Understanding the effect of light and temperature to control flowering Practical Assignments: 1) Transverse section and observing various tissue systems in dicot shoot & root 2) Transverse section and observing various tissue systems in monocot shoot & root 3) Transverse section and observing various tissue systems in dicot & monocot leaf 6. title: Animal Physiology
description_handout: Basic functional processes in animals; like homeostasis, membrane physiology, digestive, respiratory, excretory, circulatory, reproductive, nervous, sensory, muscular, endocrine systems will be studied at structural, functional, cellular and molecular level.
scope_objective: This course attempts to bring the awareness among students for major features of animal physiology and co- relate that to the human physiology. Emphasis will be on structure and function relationship and importanc of every organ. In addition, the course will also discuss about some of the diseases that are associated with complication in different organs.
learning_outcomes: a. Integration of multiple organ systems to regulate and maintain homeostasis between the internal and external environments. b. Explore the process of enzymatic digestion and its physiological outcomes within the digestive tract. c. Functional mechanisms of the human kidneys in regulating fluid homeostasis and urine formation. d. Overview of the cardiac cycle, electrocardiogram (ECG) interpretation, types of circulatory vessels, regulation of systolic and diastolic blood pressure, and the various cellular components of blood. e. Anatomical and functional organization of nervous system, including its structural and spatial characteristics. f. The role of hormones in regulating homeostasis and supporting essential physiological functions. g. Understanding gas partial pressures, intrapleural pressure dynamics, lung volumes and capacities, respiratory disorders, and the oxygen-carrying capacity of hemoglobin. h. Study of sarcomere structure, the molecular mechanism of muscle contraction, the physiological basis of rigor mortis, and the phenomenon of muscle twitching. i. Exploration of the regulatory mechanisms governing gametogenesis, fertilization, and progression of pregnancy. 5. Text Books: Sherwood, L., Klandorf, H. and Yancey, P.H., Animal Physiology: From Genes to Organisms, 2nd edition, 2013, Brook/Cole Cengage Learning, Singapore Reference Books: Sherwood, L. Principles of Human Physiology, 2007, Brook/Cole Cengage Learning, BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 2

title: Biomolecular Modeling
description_handout: Biomolecular Conformations, Structural genomics and proteomics, protein folding, Forcefield, Simulation, Conformational analysis, ab initio structure prediction, comparative modeling, lattice models, usage of modeling packages.
scope_objective: The course is designed to provide students the firsthand experience of potential utility of biomolecular modeling especially in concurrent pharmaceutical research, and in cell and structural biology. It describes the functionality, advantages, and limitations of standard computing strategies for the simulation of biomolecules. Provide a working knowledge of freely available software to carry out independent research projects in biomolecular modeling and explore the possibilities for modeling to assist in the process of determination, analyzing, evaluating, displaying, and retrieving of 3D structure data in a research or industry laboratory environment. 3. Text Books: “Molecular modeling: Principles and Applications” By Andrew R Leach, 2nd Edition, 2001, Pearson Education Lim. 4. Reference Books: (1) “Molecular Modeling and Simulation - An Interdisciplinary Guide” By Tamar Schlick, Springer, New York, 2002 (2) “Principles of protein structure” By Schulz, G.E. and Schirmer, R.H., New York, Springer-Verlag, 1979 (3) “An Introduction to Computational Biochemistry” – By C. Stan Tsai, Wiley-Liss, Inc, 2002. (4) “Bioinformatics: genes, proteins and computers” – Edited by C. Orengo, D. Jones, J. Thronton, BIOS Scientific Publishers Ltd., UK, 2003. 5. (3-8 Lectures) Protein structure and conformation R-1 (3-4) Amino Acid Building Blocks, Rotameric Structures Protein Conformation Framework, Ramachandran Plots, Conformational BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 2 Hierarchy, Structural motifs 3. (9-13 Lectures) Conformation and Variability in DNA and RNA structures R-1 (5-7) Basic Building Blocks, Conformational Flexibility, Canonical DNA Forms, DNA Sequence Effects, Non- coding RNA structure and function, Challenges in RNA structure modeling and prediction 4. (14-17 Lectures) Molecular graphics and Visualization R-3 (4), Web resources Introduction to graphic representation, Representation of molecular structure, Database of macromolecular structures, Usages of freely available visualization packages like VMD, ChimeraX, Rasmol, Pymol, SpdbViewer etc. 5. (18-24 Lectures) Protein structure prediction and protein folding problem R-4(8-9) First principle methods for predicting protein structure, comparative modeling, threading , CASP, Protein folding theories, AlphaFold 6. (25-28 Lectures) Energetics and Forcefield T (4) Different types of interactions and formulation of forcefield 7. (29-31 Lectures) Molecular mechanics T (5) Basic algorithm of MM and their utilities, Hand on sessions 8. (32-35 Lectures) Molecular dynamics T (6-7) Basic MD algorithm, Its limitation, treatment of long range forces, Enhanced sampling techniques 9. (36-38 Lectures) Conformational analysis T (9) Analysis of molecular dynamics trajectories 10. (39-41 Lectures) Lab on MD GROMACS Online tutorials Hand on session on molecular Dynamics 6. title: ENZYMOLOGY
description_handout: Enzyme nomenclature and classification; isolation and purification; structures; kinetics; regulation of enzymatic reactions; evaluation of enzymes and other proteins.
scope_objective: This course is designed to provide a broad introduction about enzymes, including their isolation, purification, structure and kinetics. Efforts will be made to understand the molecular basis of how enzymes catalyze the biological and non-natural reactions. Emphasis will be given to study the practical and industrial application of enzymes. This course integrates basics as well as current advances in enzymology and will create research interest among the students. 3. Text Books: 1). Trevor Palmer and Philip Bonner, Enzymes: Biochemistry, Biotechnology, Clinical Chemistry., East- West Press Private Limited, New Delhi, 2nd Edition, 2008. 4. Reference Books: 1). Lehninger Principles of Biochemistry. David L. Nelson, Michael M. Cox. W.H. Freeman & Company, NY, USA, 7th Edition, 2017. 2). Methods in Enzymology - Guide to Protein Purification, Vol 463, Edited by BR Richard & Murray P. Deutscher. Academic Press, 2nd Edition, 2009. 3.) Fermentation Microbiology and Biotechnology, Edited by El-Mansi EMT, Bryce CFA et al., CRC Press, Taylor & Francis Group, USA, 3rd Edition, 2012. 4.) Peer-reviewed articles and relevant web-based resources will be discussed to enhance coverage of select topics. BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 2 5. Course Plan: Module No. Lecture Session Reference Learning outcomes I Course & Class Introductions L#1-2: Broad overview of the subject and field of Enzymology and Quick preview of the entire course contents. Chap 1, T1 Getting introduced to the basic concept of enzymes, their significant properties, and varied applications in medicine, biotechnology and industry . II Enzyme nomenclature and classification L# 3-4: Brief history of Enzymology; EC system of classification; Main classes of enzymes, with examples. Chap 1, T1 Will be familiarized with the scientific system of enzyme naming and the different types of enzymes. III Enzyme structure, conformations, and specificity of enzyme actions L# 5-7: Enzyme structure and conformations; Types of enzyme specificity; Specificity Hypotheses. Chap 2, T1; Chap 4, T1 Will be able to appreciate the close association between enzyme protein structure and its biologic function. IV Enzyme Kinetics & Mechanism of enzyme action and regulation L# 8-11: Introduction to catalysis and kinetics; Kinetics of single-substrate enzyme-catalyzed reactions; Enzyme inhibition; Kinetics of multi- substrate enzyme-catalyzed reactions. Mechanisms of catalysis with examples; Enzymes and metabolic regulation; Investigation of active site structure. Chap 6-9, T1; Chap 10, 11, 14, T1; R1 Will understand the different aspects of enzyme reaction kinetics, and mechanistic basis of bio-catalysis. V Isolation and Purification L# 12-19: Extraction of enzymes; Enzyme assay methods; Enzyme purification techniques. title: BIOSTATISTICS & BIOMODELING
description_handout: Biostatistics and Biomodeling course has two components. Biostatistics part will provide an introduction to the basic concepts of statistical methods to equip students with statistical reasoning in their fields of study. Topics include variables in biology, Standard deviation; correlation and regression analysis; significance tests; chi square, t-test, ANOVA etc. Emphasis is placed on the application of fundamental concepts to real world situations. Biomodeling is designed to provide students the first-hand experience of modelling biomolecules to elucidate the relationships between sequence, structure and function. Specifically, different computing strategies for the simulation of biomolecules will be discussed with regard to their utility, advantages, and limitations.
scope_objective: The student would learn how to collect data suitable for statistical analyses, understand the general features of the data collected, making statistical inferences and likelihood of occurrence of an event using probability calculations and tests of significance. 3. title: INTRODUCTION TO BIOLOGICAL SCIENCES
description_handout: Properties of living systems, Biological macromolecules, Basic physiological processes, Genetics, Photosynthesis, Metabolism and Cellular systems. title: Food Biotechnology
description_handout: The food sector is very important from the economical point of view, and is one of the industrial areas where Biotechnology has played and still plays a pivotal role. In this course, a general view of the basic aspects (physical-chemical aspects, structure, spoilage), of foods and their processing and preservation techniques will be taught. Further the most relevant aspects for a future biotechnologist in the food industry will be studied: role of microorganisms and enzymes for the production and transformation of foods and most recent advances in foods made of/with genetically modified organisms. In addition, food safety and quality management along with food waste management will be covered. Finally, case studies of successful entrepreneurship ventures in Food Biotechnology will be discussed.
scope_objective: The aim of this course is providing the students with basic knowledge about the applications of Biotechnology in the food industry and in food-related sectors. These include the preservation tools used, production of recombinant proteins and additives to use in food technology, transgenic foods, diagnostic system used in food industry including advanced techniques like biosensors and artificial intelligence, and ethics and safety of food biotechnology. 3. title: Social Conduct 1
description_handout: Emotional & Social Intelligence, Relationships & Identity, Laws & Campus Policies and Practice, Inappropriate Behavior & Consent, Substance Abuse, Emotional Maturity & Communication, Recognizing Harm & Promoting Safety.
scope_objective: This is the first of a two-part course that is a General Institute Requirement, for all students in the first year of any program. It is intended to equip students with core emotional, social and legal literacy for a healthy campus life. This includes conversations around gender, sexuality, mental health, understanding of boundaries and consent, prevention of sexual misconduct, promoting responsible digital behavior and building awareness against substance abuse.
learning_outcomes: At the end of this part of the course, the student will be able to CLO1.Recognize and apply core emotional and social skills for campus well-being, including stress management, empathy, and self-awareness. CLO2. Understand and navigate relationships with peers, faculty, and family, with sensitivity to gender identity, sexuality, and high achievement pressures. CLO3. Identify and challenge harmful social myths and stereotypes related to gender roles, masculinity, and interpersonal dynamics. CLO4. Establish and respect personal boundaries in social, academic, and digital contexts. CLO5. Demonstrate awareness of campus policies, legal protections (including POSH), and the consequences of sexual misconduct. CLO6. Understand reporting mechanisms and institutional responsibilities in promoting a safe and inclusive campus environment. CLO7. Engage with mental health literacy, recognize signs of emotional distress, and promote openness around mental well-being. CLO8. Reflect on individual responsibility in building a safe, respectful, and accountable student community.

title: ENGINEERING GRAPHICS
description_handout: The course includes fundamentals and techniques of technical drawing and standard practices of the same so that design ideas can be adequately communicated and produced. It introduces students to the theories of projection and the concepts of engineering drawing using the most widely used CAD application software, AutoCAD. Basic AutoCAD 2023 commands will also be introduced. The course covers the following topics: Introduction to AutoCAD basic commands; theory of projections; orthographic projections; isometric projections; projection of points, lines, planes and solids; section of solids; developments of surfaces.
scope_objective: Computerized drafting provides accurate and easily modifiable graphics entities, easy data storage and retrieval facility and enhances creativity. Upon successful completion of this course, the student will be able to:  Read and interpret engineering drawings  Identify the three principal projection planes  Draw 2-dimensional orthographic projections from given 3-dimensional views  Create an isometric drawing using AutoCAD  Comprehend orthographic and multiview projection  Apply the concept of cutting planes to create the various types of sectional views  Become conversant with appropriate use of AutoCAD software for drafting. 3. title: Science, Technology and Modernity
scope_objective: This course is designed to provide students with a comprehensive understanding of how science and technology interact with societal structures, economic systems, and global governance. The course begins with an introduction to foundational perspectives on technological change and scientific knowledge systems, offering a basic orientation to how technologies are developed and adopted. It then moves to the examination of Intellectual Property Rights and Innovation, focusing on real-world issues such as patent disputes, corporate competition, and the strategic control of innovation. The third and final module explores Science, Technology, and Social Stratification, encouraging students to consider how power, inequality, and institutional interests influence technological priorities and outcomes. Overall, it critically assesses the societal responsibilities and consequences of scientific and technological work in contemporary settings. 2. Text Book: Sismondo, Sergio, An Introduction to Science and Technology Studies, UK: Wiley-Blackwell, 2010. Jacob, Margaret. 1997. Scientific Culture and the Making of the Industrial West. New York: Oxford University Press. Friedman, Thomas L. 1999. The Lexus and the Olive Tree. New York: Anchor Books. 3. Reference Material- Books/Papers: Book chapters, Journal papers, and newspaper reports will be shared as reading materials with the students.

title: General Mathematics III
description_handout: Linear equations and matrices, Determinants, Basis of Rn , Eigen Value, Eigen Vector, Linear transformations on Rn . Linear Programming: Geometric Solutions, Simplex Method, Duality, Post optimal Analysis, Transportation and Assignment Problem. Nonlinear Programming (Unconstrained optimization).
scope_objective: The course is made for Pharmacy students keeping in mind the importance of Linear Algebra and Linear programming problems and their possible applications in various fields of science and engineering. Linear algebra begins with vectors and matrices – two of the most important practical concepts in mathematics. Whereas Linear programming is a method to achieve the best outcome in a mathematical model whose requirements are represented by linear relationships. Linear programming can be applied to various fields of study. It is used in business and economics, but can also be utilized for some engineering problems. Industries that use linear programming models include transportation, energy, telecommunications, and manufacturing.
learning_outcomes: CLO1. Apply the concepts of matrix algebra, systems of linear equations, vector spaces, linear transformations, and eigenvalues/eigenvectors to solve mathematical problems arising in science and engineering. CLO2. Formulate and solve linear programming problems using graphical and simplex-based methods, analyze duality and post-optimality, and apply optimization techniques to transportation and assignment problems. CLO3. Analyze and solve basic nonlinear optimization problems using appropriate numerical optimization techniques, and interpret the results in the context of engineering and pharmaceutical applications.

title: PROCESS ENGINEERING
description_handout: Basic concepts related to heat transfer, mass transfer and flow of fluid, processes and equipment involved in extraction and filtration; mixing and granulation; size reduction and classification, evaporation and distillation, drying and crystallization, humidification and dehumidification. scope_objective: This course introduces students to the fundamental principles and practical aspects of pharmaceutical engineering, with a focus on key unit operations involved in the development and manufacturing of pharmaceutical formulations. The course emphasizes the selection, operation, and application of various equipment used in the pharmaceutical industry.
learning_outcomes: a. Complete understanding of the principles of key pharmaceutical unit operations b. description_handout: Environment, human population, and industrialization; natural resources and the impact of man-made activities on them; structure and function of ecosystem, population ecology, biodiversity and its conservation, environmental pollution, social issues and the environment, and environmental impact assessment.
scope_objective: The United Nations Conference on Environment and Development (UNCED) held in Rio De Janero in 1992, the 1994 conference on United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), and a very recent 2015 Paris Agreement have created awareness among the people around the globe about the deteriorating condition of Earth’s environment. It has warned us not to be ignorant of the environmental issues. In lieu of the situation, the Hon’ble Supreme Court directed the UGC to introduce a basic course on environment for undergraduate students in India. The course is designed to cover all aspects of environment [Ecological including biotic (flora- fauna) and abiotic (air, water, soil & geography), social, economic and aesthetical]. The course is of interdisciplinary nature dealing with social, biological & engineering aspects of environment. The role of biotic and abiotic factors in the functioning of the environment, the impact of anthropogenic activities on the environment, different environmental pollutants, its impact and management strategies; and ecological, socio-political and economic issues will be discussed with appropriate real-life examples and case studies. The course would also provide insight into practical solutions to different environmental issues. Finally, important concepts of environmental impact assessment from all the above mentioned sources would be dealt with. The interested students can take the learnings forward from this point and enrich themselves further by doing other electives/projects in these areas. 3. title: Foundations of Data Structures and Algorithms
description: Data Structures and Algorithms or Foundations of Data Structures and Algorithms 3 3 1 1 4 4
description_handout: Algorithm Analysis – Mathematical preliminaries, Sorting Algorithms, Search Algorithms, Linear Structures, Non-Linear Structures, Hashing, Graphs and Algorithms. (Open elective for non-B.E. Computer Science students)
scope_objective: A data structure is a way to organize large amounts of data, their relationships, and the opera- tions that can be applied to them. This course focuses on applying data structures like stacks, queues, linked lists, heaps, trees, and graphs, along with algorithmic techniques such as brute- force, greedy, divide-and- conquer, and dynamic programming, to solve real-world problems, in- cluding shortest paths in maps, spell checking, and social network analysis. Objectives • Apply basic data structures (stacks, queues, linked lists, trees) to solve programming prob- lems. • Implement advanced data structures (graphs, balanced search trees, hash tables, priority queues) for complex applications. • Use algorithmic techniques (brute-force, greedy, divide-and-conquer, dynamic programming) to address real-world challenges. • Develop skills to design and implement data abstractions for problem-solving.
learning_outcomes: CLO1. Apply appropriate data structures such as arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, trees, graphs, and hash tables to solve computational problems. CLO2. Perform a basic analysis and comparison of algorithms based on correctness, effi- ciency, and suitability for different problem domains. 1 CLO3. Design and implement solutions using fundamental algorithmic paradigms, including divide-and-conquer, greedy, and dynamic programming. CLO4. Develop efficient programs by selecting suitable data structures and algorithms for real-world applications.

title: Introduction to Engineering Design
description_handout: This course provides students with a foundation in engineering design practice and prepares them for discipline-specific advanced courses in engineering design. Students will gain experience in the use of digital design techniques and management of larger open-ended, team-based engineering design tasks in a project-based learning environment. Students will learn to create detailed designs of real-world products and systems by applying design thinking and scientific principles. Students will learn a range of design techniques to contextualize, evaluate, and communicate designs, from generating ideas via sketching to development of digital models and detailed technical drawings that meet the international standards. Students will develop foundation skills in computer-aided design (CAD) techniques to generate 3D models of products and assemblies and learn to integrate them in augmented and virtual reality tools. 2. Course Contents: Engineering Design process, Introduction to Engineering Drawing, Introduction to Orthographic Projections, Projections of points, lines, planes, and solid objects, Sectional views, Manufacturing processes and materials, Fits and Tolerances, Isometric Drawing, Introduction to Solid Modelling, Assembly drawings 3. Scope and Objective of the Course: The scope and objectives of the course are as follows: 1. Apply key elements of the design process and scientific principles to create detailed design of a product that meets engineering requirements and standards. 2. Generate and interpret engineering technical drawings of parts and assemblies according to engineering design standards; and 3. Use CAD software to generate a computer model of a well-defined part or assembly. 4. Text Books: Engineering Drawing and Design, 6th Edition David A Madsen, Cengage Learning 5. Reference Books: 1. Engineering Graphics Essentials with AutoCAD 2023, Kirstie Plantenberg, SDC Publications. BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 2 6. description_handout: This course introduces the fundamental concepts and analytical tools of game theory for studying strategic interactions among rational decision-makers. It covers the construction and classification of games with complete and incomplete Information, strategic behavior, and solution concepts, including dominant strategy equilibrium, iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies (IESDS), Nash equilibrium, mixed strategy equilibrium, and static and dynamic games with and without complete Information. It also includes extensive-form games, finite- and infinitely-repeated games, Bayesian games, and the integration of linear programming with game-theoretic analysis. Emphasis is placed on applications to economics and public policy, including social choice and voting theory, trade, environmental economics, industrial organization, auctions, negotiations, and other strategic decision-making problems.
scope_objective: Game Theory is a tool and is a beautiful mix of mathematics, economics, and psychology. Game theory is a technique for analyzing strategic problems across diverse settings. The foundation of Game Theory was laid by John von Neumann, who proved the fundamental minimax theorem in 1928 and published a book (co-authored with Oskar Morgenstern), Theory of Games and Economic Behavior, in 1944. Game Theory became a buzzword and attained particular glamour, with the Nobel Prize going to John Nash for his contributions to the Field, which has found applications in almost every branch of knowledge. Broadly, Game Theory can be divided into cooperative and non-cooperative game theory. This course deals only with non-cooperative games. The main objective is to introduce students to Game Theory & Its applications to the real world as a tool for logical thinking in a strategic interaction setting.
learning_outcomes: The course would aim to illustrate economic & other real-world concepts and to make students adept at approaching financial problems from a game-theoretic perspective. CLO1) Understand the Fundamentals of Game Theory, including game construction, analysis, and solutions. CLO2) Able to apply game theory tools to real-world contexts such as economic, political & environmental settings, trade negotiations, environmental agreements, cartels, oligopolistic competition, and in social choice contexts, among others. CLO3) Understand the collective decision-making mechanisms using game-theoretic tools. CLO4) Gain exposure to games with imperfect Information, including understanding the basic concepts of Bayesian games (types, beliefs, and strategies). CLO5) Develop problem-solving and strategic thinking skills.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Robotics
description_handout: This course provides a comprehensive introduction to artificial intelligence techniques for robotic systems with emphasis on adaptive learning, machine learning, and cognitive decision making. Topics include: Evolution of intelligent robotics; adaptive learning algorithms; biologically inspired learning using Dynamic Hebbian Learning and adaptive oscillators; statistical learning and adaptive estimation; data-driven modelling of serial-chain manipulator kinematics using neural networks; reinforcement learning for robot trajectory planning and decision making; and high-level robot control through large language models/vision language models (using camera sensors). Each module contains hands-on sessions and project-based learning to emphasize implementation of intelligent algorithms for adaptation, learning, and autonomous algorithm for robotics.
scope_objective: This course introduces the fundamental concepts of Artificial Intelligence for Robotics through the lens of adaptive, data-driven, and cognitive robotic systems. Unlike conventional robotics courses that primarily focus on analytical modelling and control, this course emphasizes how robots can learn, adapt, and make intelligent decisions using modern AI techniques while remaining grounded in classical robotics principles. Students will explore multiple paradigms of robot intelligence, ranging from adaptive learning algorithms and biologically inspired learning mechanisms to neural networks, reinforcement learning, and high-level cognitive reasoning using vision and large language models. Through hands-on experiments, students will investigate how intelligent algorithms can be applied to serial-chain robotic manipulators for learning kinematics, trajectory generation, sensor adaptation, and autonomous task execution. Course Outcome: Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to: CO1 Explain and compare adaptive, statistical, machine learning, and AI-based approaches for developing intelligent robotic systems. CO2 Develop and implement adaptive learning algorithms, including Dynamic Hebbian Learning and statistical learning methods, for robotic sensing, adaptation, and motion generation. CO3 Design and evaluate neural network and reinforcement learning approaches for solving robot kinematics and trajectory planning problems in serial-chain manipulators. CO4 Develop AI-enabled robotic applications that integrate vision to generate high-level task commands for autonomous robotic manipulation. title: FUZZY LOGIC & APPLICATIONS
description_handout: Fuzzy sets, fuzzy binary relations, fuzzy logic, fuzzy reasoning, applications in decision making, control theory, expert systems, artificial intelligence etc.
scope_objective: The course aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the fundamental concepts of fuzzy sets, fuzzy relations, fuzzy logic, and fuzzy reasoning, along with their applications in decision making, control theory, expert systems, artificial intelligence, and other interdisciplinary areas. Emphasis is placed on developing analytical, computational, and problem-solving skills through real-world applications. title: Human Computer Interaction
description_handout: Introduction to HCI in the AI era; Understanding People: Perception, Motor control, Cognition, Needs, and Experience; User Research: Interviews, Field research, and Survey research; Understanding Interaction: Usability Engineering, Information and control, Dialogue, Tool use, Automation, and Rationality; User Interfaces: Input devices, Displays, Interaction techniques, and Reality-based interaction; Design: Cognition, Practice, and Processes; Engineering: Systems, Design engineering, Safety and risk, and Computational representations and models; Evaluation: Analytical methods, Think-aloud studies, and Experiment.
scope_objective: At the completion of this course, students will be able to: • Understand the concepts and theories of human-AI interaction. Furthermore, they will be able to explain basic concepts from the relevant theories in cognitive and social sciences. (LO1) • Illustrate and compare methods of “user-centered engineering (UCE)”, involving future users in various stages of the design and development process of AI systems. title: Introduction to Gender Studies
description_handout: Introduction to Gender Studies and Feminist Movements; Theories of Gender; Sex, Gender and Sexuality; Social Construction of Gender; Intersectionality and Social Location; Marriage, Family and Gender Discrimination; Gender and Labour Politics; Productivity and Labour Issues; Unpaid Domestic Work and Gendered Labour; Globalization, Global Assembly Line, Care Work and Emotion Labour; Ideal Worker Norm and Second Shift; Gender Discrimination in the Workplace; Media Representations and Male Gaze; Theories of Masculinity; Gender Based Violence.
scope_objective: To develop the knowledge necessary for addressing issues of gender equity and understanding gender roles. The course would help students get a greater insight into women’s rights, their role in shaping political, social, economic and cultural institutions. Emphasis would be laid on understanding the dynamics of gender relations in educational institutions, work and home. The course would further aim at gender sensitization in the context of societal stratifications.
learning_outcomes: • Familiarity with the foundational concepts, scope and relevance of Gender Studies as a discipline. • Understanding of the historical trajectory of feminist movements and their theoretical contributions. • Understanding of the social construction of gender, sex and sexuality through key theoretical frameworks. • Understanding of intersectionality as a framework for analysing overlapping systems of identity and inequality. • Evaluating the dynamics of gender discrimination within institutions of marriage and family. • Understanding the gendered dimensions of labour politics and workplace discrimination. • Evaluating the politics of unpaid domestic work and its relationship to gendered labour. • Understanding the impact of globalization on gendered labour, care work and emotion labour. • Understanding the ideal worker norm and the second shift as frameworks for analysing gender discrimination in the workplace. • Evaluating media representations of gender and the concept of the male gaze. • Understanding theories of masculinity and their relationship to gender-based violence. title: Introduction to Nano Science
description_handout: Nanotechnology is widely regarded as a transformative field with the potential to address critical challenges in energy, healthcare, electronics, and advanced manufacturing. This course is designed to introduce students to the fundamental concepts of nanoscience and nanotechnology, preparing them for further academic research or industrial careers in this rapidly evolving area. The course focuses on the fundamental science behind nanomaterials, their synthesis and properties of nanomaterials, with emphasis on their size-dependent physical, chemical, electrical, optical, and thermal properties. Applications of nanomaterials in electronics, medicine, MEMS, photonics, catalysis, energy systems, and heat transfer will be discussed. The course also introduces essential quantum mechanical concepts relevant to nanoscale systems. In addition, emerging trends, large-scale manufacturing challenges, and future directions in nanoscience and nanotechnology are covered.
scope_objective: The course is structured to provide a comprehensive and interdisciplinary overview of nanoscience and nanotechnology. Students will learn common methods for the synthesis of nanoparticles and nanostructures. Special emphasis is placed on understanding the unique properties of nanomaterials and the scientific principles governing their behavior at the nanoscale. The course highlights real-world motivations and applications of nanomaterials across multiple technological domains. This course is well suited for students seeking foundational knowledge and practical exposure to nanoscience and nanotechnology, and serves as an effective entry point into advanced study or research in the field.
learning_outcomes: After successful completion of this course, the student will be able to: 2 BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus ACADEMIC— UNDER GRADUATE STUDIES DIVISION ◦Explain the fundamental principles of nanoscience, including size-dependent properties and quantum effects at the nanoscale. ◦Describe and compare common synthesis techniques used for nanomaterials. ◦Analyze the structure–property–application relationships of nanomaterials in areas such as electronics, energy, catalysis, and biomedical systems.

title: Nanotechnology for Renewable Energy and Environment
description: Nanotechnology for Renewable Energy and Environment 3 1 4
description_handout: This course provides an introduction to nanotechnology, emphasizing its applications in renewable energy and environmental engineering. It covers fundamental concepts, including the distinction between the macro- and nanoscale, nanoscale phenomena, and the distinctive properties of nanomaterials that enable them to outperform many conventional materials. The course also discusses the fundamentals of fabrication, characterization, and operating principles of advanced energy devices, including organic, quantum dot, and dye-sensitized solar cells, fuel cells, batteries, and carbon nanotube-based energy storage systems, and the application of nanomaterials for hydrogen production and storage. In addition, it examines the application of nanotechnology in improving solar cells, nanoelectrodes, nanocoating, catalyst materials for fuel cells, and battery technologies. The course further explores the role of nanotechnology in environmental sustainability, including groundwater remediation, nanoadsorbents, ecotoxicology, nanomaterial toxicity, transport and fate of nanomaterials in the environment, and the broader societal impacts of nanotechnology.
scope_objective: Nanotechnology is widely regarded as a transformative technology with the potential to significantly benefit society across diverse fields. This course is designed to equip students with the fundamental knowledge and skills required for advanced academic research or industrial careers in nanotechnology, with particular emphasis on applications in renewable energy and environmental sustainability. The course is divided into 3 modules as decribed below. o Module 1: General introduction to principles of nanoscience and technology o Module 2: Nanotechnology applications in the renewable energy sector o Module 3: Nanotechnology applications in the environmental sector. The specific topics covered under each module are listed in the course plan (refer to section 6 of this handout).
learning_outcomes: o Introduce the importance and application of nanomaterials and the origin of their unique properties. o Summarize the fabrication methods, characterization techniques, and operating principles of solar cells, fuel cells, batteries, and CNT-based energy storage systems. o Explain the merits and motivation in the renewable energy and environmental sectors. o Define toxic effect of nanomaterials on human and environment, relative remediation and precautions.

scope_objective: In recent years the manufacturing industries are facing problems of survival. They find it difficult to maintain a long term competitive advantage due to uncertainty in environmental conditions. The ideal production system for such environment is Flexible Manufacturing Systems (FMS), which are considered to meet the demand for a variety of products with improvement of productivity in mid-volume manufacturing. This course will highlight the fundamentals of FMS and modelling for design, planning and control of FMS.
learning_outcomes: CLO1. Comprehend importance of adaptability of changes in product type and quantity in industry. CLO2. Understand how labor cost can be reduced by automated the manufacturing system using FMS. CLO3. Comprehend CNC technology and role of CAM in FMS.

title: Pattern Recognition
description_handout: This is a ﬁrst course on Pattern recognition. It begins with an introduction to the fundamentals of digital images and develops the theoretical background for the pattern recognition. It goes on to discuss the different aspects like the preprocessing of a digital image, segmentation, representation and description and ﬁnally the object recognition. During the course, a ﬂavour of matlab programming will also be given.
scope_objective: Over the past 30 years or so, pattern recognition and automation have evolved into a mature subject embracing many topics and applications: these range from automatic (robot) assembly to automatic vehicle guidance, from automatic interpretation of documents to veriﬁcation of signatures, and from analysis of remotely sensed images to checking of ﬁngerprints and human blood cells. Currently, pattern recognition and automatic visual inspection are undergoing very substantial growth, neces- sary improvement in quality, safety and cost effectiveness being the stimulating factors. The course introduces the students to the fundamentals of digital images and various processing techniques that are applied to them not only to improve their quality but also to recognize them. 3. Textbooks: TB1. Digital Image Processing, R. C. Gonzalez and R. E. Woods, 3rd and above, Pearson Education Asia, 2007. References: Ref1. Image Processing, analysis and machine vision, M. Sonka, V. Hlavac and R. Boyle, 2nd Ed., Thompson Asia, 2003.

title: New Venture Creation
description_handout: The purpose of this course is to not only study entrepreneurship but also practice it. Student teams are expected to create a technology product-based or service/SaaS-based startup and complete the business model canvas, including all the building blocks of creating a venture. In order to create a successful startup, student entrepreneurs will be required to comprehend the five phases of startup creation: (1) idea and problem validation; (2) solution validation and product market fit (PMF); (3) go to market (GTM) and scalability; (4) operations and institutionalization; (5) Startup teams will work on customer discovery, product development, market research, technology viability, fundraising, competitive analysis, team formation, marketing & sales strategy, and storytelling. The course features workshops/guest- lectures from entrepreneurs, investors and academicians with strong experience in creating and running Startups. Participating teams will be assigned an experienced, dedicated entrepreneur mentor who will guide them through the semester and can choose to mentor after the course is concluded. The top teams may be invited to compete for seed funding in early 2027 to pursue their business idea for incubation after the completion of the NVC course and thereby launch the business.
scope_objective: NVC’s mission is to empower student founders with the choice and tools to become entrepreneurs Hence, the course aims to provide students with an opportunity to launch/ prepare to launch startups post-NVC. NVC helps them to think and act entrepreneurially. The central mystery of entrepreneurship is how to transform an idea into an organizational entity where people can channel their energy and creativity to produce a reliable output that creates economic value. Some of the questions that will be addressed are: Which specific market segment of customers should you focus on? How do you plan for a new venture? How do you build an effective venture team? How do you establish your venture’s identity and legitimacy? How do you win customers? How will your venture make money? How do you manage your venture’s dependence on key external partners? 3. Text Book: Steven G. Blank: The Four Steps to the Epiphany, Lulu.com, second ed. Available online: http://web.stanford.edu/group/e145/cgi- bin/winter/drupal/upload/handouts/Four_Steps.pdf 2 4. Reference Books: ● Osterwalder & Pigneur: Business Model Canvas, Wiley 2010 ● Eric Ries: The Lean Start up, Penguin 2011 5. title: Introduction to Large Language Models
description_handout: Introduction to Large Language Models (LLMs); prompt engineering techniques (e.g., zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought), autonomous prompt optimization; retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), vector databases, multi-modal RAG methods; tool and function calling; multi-agent workflows (memory, planning, action, reflection); safety, guardrails, reliability; LLM-based evaluation, human evaluation; life cycle of LLM training, LLM architecture, fine-tuning LLMs using supervised learning or reinforcement learning; inference optimization; Mechanistic Interpretability; real-world case-studies
scope_objective: s: By the end of this course, students will be able to: a. Understand and apply prompt engineering techniques to control the behavior of LLMs. b. Build retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines for combining LLMs with external knowledge bases. c. Fine-tune LLMs for specific tasks using publicly available models. d. Leverage tool calling to enable LLMs to interact with external systems and APIs. e. Design and implement multi-agent workflows where multiple LLMs interact to solve complex tasks. f. Implement guardrails to ensure the safe and ethical deployment of LLMs in production environments. g. Understand the internal architecture of LLMs and the entire life cycle of LLM Training and Fine-Tuning. h. Evaluate the performance and accuracy of LLM-powered applications using appropriate metrics. i. Understand the principles of inference for deploying LLM models efficiently at scale. 3. title: Environmental Impact Assessment
description_handout: Environment and global problems; Framing Environmental issues; effects of infrastructure development on environment; prediction and assessment of environmental impacts of infrastructure projects: technical and procedural aspects, guidelines and legal aspects of environmental protection, impacts on air, water, soil and noise environment, valuation, strategic assessment, mathematical modeling for environmental processes; social impact assessment (SIA), dislocation/disruption impact of Infrastructure projects; Life Cycle Assessments (LCA) and risk analysis methodologies; mitigation of environmental impacts; case studies; environmental management plan (EMP), national and international certification and guidelines including ISO.
scope_objective: The course focuses on understanding environmental issues linked to infrastructure development, emphasizing technical, procedural, and legal aspects of environmental impact assessment (EIA). It covers prediction and mitigation of impacts on air, water, soil, and noise environments, supported by modeling tools. Strategic assessments, LCA, risk analysis, and SIA are addressed alongside valuation and management frameworks. Case studies and EMP formulation are discussed with reference to national and international standards, including ISO, ensuring comprehensive exposure to certification protocols and regulatory compliance.
learning_outcomes: a. Identify and frame environmental issues arising from infrastructure development, including physical and social dimensions. b. Apply procedural and technical approaches for impact prediction, assessment, and valuation using modeling tools and legal guidelines. c. Formulate environmental management plans (EMP) and assess projects in line with national and international frameworks, including ISO.

description_handout: This course deals with the research and development work in assigned areas of professional interest. Each student will work under the overall guidance and supervision of a faculty member/professional. References and bibliography in standard format are also to be included in the report.
scope_objective: The aim of this course is to carryout a research and development project in assigned areas of professional interest. An attendance sheet is being provided for this purpose to the supervisor. g) The candidate should apply and seek prior permission of his supervisor for going on leave for any genuine needs. If leave of absence exceeds seven days in entire semester, recommended BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 2 final grade may be revised by supervisor. h) The following format for Dissertation Abstract should be used. A check-list of various items is provided and students should carefully go through these. Supervisors are also requested to examine the draft of the FINAL REPORT keeping in view the items in the checklist. Title of the thesis should be proper and should be indicative of the type of work done. 4. EVALUATION Evaluation in this course is essentially individual oriented. Current literature (journals, books, etc.) must be methodically reviewed and the status of the work in the field must be considered. The detailed outline of work must reflect a survey of the current literature in the same area and must include topic of research, objective, background of previous work in the area, methodology and a work plan with a time schedule clearly indicating the intermediate milestones and the estimated time to achieve the same along with references and bibliography. b) Within two weeks of registration, the student should give his Dissertation particulars to the Head of Department in TS-1 Performa. c) The student should regularly interact with his supervisor and present seminars and submit reports on the scheduled dates. Proposed examiners and other faculty in relevant area may be requested to attend the presentations. d) Supervisor will announce the Mid-semester grade to his student and send the MID-SEM Evaluation Form to the Head of Department. e) Typed copy of Final Dissertation Report and Abstract are to be submitted to the supervisor on or before the last day of class work in each semester. f) Every student has to sign his attendance regularly with the supervisor or as per the alternative arrangement made by the supervisor. A check-list of various items is provided and students should carefully go through these. Supervisors are also requested to examine the draft of the FINAL REPORT keeping in view the items in the checklist. title: Foundations of Measurements and Experimentation
description_handout: This course introduces scientific and engineering inquiry through the principles of measurement and experimentation. It covers fundamental concepts, such as accuracy, precision, calibration, error analysis, and uncertainty, as well as the hands-on use of sophisticated instruments across multiple disciplines. The course includes data acquisition, visualization, and analysis using modern computational tools. It emphasizes experimental design, hypothesis formulation, and experimental validation. It also focuses on correlating measurements with real-world problems, documenting and interpreting results, and communicating findings effectively with due consideration to ethical practices in experimentation.
scope_objective: The course aims to provide a foundational understanding of measurement as an essential element of engineering and scientific practice. It covers key measurement concepts, exposure to a variety of instruments and sensors across disciplines, and methods for reliable data acquisition and analysis. The objectives of the course are to enable students to: (i) Understand fundamental measurement concepts such as accuracy, precision, resolution, cali- bration, and uncertainty. (ii) Use appropriate measuring instruments and sensors for acquiring experimental data across dif- ferent domains. (iii) Apply techniques for data acquisition, visualization, and analysis using modern computational tools. (iv) Develop an understanding of experimental methodologies, including hypothesis formulation, experimental design, and validation. (v) Interpret experimental results and correlate them with underlying scientific and engineering principles. (vi) Communicate experimental findings effectively and adhere to ethical practices in experimen- tation and technical reporting. BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 2
learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: CO1: Understand and apply fundamental measurement concepts such as accuracy, precision, resolution, calibration, and uncertainty. CO2: Use appropriate measuring instruments/sensors to solve a problem and acquire experimental data across different disciplines. CO3: Analyze experimental data using graphical and statistical methods, including error estimation and uncertainty propagation. CO4: Formulating hypotheses and their validation through design and conducting experiments. CO5: Interpret experimental observations using fundamental scientific and engineering principles. CO6: Document and communicate experimental findings effectively through structured reports and presentations.

title: Renewable energy
description_handout: Introduction of renewable energy, advantages, potential, status of development, broad details of different renewable energy systems such as solar, wind, biomass, microhydel, geothermal etc; Renewable energy development policy, Renewable energy industries, international co-operation, HRD and career growth opportunities, consultancy areas and future thrust areas in renewable energy development. Scope: State-of-the-art treatment of different sources of renewable energy, their utility, and techno- economic assessment. Course Objective: 1. Evaluation: Evaluate: To determine the power output and evaluate the performance of simple thermodynamic cycles for power generation technologies in terms of thermal efficiency. 2. Evaluation: Evaluate: To be able to analyze and evaluate the performance of coal-based or gas-based power generation technologies. 3. Evaluation: Estimate: To be able to estimate the performance of wind, geothermal, ocean, and solar power technologies with/without energy storage for a given geographical site, in terms of their efficiency or potential. 4. Analysis: Analyze: To be able to analyze bio-chemical and thermo-chemical conversion technologies of biomass and organic waste in terms of their potential and conversion efficiency. 5. Analysis: Analyze: To analyze and compare the performance of fuel cell technologies in terms of operating conditions, efficiency and applications. Text book: 1. Kothari, D.P., Singal, K. C., Ranjan, Rakesh, Renewable Energy Sources and Emerging Technologies, Third Edition, PHI Learning Private Ltd., New Delhi, 2022. ISBN: 978-81- 203-4470-9 Reference books: 1. G. N. Tiwari, and M. K. title: SURVEYING
description_handout: The compulsory disciplinary course has been designed to introduce the basic concepts of geodesy (surveying) for Civil Engineering students. Different basic and advanced methods of measurements and traversing have been included so that the student will be able to handle a given project independently, irrespective of whether it is a road or any other infrastructure project. Important issues like curve setting, calculation of areas and volumes, which form part and parcel of any field civil engineer in his/her day-to-day activity. Hence, in this course, these areas have also been included. Scope & Objective: The course introduces the students to various basic techniques in surveying, viz., chain, compass, theodolite, plane table, tacheometry, traversing, and calculation of areas and volumes, along with fundamentals of a few advanced surveying techniques. Course Learning Outcomes: After successful completion of this course, students will be able to: ▪ Understand and apply the fundamental concepts of surveying, including methods of linear measurements and handling common field equipment such as chains, tapes, and compasses. ▪ Execute and analyze compass traversing, including the computation and correction of bearings, and apply techniques for accurate plotting and area determination. ▪ Perform differential and profile levelling and interpret level books for reduced level determination, accounting for curvature and refraction. ▪ Conduct contouring operations and generate contour maps using field measurements and appropriate plotting techniques. BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 2 ▪ Carry out plane table and tacheometric surveys and apply relevant graphical and mathematical methods for plotting and distance/elevation computations. ▪ Design and set out simple and transition curves for civil infrastructure projects using chain, tape, and theodolite methods. ▪ Compute areas and volumes from cross-sections and contour maps and interpret mass haul diagrams relevant to earthworks. ▪ Demonstrate knowledge of modern surveying technologies, including total stations, photogrammetry, and remote sensing, and their practical applications. ▪ Analyze sources of error in surveying measurements and apply appropriate corrections to enhance the accuracy and reliability of data. ▪ Apply theoretical knowledge in field conditions by conducting various practical exercises such as chain surveying, curve setting, and use of total stations and GIS software. Textbooks: T1. Duggal S.K.; Surveying; Tata McGraw-Hill, New Delhi, Vol I and II, 4th Edition (2013). T2. Moondra, H.S. and Gupta Rajiv, Lab Manual for Civil Engineering, CBS, 2nd edition, (2000). Reference Books: R1. Punmia B.C; Surveying; Laxmi Publishers, Vol I, II and III, (1990). R2. Agor, R; A Text Book of Surveying & Levelling, Khanna Publishers. New Delhi. R3. N N Basak: Surveying & Levelling, McGraw Hill Education (India) Private Limited, New Delhi, 2nd edition, 2014. R4. Venkatramaiah, C; Textbook of Surveying, University Press, Second Edition, 2011. R5. Bhavikatti, S.S; Surveying Theory & Practice, Ik International Publishing House Pvt Ltd, New Delhi, 2013. title: Civil Engineering Materials
description: Civil Engineering Materials 3 2 4 DISCIPLINE ELECTIVE COURSES Track - 1: Environment and sustainable design
description_handout: Different types of cements, chemical composition, properties and tests, coarse and fine aggregate for concrete, tests on aggregates, grading of aggregates and its effect on concrete properties, chemical and mineral admixtures, properties and tests on fresh and hardened concrete; transportation and placing of concrete, non- destructive testing of concrete, durability of concrete, quality control and acceptance criteria of concrete, Factors in the choice of mix proportions, Proportioning of concrete mixes by various methods – BIS method of mix design; Introduction to special concretes. Manufacturing/sources, classification, applications, properties and testing of bricks, blocks, tiles, aggregates, lime, timber, paints, glass, bitumen, cutback, emulsion, modified bitumen, steel, non-ferrous metals, polymeric materials, geo-synthetics, etc. Low cost and waste material in construction. Latest, BIS, IRC & ASTM specifications and guidelines of all above- mentioned material, and construction equipment.
scope_objective: The course deals with properties, characterization, testing, selection and quality control of construction material. For economical, durable and high performance of structure, it is imperative to have knowledge on construction materials and their wider applications. This course provides a basic and enhanced overview of various construction materials presently used in practice.
learning_outcomes: By the end of this course, students will be able to: a) Identify and classify common civil engineering materials such as concrete, steel, wood, aggregates, asphalt, and modern composites. b) Explain the physical, mechanical, and chemical properties of construction materials and how these properties affect material performance and selection. BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 2 c) Perform standard laboratory tests to evaluate the properties and behaviour of civil engineering materials, including tests for strength, and workability. d) Interpret test data and analyse results to assess material suitability for specific applications in civil engineering. e) Understand the influence of material properties on the structural performance, serviceability, and durability of civil infrastructure. f) Compare and evaluate materials based on environmental impact, cost-effectiveness, availability, and sustainability. g) Demonstrate awareness of current trends and innovations in civil engineering materials, including smart materials, green materials, and recycled materials. h) Apply appropriate material selection in the design and construction of civil engineering structures in accordance with relevant codes and standards.

title: Fluid Mechanics
instructor_handout: Dr. Guntu Ravikumar (M W 5 Th 10 at 6104)
description_handout: Fluid Mechanics is an introductory course that covers the fundamental aspects of fluid mechanics, especially the classical and well-established laws. This course emphasizes understanding these governing laws and their widespread engineering applications in fluid related problems by covering the following topics: Concepts and definitions, compressibility of fluids, fluid pressure and measurement, fluid statics, buoyancy, rigid body motion, fluid kinematics, conservation laws: control volume approach, differential analysis of fluid flow, study of flow pattern through orifices and mouthpieces, notches and weirs, analysis of flow through pipes, viscous fluid flow analysis: analysis of flow through pipes, dimensional analysis and similitude. The contents of this course will enable the students to tackle real-life fluid mechanics problems and provide a broad overview of the subject. Moreover, this course will be helpful to students as a prerequisite for further advanced courses in fluid mechanics at undergraduate and graduate levels.
scope_objective: • Introduction to different fluid properties and their engineering applications • Learn about pressure exerted by fluids and pressure measurement techniques • Estimate hydrostatic forces on surfaces • Learn about buoyancy and evaluate stability of submerged and floating bodies • Understand concepts of fluid kinematics, methods of describing fluid flow, types of fluid flow, control mass and control volume, rate of flow, continuity equation, potential and stream functions • Study dynamics of fluid flow, Euler’s equation, Bernoulli’s equation and its applications, Navier Stokes equation, and pipe bend problems • Compute fluid discharge through orifices and mouthpieces, and flow over weirs and notches • Analyze flow of viscous fluids through pipes and plates, and compute head loss due to friction • Compute different types of energy losses and determine hydraulic gradient and total energy line for flow through pipes. Become adept at solving problems pertaining to syphon, flow through pipes in series, parallel and branched pipes, power transmission through pipes, and flow through nozzles • Perceive the concepts of dimensional analysis and similitude
learning_outcomes: On completion of this course, the students will be able to, 1. Demonstrate the difference between solid and fluid, its properties and properties in static and dynamic conditions 2. Estimate pressure exerted by fluids and experiment with pressure measurement devices BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 3. Apply conservation laws applicable to fluids and its applications through fluid kinematics and dynamics 4. Perceive and formulate relationship among the parameters involved in the given fluid phenomenon and apply concepts of similitude in analyzing models and prototypes 5. Estimate the losses in pipelines for both laminar and turbulent conditions and analysis of pipes connected in series and parallel.

title: Hydraulic Engineering
description_handout: This course introduces Civil Engineering students to the core concepts of hydraulic engineering, focusing on the Behaviour of real fluids: boundary layer theory, turbulent flow through conduits; analysis of closed-conduit hydraulic systems including pipes, valves, fittings, and pumps, water hammer in pipes, pipe networks analysis: Hardy cross method; Open channel hydraulics: uniform and non- uniform flow; flow past immersed bodies: drag and lift; Analysis of Impact of jets; Introduction to fluid machinery.
learning_outcomes: (CLOs): Upon the completion of this course, students will be able to perform the following: BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 2 CLO1. Explain the behaviour of real fluids, including boundary layer development and turbulent flow through conduits, and apply these concepts to practical hydraulic engineering problems. CLO2. Analyze closed-conduit hydraulic systems by evaluating head losses, pipe flow characteristics, pumps, valves, fittings, and the effects of water hammer in pressurized pipelines. CLO3. Analyze and solve pipe network problems using the Hardy Cross Method for the design and operation of water distribution systems. CLO4. Analyze uniform and non-uniform flow in open channels using fundamental hydraulic principles and empirical equations for engineering design and performance assessment. CLO5. Evaluate fluid forces on immersed bodies, including drag, lift, and the impact of jets on stationary and moving surfaces, for engineering applications. CLO6. Explain the classification, operating principles, and applications of fluid machinery, particularly hydraulic turbines and pumps, and relate them to hydraulic engineering systems.
