title: DESIGN OF REINFORCED CONCRETE STRUCTURES
description_handout: Design Philosophies: Introduction to working stress design philosophy; Limit State design philosophy, Limit State design of Singly reinforced and doubly reinforced rectangular and flanged section beams; Design of one-way and two-way slabs in flexure; Design of beams and slabs for shear; Design of beams and slabs for bond, anchorage and development length; Design of beams and slabs for serviceability; Limit state design of columns subjected to axial load, and axial load plus uni-axial and bi-axial bending; Design of footings under the columns; Design of simple staircases.
scope_objective: In this course, the students will be introduced to the various design philosophies used in the design of Reinforced Concrete (RC) structures, with a particular focus on the Limit State Design method. The course will provide an in-depth discussion of the concepts of Limit State Design method. Subsequently, the Limit State Design method will be employed to the design of singly and doubly reinforced rectangular- and T-section beams and one-way and two-way slabs, for flexure, shear, anchorage, bond, and serviceability requirement. Additionally, the course will cover the design of columns subjected to axial loads, and axial load plus uniaxial and biaxial moments. Moreover, the course will explore different types of staircases, with a specific emphasis on the design of dog-legged staircases. At the end of this course, students will be able to design the basic structural elements of an RC buildings. 3. Text Book and References TB: S. title: In-situ Testing Methods in Geotechnical Engineering
description: In-situ Testing Methods in Geotechnical Engineering 3 0 3
description_handout: In-situ Testing Methods in Geotechnical Engineering is an introductory course to various in-situ test methods pertaining to geotechnical engineering and analysis of in-situ test results, including drilling and sampling, standard penetration test (SPT), cone-penetration test (CPT), piezocone penetration test (CPTu), vane shear test (VST), non-destructive tests (NDT) using body waves and surface waves - seismic reflection test, seismic refraction test, and spectral analysis of surface waves (SASW) test. Structure and components of geotechnical reports and data presentation techniques using borehole logs will be discussed. The contents of this course will enable students to utilize different in-situ test results for soil property interpretation, direct and indirect applications for the design of geotechnical structures, and liquefaction assessment. This course will be helpful to students when they start working as practicing engineers or for further graduate-level advanced courses in geotechnical engineering. Scope and Objective: Introduction to in-situ testing, drilling, and sampling, advantages and disadvantages of in-situ testing, and scope of using the test results for direct and indirect design of geotechnical structures. • Learn about SPT, test procedure, SPT corrections, and frequently used correlations to estimate different geomaterial properties. • Become familiar with some of the frequently used methods for the design of foundations using SPT data. • Learn about CPT, test procedure, and frequently used correlations to estimate different geomaterial properties. • Design of foundations based on CPT results. • Assess liquefaction potential for a site based on SPT and CPT results. • Estimate seismic wave velocities and interpret subsurface profiles based on seismic reflection and refraction tests, and SASW test. • Structure and components of geotechnical reports and data presentation techniques using borehole logs based on exploration findings will be discussed. Course Learning Outcome: • Remember different in-situ testing methods related to geotechnical engineering. BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 2 • Understanding of different widely used in-situ testing procedures and principles pertaining to geotechnical engineering. • Knowledge of appropriate correlation equations available to interpret different geomaterial properties using in-situ test results. • Apply different direct design methods for designing foundations. • Analyze and compare different in-situ test results for tests conducted at the same site and decide suitability of different test methods. • Evaluate the suitability of different test methods based on site details and purpose of testing, select suitable method for foundation design using in-situ test results and assess potential for liquefaction. Textbooks and references: TB1. In-situ Testing Methods in Geotechnical Engineering by Alan Lutennegar RB1. In-situ Testing in Geomechanics: The Main Tests by Fernando Schnaid RB 2. Geotechnical Earthquake Engineering by Steven Kramer RB 3. Manual on Subsurface Investigation (NCHRP W 258) RB 4. Guide to Cone Penetration Testing by P.K. Robertson and K. Cabal RB 5. title: Applications of Artificial Intelligence in Civil Engineering
description: Applications of Artificial Intelligence in Civil Engineering 3 0 3
description_handout: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence and soft computing; Neural networks: Introduction, models, and its application in civil engineering, fuzzy logic and its application in decision making, Clustering; Genetic algorithms; Expert systems; Introduction to machine learning (Support Vector Machine), case studies. Scope and Objective: Artificial Intelligence (AI) may be considered a field of computer science that attempts to build technology to inculcate human cognition in computer systems, but applications are not limited to. A primary goal of AI is to build intelligent entities. This course is structured to give an overview of the area, as well as some important soft computing techniques which are essential to solve the complex problems in terms of the fundamentals. The attributes of human intelligence such as reasoning, planning, learning etc. will be attempted to be understood to incorporate in problemsolving. Course learning outcomes: By the end of the course, the students should have a. Out of various techniques, emphasis will be on Genetic algorithm, Artificial Neural Network, and Fuzzy Systems a. General knowledge of the field of AI b. They should be able to recognize when and how to use AI techniques to solve civil engineering problems. c. The students should also be able to evaluate new techniques they encounter. d. Students will take up a group project/ term paper to study in detail the theoretical details of an intelligent system and implement that during the semester. Text books and references: TB1: Artificial Intelligence A Modern Approach; Stuart J.Russell, Peter Norvig, Third Edition Pearson Education, Inc., India TB2: Neural Networks, Fuzzy logic, and Genetic Algorithms Synthesis and Applications; S. Rajasekaran, G.A. Vijayalakshmi Pai, PHI Learning Pvt. Ltd, Delhi. Method of conduct of the course: The traditional method of teaching by chalk and board has been highly regarded for many educational levels. The chalk-and-board teaching system has been appreciated for creating an opportunity for direct and personal communication between teachers and students to engage with each other face to face. Approaches such as blended learning, collaborative strategies, and experiential learning promote engagement, critical thinking, and lifelong learning. title: Green Buildings and Energy Conservation
description_handout: Climate zones and sun path diagram, thermal comfort, heat flow through building materials, energy efficient building design factors like site planning, plan form and orientation, construction techniques, materials and finishes, natural day lighting and ventilation strategies, thermal performance of building elements, simple techniques to recycle and reuse water, harvest rainwater, green building rating system, case studies of traditional architecture and contemporary buildings, building design using AUTOCAD/ GIS/ AI Scope and Objective: The course introduces green architecture and intends to equip students with technical knowledge of energy- efficient green building. The course covers various aspects of green architecture like climatology, passive solar architecture, water management. The course will also guide students, through projects, to apply concepts and ideas for the design of a green building. Course learning outcomes: By the end of the course, the students should have 1. title: Environmental Impact Assessment
description_handout: Environment and global problems; Framing Environmental issues; effects of infrastructure development on environment; prediction and assessment of environmental impacts of infrastructure projects: technical and procedural aspects, guidelines and legal aspects of environmental protection, impacts on air, water, soil and noise environment, valuation, strategic assessment, mathematical modeling for environmental processes; social impact assessment (SIA), dislocation/disruption impact of Infrastructure projects; Life Cycle Assessments (LCA) and risk analysis methodologies; mitigation of environmental impacts; case studies; environmental management plan (EMP), national and international certification and guidelines including ISO.
scope_objective: The course focuses on understanding environmental issues linked to infrastructure development, emphasizing technical, procedural, and legal aspects of environmental impact assessment (EIA). It covers prediction and mitigation of impacts on air, water, soil, and noise environments, supported by modeling tools. Strategic assessments, LCA, risk analysis, and SIA are addressed alongside valuation and management frameworks. Case studies and EMP formulation are discussed with reference to national and international standards, including ISO, ensuring comprehensive exposure to certification protocols and regulatory compliance.
learning_outcomes: a. Identify and frame environmental issues arising from infrastructure development, including physical and social dimensions. b. Apply procedural and technical approaches for impact prediction, assessment, and valuation using modeling tools and legal guidelines. c. Formulate environmental management plans (EMP) and assess projects in line with national and international frameworks, including ISO.

title: Fundamentals of Systems Engineering
description_handout: Systems Engineering is an interdisciplinary field that focuses on the structured development, integration, and management of complex systems across their entire life cycle—from conceptual design and planning to operation, maintenance, and retirement. In the context of infrastructure, it addresses technical, organizational, and stakeholder-related complexities by employing a holistic, systems-oriented approach. This course introduces students to the fundamentals of systems engineering with a focus on civil and infrastructure systems, preparing them to think critically and act strategically in dynamic, real-world environments.
scope_objective: The course is designed to build a strong foundation in systems engineering methodologies while contextualizing their application to infrastructure planning, development, and management. Students will explore systems architecture, modeling, simulation, optimization, and decision-support frameworks relevant to the life cycle of infrastructure systems. The course also integrates modern tools such as AI, IoT, digital twins, and life-cycle costing techniques to support informed decision-making and innovation. The overarching objective is to develop technically sound, system-aware professionals capable of solving real-world infrastructure problems through interdisciplinary thinking, structured analysis, and evidence-based planning.
learning_outcomes: a. Understand systems engineering principles and their application to infrastructure life-cycle management. b. Apply systems thinking and modeling techniques to analyze complex infrastructure systems. c. Use optimization, simulation, and decision-support tools for infrastructure planning and operations. d. Evaluate infrastructure projects using life-cycle costing and basic investment analysis methods. e. Introduction to Integrating emerging technologies such as AI and IoT into infrastructure systems design and management.

title: Water Resources Planning and Management
scope_objective: The course CE G525 Water Resources Planning and Management aims to equip students with a comprehensive understanding of the engineering, economic, and environmental aspects involved in the sustainable planning and management of water resources. It covers both quantitative and qualitative assessments of water systems, integrating surface and groundwater hydrology, water quality modeling, and watershed management. The course emphasizes decision-making under uncertainty, project analysis, and the application of mathematical modeling and optimization techniques, including linear, non-linear, and multi-objective programming. Through the study of pollution sources, water conservation strategies, and demographic considerations, students gain insights into integrated water resource planning. Modern computational tools such as fuzzy logic and artificial intelligence are introduced alongside real-world case studies and laboratory experiments, enabling students to address complex, multidisciplinary challenges in water resource systems. The course ultimately prepares students to contribute effectively to socially and environmentally responsible water resource development and policy-making.
learning_outcomes: Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to: a. Understand the structure, components, and modeling approaches of water resource systems. b. Apply principles of engineering and economics in water resource planning and project

title: Pavement Material Characterization
description_handout: [as per the Bulletin] This course covers topics related to characterization of pavement materials including soil, aggregates, bitumen,bituminous mixtures and pavement quality concrete (PQC). Soil characterization includes description of characteristics and desirable properties, classification, compaction, strength and modulus of subgrade soil. For aggregates, origin and production, mineralogy, physical properties and aggregate properties for mix design would be discussed. Detailed description of bituminous binder would include origin, production and it application, chemical composition, physical and rheological properties, grading system, modification of bitumen, cutbacks and emulsions. Bituminous mixtures include production, desirable properties, mix design and performance testing. For PQC, materials and selection of mix proportions would be covered along with design example.
scope_objective: The main objective of this course is to understand the different material components typical in pavement and learn about the importance of the properties of these components for effective functioning of the pavement. In this course, we would also look into the guidelines outlined for testing, specifications and characterization of various material used in pavements (both nationally and internationally). A brief about the ongoing worldwide research on various material aspects of pavements will also be covered as a part of different lectures.
learning_outcomes: a. . To characterize pavement materials b. . To perform bituminous mix design c. . To perform mix design of concrete

title: AIRPORT PLANNING & DESIGN
description_handout: The course deals with complete planning and design of airports with greater emphasis on planning not restricted to airports, but air transport at large. The course will also touch base on several other connected aspects of air transportation such as forecasting air transport demand, evolution of aircraft and pavements, air transportation business, sustainability aspects etc.
scope_objective: The scope of the course is to know the various aspects of airport planning and design. This course is expected to provide a broad overview on various topics as mentioned below. ➢ To understand briefly air transport and aviation industry [Module I] ➢ To understand the need to forecast air transport demand [Module II] ➢ To get the overall idea about aircraft and its influence on entire planning [Module III] ➢ To get a comprehensive overview about airport system and master planning [Module IV] ➢ To get an overview about the factors affecting the airport capacity [Module V] ➢ To comprehensively analyze the airside configuration and geometric design [Module VI] ➢ To understand the structural pavement design and airport drainage [Module VII] ➢ To get a quick overview about different visual aids in airport and in airspace [Module VIII] ➢ To acknowledge the importance of maintenance and rehabilitation of pavement [Module IX] ➢ To know the parameters influencing the airport performance including benchmarking [Module X]
learning_outcomes: o Complete comprehensive understanding of airport planning process o Structural pavements, maintenance and failures o Detailed insights into various guidelines and standards

title: Pavement Failure Evaluation and Rehabilitation
description_handout: This course covers topics related to pavement failure, evaluation and rehabilitation such as pavement deterioration, distress and different types of failures, methods of measurement and treatment, use of modern equipment for pavement surface condition measurements, analysis of data, interpretation, Structural deterioration of pavements: causes, effects, methods of treatment, structural evaluation of flexible pavements by rebound deflection method, analysis of data, design of overlay, use of FWD and other methods for evaluation of flexible and rigid pavements and their application, pavement testing under controlled conditions, test track studies, Instrumentation for pavement testing.

title: Rural Road Technology
description_handout: Network planning, accessibility and mobility; road alignment and survey; geometric design: cross sectional elements, sight distance, horizontal and vertical alignments; road materials and use of marginal materials; pavement design, drainage, culverts and small bridges; construction and specifications; quality control in construction; pavement failures; maintenance; preparation of detailed project report (DPR); community participation in planning, design, construction and management.
scope_objective: Rural roads are the key components for the development of rural community. In this regard, the Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY) was launched by the Govt. of India to provide connectivity to unconnected Habitations as part of a poverty reduction strategy. Subsequently, the various strategies have been adopted in planning and construction of rural roads with the aid of technologically advanced construction practices. The scope of the course is to know the various aspects rural roads construction and the various processes associated with the construction. In the recent past, special emphasis is on the use of green technology for road construction in many states. Rural road technology is fast evolving at an urban pace. The course aims to cover various technological advancements that have taken place not only in India, but also on the global stage.
learning_outcomes: a. . To perform the geometric design of rural roads b. . To design the flexible and rigid pavement c. . To prepare the detailed project report

title: DYNAMICS OF STRUCTURES
description_handout: Introduction and Scope of dynamic analysis of structures; origins of vibration theory and experiment; review of earlier concepts: D’Alembert’s principle, equations of motion. Elements of a structural system: springs, dashpot, mass; Springs in parallel and series; methods to formulate equations of motion; Formulation (equation of motion) and solution of undamped and damped free vibration analysis of S.D.O.F system; Formulation (equation of motion) and solution of undamped and damped forced vibration analysis of S.D.O.F system; Forced vibration under harmonic, periodic, impulse, step, ramp, general dynamic forces (time and frequency domain analysis) and response spectrum load, support excited vibration, seismic pickups; Numerical techniques for evaluation of dynamic response of SDOF system; time domain analysis; direct integration techniques; finite difference method (Central Difference method); Newmark beta method; average and linear acceleration method; Development of equation of motion and solution for two degree of freedom systems; Free vibration analysis of MDOF systems; frequencies; mode shapes and response; orthogonality condition of mode shapes; Approximate methods for obtaining natural frequencies and mode shapes; Holzer method; Stodola’s method; Rayleigh’s method; Rayleigh-Ritz method; Inverse iteration method; Vector iteration method; Rayleigh’s Quotient iteration method; Matrix iteration method; Generation of damping matrix for MDOF; dynamic properties; modal damping; classical damping; damped response with Rayleigh and Caughey damping.Mode superposition method; mode acceleration method; modal combination rules using absolute sum, SRSS and CQC method.
scope_objective: Natural phenomena and human activities impose forces of time-dependent variability on various civil engineering structures. This course deals with analysis and design of structures subjected to dynamic loads, which involve consideration of time-dependent forces. Based on this scope, the following objectives have been listed:  To make this course necessary for students who are desirous of joining design offices/ industry related to buildings, industrial plants, bridges, tanks, offshore structure, tall chimneys etc.  To determine the behavior of structures under dynamic loading and design a structure which is resistant to dynamic loading such as seismic, wind, seawave, vehicle induced vibration force etc.
learning_outcomes: a. Development of software for the analysis of framed/skeleton structures. b. Capability development for the use of structural dynamics concept and its applications for framed structural analysis and design under dynamic loading. c. Determine the behavior of structures under dynamic loading and design a structure, which is resistant to dynamic loading such as seismic, wind, seawave, vehicle induced vibration force etc.

title: ADVANCED CONCRETE STRUCTURES
description_handout: The course deals with various aspects of concrete structures with emphasis on design of various elements and exposure to different code provisions. Materials; high strength concrete, flexure analysis and design; shear and diagonal tension; bond and anchorage; serviceability; torsion; columns; joints; indeterminate beams and frames; yield line analysis; strip method for slabs; composite construction; footing and foundations; concrete building system; concrete tall buildings, detailing in concrete structures
scope_objective: The concrete structures are quite common in India for both low-rise and high-rise buildings due to the strong performance in the last many decades even during strong wind & earthquake ground motion. The concrete structures are used in most of the infrastructure applications such as construction of buildings, bridges, roads, airport structures, stadiums, water tanks, chimneys, storage bins, nuclear reactors etc., The codal provisions are continuously changing with changing times due to technological advancements and our improved understanding of the behavioral characteristics of concrete. Though concrete structures are design are not anything new, but certain aspects of design and construction still needs further research and understanding. The beam-column joint is hardly 50 years old and was totally unexplored before 1970s. Today, it was observed that beam-column failure is one of the most important reasons for the failure of RC framed structures. On the other hand, RC structures are only framed form, but different structural configurations evolve over the years to accommodate the tall buildings with safety and economy. The present course aims to highlight the design and construction aspects of wide range of structures, ranging from traditional RC framed structures to tall buildings to certain specialized structures such as chimneys and water tanks. The emphasis will be more on the performance of structure under earthquake loading conditions. The codal provisions will be discussed for the better understanding. ➢ To understand the concrete structures and its applications [Module - I] ➢ To study different structural configurations for the concrete structures [Module-II] ➢ To understand and design few important components of RC framed structures including beam-column joints and other vital structural elements [Module-III] ➢ To understand the concept of shear wall frame structures [Module IV] ➢ To understand the behavioral and design aspects of shell structures and folded plates [Module V] ➢ To understand the ductile behavioral aspects of structures under earthquake [Module VI] ➢ To understand the design and detailing aspects of water tanks and chimneys [Module VII] ➢ To understand the design aspects of RCC poles and pipes [Module VIII] BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 2 ➢ To discuss the case studies of different RC structures and its failures [Module IX] ➢ To discuss the various advancements in concrete structures and the research scope [Module X]
learning_outcomes: o Comprehensive understanding of design aspects of concrete structures o Structural elements and code provisions o RC detailing of critical structural elements o Tall buildings behaviour and structural systems

title: PRESTRESSED CONCRETE STRUCTURES
description_handout: Introduction to basic concepts of prestressing; prestressing systems; analysis of prestress; losses in prestress; deflection; design of anchorage zone, design of prestressed concrete girders.
scope_objective: s The universal use of prestressed concrete as a versatile construction material is well established due to its suitability in multifarious types of structural applications. The application of prestressed concrete is increasing with the development of technology. Prestressing is the application of an initial load on a structure to enable it to counteract the stresses arising from subsequent loads during its service period. In this course, the students will be introduced to prestressed concrete and its applications. The course would cover important topics of prestressed concrete, including the design of structural elements based on the limit state philosophy of design. It would partially fulfill the requirements of practicing structural design engineers. The course integrates science and engineering principles to design prestressed concrete members and structural systems. The application of scientific and engineering knowledge would be demonstrated in solving engineering problems associated with the design of precast prestressed building members. This course would be quite helpful for students who want to join the structural design or construction industry. At the end of the coursework, students will be able to determine the behavior of prestressed concrete structures. 2. Course Learning Outcomes Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to understand the fundamental concepts of prestressing and the different systems used in prestressed concrete construction. They will gain the ability to – ▪ Understand the basic principles of prestressing and identify various prestressing systems including pre-tensioning and post-tensioning methods. BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 2 ▪ Analyze the behaviour of prestressed concrete members under axial loads and bending, including the use of pressure/thrust lines and load balancing concepts. ▪ Calculate different types of prestress losses and understand their causes and effects on structural performance. ▪ Evaluate the flexural and shear strength of prestressed concrete members and design appropriate reinforcements. ▪ Analyze the transfer of prestress in pre-tensioned members and anchorage zone stresses in post- tensioned members. ▪ Design prestressed concrete sections for flexure using limit state concepts and apply methods such as Magnel’s approach. ▪ Compute short- and long-term deflections in prestressed concrete members and assess crack width control under service loads. ▪ Analyze statically indeterminate prestressed concrete structures, including secondary moments and concordant cable profiles. ▪ Understand and design composite structures involving prestressed and in-situ cast concrete under different support conditions. ▪ Apply engineering knowledge and analytical skills to solve real-world structural design problems involving prestressed concrete. 3. title: Advance Structural Analysis
description_handout: [as per the Bulletin] Flexibility Method; stiffness method; beam curved in plan; two dimensional and three dimensional analysis of structures; shear deformations, shear wall analysis; interactive software development for analysis of structures.
scope_objective: Advanced structural analysis techniques and methods provide efficient means and tools for analysis and design of framed structures using matrix approach. Hence learning advance structural analysis will be very useful for structural analyst and designers using computer oriented approach. The basic objective of this course is to acquire the fundamental concepts of matrix methods of structural analysis and their implementation in development of computer programs for computer aided structural analysis of structures. By the end of the course, the students will be familiar with matrix methods of structural analysis using self-developed computer programs wherein both the concepts of flexibility method and stiffness method of structural analysis will be emphasized

title: Finite Element Analysis
description_handout: Fundamentals of the finite element method (FEM); basic formulations of FEM; steps in FEM; 1-D, 2- D and 3-D elements; axi-symmetric elements, isoparametric formulations; programming aspects in FEM; plate bending elements; shell elements; material and geometric nonlinearity; Buckling and Vibration problems, application of FEM to civil engineering problems.
scope_objective: Finite element method is the most powerful numerical method widely used for solving problems in different branches of engineering especially Civil Engineering. This method is usually used to solve complex problems with regard to complexity in material, geometry, boundary, and loading conditions, such as non-homogeneous material, irregular geometry, boundary conditions, and static & dynamic loading conditions. The finite element formulation from the weak form of the governing differential equations is also covered. The course is aimed to enable students to understand the advanced concept of finite element method and its application to Civil Engineering. 3. Text Book R. D. Cook, D. Malkus, M. E. Plesha, and R. title: Environmental Impact Assessment
description_handout: Environment and global problems; Framing Environmental issues; effects of infrastructure development on environment; prediction and assessment of environmental impacts of infrastructure projects: technical and procedural aspects, guidelines and legal aspects of environmental protection, impacts on air, water, soil and noise environment, valuation, strategic assessment, mathematical modeling for environmental processes; social impact assessment (SIA), dislocation/disruption impact of Infrastructure projects; Life Cycle Assessments (LCA) and risk analysis methodologies; mitigation of environmental impacts; case studies; environmental management plan (EMP), national and international certification and guidelines including ISO.
scope_objective: The course focuses on understanding environmental issues linked to infrastructure development, emphasizing technical, procedural, and legal aspects of environmental impact assessment (EIA). It covers prediction and mitigation of impacts on air, water, soil, and noise environments, supported by modeling tools. Strategic assessments, LCA, risk analysis, and SIA are addressed alongside valuation and management frameworks. Case studies and EMP formulation are discussed with reference to national and international standards, including ISO, ensuring comprehensive exposure to certification protocols and regulatory compliance.
learning_outcomes: a. Identify and frame environmental issues arising from infrastructure development, including physical and social dimensions. b. Apply procedural and technical approaches for impact prediction, assessment, and valuation using modeling tools and legal guidelines. c. Formulate environmental management plans (EMP) and assess projects in line with national and international frameworks, including ISO.

title: Chemical Process Calculations
description_handout: Historical overview of Chemical Engineering, Principles of balancing with examples to illustrate differential and integral balances lumped and distributed balances, Material balances in simple systems involving physical changes and chemical reactions, Systems involving recycle, purge and bypass, Properties of substances: single component & multicomponent, single and multiphase systems. Ideal liquid and gaseous mixtures, Energy balance calculations in simple systems, Introduction to Computer aided calculations-steady state material and energy balances for chemical plants
scope_objective: This course provides an introduction to the basic fundamentals of chemical engineering. It deals with calculations, which form the basis of the design of a chemical industrial plant or process. It aims to inculcate conceptual knowledge as well as systematic and sound problem solving skills in the student. The concept of material and energy balances are introduced, explained, and worked with the help of examples from the real world chemical process plants. Fundamentals of this course would be required for other courses like Chemical Process Technology, Chemical Reaction Engineering, Separation Processes and Process Modelling and Simulation.
learning_outcomes: (CLO): CLO1. At the end of this course, the students must be able to apply important definitions and conventions in chemical processes. CLO2. They can solve material and energy balances for single and multiple units with or without chemical reaction and feedback/bypass. 3. title: Fluid Mechanics
description_handout: Fundamental Concepts, Fluid Statics, Integral and Differential Analysis for Fluid Motion, Dimensional Analysis, Internal and External Fluid Flow, Fluid Machinery, Flow through Packed Bed, Agitation, Introduction to Compressible Flow.
scope_objective: This course is an introduction to the field of fluid mechanics. It mainly covers the basic principles of fluid mechanics. It introduces the student to the fundamental and practical aspects of fluid flow operations that a practising chemical engineer encounters regularly. The physical concepts of fluid mechanics and analysis methods, beginning from basic principles, shall be dealt with in this course.
learning_outcomes:  Recognize and define key fluid properties (such as pressure, density, temperature, viscosity, and velocity fields), calculate shear stresses and viscous forces, and apply fundamental fluid laws including the ideal gas law, surface tension, and speed of sound.  Evaluate pressure distributions in hydrostatic fluids and submerged surfaces across various geometries, and predict buoyancy forces on floating bodies.  Apply the Reynolds transport theorem to establish conservation laws and solve problems involving the Conservation of mass and momentum using integral and differential analysis.  Apply Bernoulli and Euler equations to solve incompressible inviscid flow problems, and develop key dimensionless groups using principles like the Buckingham Pi Theorem.  Analyze fully developed laminar and turbulent pipe flows, calculate pipe losses using the Moody chart, and evaluate pressure drops across fittings, valves, and sudden expansions or contractions.  Apply boundary-layer concepts (including calculating thickness and pressure gradients), evaluate Drag on immersed bodies, analyze fluid flow through solid beds, and determine minimum fluidization velocities.  Understand the characteristics and operations of pipes, fittings, and valves, and select and design pumps based on specific process requirements.

title: Engineering Chemistry
description_handout: Introduction to basic principles of various branches of chemistry and their applications in chemical Industries. Organic chemistry (Important functional groups and their reactions, Some important name reactions commonly used in the chemical industry); Physical chemistry (Thermodynamic processes, Thermochemistry, Electrochemistry, Adsorption, Catalysis), Chemical methods of analysis (volumetric analysis: neutralization, redox, complexometric titrations), Instrumental methods of analysis ( IR, UV- vis spectroscopy, Chromatography), Engineering materials (cementing materials, refractories, polymers), Metals and alloys (Iron and steel), Corrosion (types of corrosion and corrosion control methods), Water treatment (Hardness of water, water analysis and water treatment), Fuels and combustion (Classification of fuels, Analysis of coal, Combustion, Calorific value and its determination).
scope_objective: The course aims to introduce various aspects of chemistry as applied to engineering. The course also aims to bridge the theoretical concepts and their practical engineering applications, thus highlighting the role of chemistry in the field of chemical engineering. 3. Text Books: TB: Dr. Suba Ramesh and others, Engineering Chemistry, Wiley India, 2011,1st Ed. 4. Reference Books: R1: P. W. Atkins, Elements of physical chemistry, 8th edition, Oxford University Press R2: T. W. Graham Solomons and Craig B. Fryhle, Organic Chemistry, 9th edition, John Wiley and sons R3: Perry and Green, Perry’s Chemical Engineers’ Handbook, 9th Edition, Section 2, McGraw Hill R4: Dr S. S. Dara and Dr S. S. Umare, A Text book of Engineering Chemistry, S. Chand& Company Ltd,2000 1st Ed. R5: William Kemp , Organic Spectroscopy, Palgrave, 1991,3rd Ed. title: Kinetics & Reactor Design (KRD)
description_handout: Kinetics Reaction rate, order, rate constant; Batch reactors Design + basics; Kinetic constants from batch reactor data; Ideal flow reactors Mass and Energy balances; Isothermal, adiabatic and non-isothermal operation; Catalysts, Catalytic rates, Reaction mechanisms; Internal/External transport in catalysts; Non-catalytic solid-gas reactions; Reactor design for ideal flow reactors; Kinetics of Solid Catalyzed Reactions; Yield and Selectivity; Concept of RTD; Segregation and Maximum Mixedness models.
scope_objective: This course is an introduction to the chemical reaction kinetics, design and performance of various types of chemical reactors for chemically reacting systems, which yield industrially important products. The emphasis in this course will be to understand the fundamentals of kinetics of homogeneous reactions, design and analysis of ideal reactors; and non-ideal flow.
learning_outcomes: By the end of this course the student will be able to,  Develop performance equations for reactors and design the reactors  Apply design principles to decide on reactor for appropriate processes/reactions.  Understand the basics of catalysis and develop equations for catalyst effectivness, design catalytic reactors  Understand how non ideal reactors (reactors in the real world) operate differently from ideal reactors.  Learn how the chemical engineering industry depends on reactors and their design.

title: Chemical Engineering Laboratory -1
description_handout: The course comprises of experiments in three major areas of chemical engineering, i.e., fluid mechanics, heat transfer and mass transfer. The course involves experiments designed to cover the areas related to the theory of 1. Fluid flow: flow through packed and fluidized beds, major and minor losses associated with fluid flow, flow characteristics, continuity principle, boundary layer theory and fluid moving machinery, 2. Heat transfer: conduction, convection, radiation and heat exchange equipments such as heat exchangers (shell and tube, double pipe, plate type, finned tube) and condensers. 3. Mass transfer: Vapor liquid equilibrium (VLE), separation based on volatility, mass transfer equipments such as distillation column, packed bed adsorber, and mass transfer with reaction and other relevant concepts.
scope_objective: The main objective of this course is to familiarize the students on different principles of chemical engineering through hands on experimentation. The experiments are designed to enable students to apply the theoretical background assimilated in the relevant chemical engineering courses to practice in a laboratory environment. Emphasis is laid on employing scientific methodology in practice: each experiment requires planning, data collection, calculations based on chemical engineering principles, critical analysis, discussion and presentation of the observed result. Additionally, the students will also learn the operation of laboratory scale scientific equipment.
learning_outcomes:  Gain fundamental hands on experience working with Chemical Engineering laboratory conditions and equipments.  Learn how to apply important Chemical Engineering theory for calculations and performing experiments.  Learn how to get proper data, how experimental data can be analyzed and how suitable conclusions can be attained.

title: Atomic and Molecular Simulations
description_handout: This course is to equip students with the knowledge of a variety of modern simulation methods at the atomic and molecular levels. The course will deal with several atomic and molecular simulation methods e.g., ab initio methods, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, Monte Carlo (MC) methods, free energy algorithms, coarse-graining, and multiscale methods. The course will provide hands-on training for simulations using GROMACS or LAMMPS or similar and hands-on simulations using any DFT packages such as VASP, Quantum Espresso or similar. The course also introduces concepts and algorithms based on programming languages (e.g., Matlab, C, C++, Molecular Modelling Software, and Visual Software). Case studies and examples of several real-life applications will be presented for all the simulation techniques.
scope_objective: This course aims to give an overall introduction to various types of particle-based simulation techniques in the sub-micro level phenomena with hands-on training. Currently, with the advances in computational tools, more and more industries/researchers are focusing on using computational tools to study material properties for various applications. The course will include computational multi-scale methods, from first principle ab initio calculations to molecular mechanics, offering potential pathways for studying advanced materials for several applications such as molecular electronics, energy storage/generation, separation, and purification, to name a few. After successful completion of the course, the students will be equipped with the theoretical basis and algorithms of several atomic and molecular simulations techniques (DFT, MD, MC) with their typical application areas and will be able to solve real- world problems by choosing the right simulation techniques.
learning_outcomes:  Understand and apply fundamental atomic and molecular simulation techniques, including DFT, MD, MC, and multiscale methods.  Select and apply appropriate simulation approaches to solve real world problems by understanding the phenomena in atomic and molecular scale .  Analyze and evaluate simulation data to extract meaningful physical and chemical insights for advanced materials applications. title: Advanced Transport Phenomena | ATP
description_handout: Viscosity, thermal conductivity and diffusivity, Shell momentum and energy balance, equations of change for isothermal and non-isothermal systems, Concentration distribution in solids and laminar flows, momentum, thermal and concentration boundary layers near walls, origin of turbulence, length scales in turbulent flows, Reynolds (RANS) equations, estimates of Reynolds stress (k-epsilon and k-omega type models), turbulent shear flow near a wall, turbulent flow in pipes and channels, turbulent heat transfer, Introduction to large eddy simulations models, rheology and material functions, non-Newtonian viscosity and generalized Newtonian models, Linear and non-linear visco-elasticity, radiation heat transfer, multi-component systems, Coupled heat and mass transfer, evaporation, boiling and condensation, chemical reactions, Special topics: Flow through porous media, compressible flows, multiphase flow, Transport phenomena in biochemical systems.
scope_objective: Transport phenomena is one of the basic subjects of chemical engineering and includes study of fluid dynamics, heat and mass transfer. The governing equations for the aforementioned transport processes are analogous in nature as the underlying molecular mechanisms are very closely related. The objective of this course is to cover advance topics in this area like the transport of momentum, heat and mass in turbulent flow, creeping flows, flow through porous media, flow over flat plates and curved surfaces, interphase transport, etc. A balanced overview and fundamental equations for transport processes would be provided along with illustrations regarding solving relevant problems. Further, some special cases which are frequently encountered would also be covered. 3. Text Book (TB | T): T1 Bird, R. title: COMPUTATIONAL FLUID DYNAMICS
description_handout: Philosophy of Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD); governing equations of fluid dynamics; mathematical behaviour of partial differential equations and their impact on CFD; finite volume and finite difference discretization, the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations. Iterative methods, simulation procedures for sample chemical engineering problems using FLUENT.
scope_objective: This course aims to apply numerical methods and transport phenomena to understand and use CFD as a scientific tool. The course is research-oriented. A student is expected to do an extensive guided reading of CFD applications and practice with building CFD models using ANSYS and COMSOL. The students will review and present research papers using CFD as investigative tools in class.
learning_outcomes: By the end of this course, students will be able to: 1. Explain the philosophy, scope, and applications of Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) in research and engineering design contexts. 2. Derive and interpret the governing equations of fluid dynamics and explain their physical significance in various flow conditions. 3. Classify and analyze partial differential equations relevant to CFD and evaluate their physical and computational implications. 4. Apply finite difference and finite volume methods for the discretization of governing equations and assess stability, accuracy, and convergence of numerical schemes. 5. Demonstrate the concepts of grid generation, transformation, and meshing techniques for CFD simulations. 6. Implement various CFD numerical techniques (e.g., Lax-Wendroff, MacCormack, ADI, Pressure Correction) for solving fluid flow problems. 7. Simulate incompressible Couette flow and other benchmark problems using appropriate implicit methods and pressure correction algorithms. 8. Use commercial CFD software (e.g., ANSYS Fluent, COMSOL) to model and analyze different types of fluid flow, heat transfer, species transport, combustion, multiphase flows, and moving mesh problems. 9. Critically review and present research literature applying CFD to chemical engineering and related fields. 10. title: Chemical Process Optimization
description_handout: Introduction to Process Modelling and simulation, Fundamentals of analytical optimization. Survey of one dimensional line-search methods, and multidimensional unconstrained and constrained numerical optimization algorithms. Applications of linear programming, nonlinear programming, mixed integer linear/ nonlinear programming, and parameter estimation in chemical engineering. Feasible-path and infeasible path techniques for chemical process flowsheet optimization, Evolutionary computation in Chemical Engineering.
scope_objective: The chemical industry has undergone significant changes during the past 25 years due to the increased cost of energy, increasingly stringent environmental regulations, and global competition in product pricing and quality. One of the most important engineering tools for addressing these issues is optimization. Optimization as the name suggests, deals with finding the optimum design parameters for maximizing the profit or minimizing the total investment on a process plant. The criteria for analysis of the economic objective function involve fulfilling a process criteria restrictions, conditions, design equations, and respecting the limits of the variables. Most problems in chemical engineering processes have many solutions, in some cases becoming endless. The optimization is related to the selection of an option that is best in a variety of efficient options but being the only one that comes closest to an economic optimum performance and operation. This course, as a subject, deals with the concepts of modeling & simulation, various methods of optimization, objective functions, constraints, theoretical & computational basis for optimization techniques, various chemical engineering examples, etc. The objective of the course is to apply the optimization techniques in chemical engineering processes for reducing the operating cost and maximizing the profit. After completing this course the students will be able to apply the principle of optimization in solving engineering problems and understand the scope of optimization in solving Chemical Engineering problems. 3. description_handout: Origin of quantum theory-black body radiation, line spectra, photoelectric effect; wave particle duality; wave equation: normal modes, superposition; postulates of quantum mechanics, time dependence, Hermitian operators, commutator; Schrödinger equation, operators, observables, solution for particle in a box, normalization, variance, momentum; harmonic oscillator, vibrational spectroscopy; rigid rotor, angular momentum, rotational spectroscopy; Hydrogen atom- orbitals, effect of magnetic field; Variation method, variation theorem, secular determinants; Many electron atoms and molecules; Born Oppenheimer approximation, VB Theory, H2 in VB, Coulomb, ex-change, overlap integrals states of H2; antisymmetric wavefunctions two electron systems, Slater determinants, HF method; SCF method; term symbols and spectra, configuration, state, Hund’s rules, atomic spectra, spin orbit interaction; basic MO theory, homonuclear diatomics-N2, O2, SCF- LCAO-MO, molecular term symbols; HMO theory-π electron approximation, conjugated, cyclic systems.
scope_objective: This is the second of the four Physical Chemistry courses designed for the integrated M.Sc. Chemistry Programme. The course introduces quantum mechanics and application of quantum mechanics to electronic structure of atoms/molecules, chemical bonding, and spectroscopy. At the end of the course the student will be able to understand fundamentals of quantum chemistry and can apply quantum mechanics to electronic structure calculation of many electrons atoms and into molecular spectroscopy.
learning_outcomes: a) Demonstrate the need of quantum mechanics to explain atomic and molecular phenomenon. b) Apply concepts of quantum mechanics to simple and exactly solvable physical systems. c) Explain bonding theories and their application to simple molecular systems. d) Illustrate various approximation methods using quantum mechanics. e) Formulate SCF methods for many electrons system which is the basic of any electronic structure calculation for geometry optimization and energy calculation. f) Application of quantum mechanics into molecular spectroscopy.

description_handout: Structure of molecules: VSEPR model; ionic crystal structure, structure of complex solids; concepts of inorganic chemistry: electronegativity, acid-base chemistry, chemistry of aqueous and non aqueous solvents; descriptive chemistry of some elements: periodicity, chemistry of transition metals, halogens and noble gases; inorganic chains, rings, cages and clusters.
scope_objective: The course is designed in consideration to growing the basic level knowledge and understanding in inorganic chemistry. It includes electronegativity, detailed study of acid-base chemistry, non-aqueous solution chemistry, concept of redox chemistry, shape and structure of inorganic covalent molecules using VSEPR model and bonding of ionic compounds in solid state. It includes the chemistry of halogen and noble gases and main group elements. There will have thorough discussion of chemistry of macromolecules containing inorganic chains, rings and cages.This course will attempt to provide the students with sufficient basic knowledge of the structure and reactivity of inorganic systems to ensure a more comprehensive understanding. By the end of semester, you will be able to learn – ➢ Different scales to define electronegativity; rationalization of unusual reactivity ➢ Shape and structure of different covalent molecules and ionic compounds ➢ Measures of acid-base strength in gas and solution phase; Relation between hardness and softness, Symbiosis ➢ Chemistry of protonic and aprotic solvents; Redox stability; Diagrammatic presentation of potential data ➢ Use (or not) of d orbitals by nonmetals; Reactivity and d orbital participation ➢ Positively charged halogens; Pseudohalogens ➢ Numerous examples in nature of inorganic chains, rings and cages – their structures and chemistry 3. title: Chemical Experimentation I
description: Chemical Experimentation I 3 PHY F212 Electromagnetic Theory I 3
description_handout: The chemical experimentation course is based on laboratory experiments in organic chemistry, and the course is available for second-year M.Sc. Chemistry students.
scope_objective: The course’s main objective is to provide students with a firsthand experience of basic techniques used in an organic chemistry laboratory. Broadly, the experiments include qualitative organic analysis, detection of known and unknown functional groups, chemical separation of a mixture of two compounds, examples of single-step and two-step organic syntheses, extraction of organic compounds from natural sources or from drugs, chromatographic separation of the pure compound from a mixture obtained in a multistep reaction, etc. 3. Textbooks: Vogel's Textbook of Practical Organic Chemistry, 5th Ed.; Lab manual will be provided 4. Reference Books: Reference sources for each experiment will be specified as necessary. 5. Course Plan: The students will perform several experiments in qualitative, synthetic organic chemistry, including single- step and multi-step synthesis, extraction of natural products, and training in chromatographic separation, with an emphasis on individual planning and execution of the experiments. The students will be divided into two sections (I & II), and each section will conduct a set of experiments (Lab I or Lab-II experiments) in the first half semester, and thereafter, interchanging of the students will proceed during the second half of the semester. Selected 20 experiments will be discussed and performed in the class. title: Organic Chemistry-III
description_handout: Applications of important reagents and reactions in organic synthesis and disconnection or synthon approach will be emphasized in this course. Common organic reagents, Organometallic reagents, Transition metal catalyzed reactions, basic principles of disconnection, order of events, chemioselectivity, regioselectivity etc. introduction to reterosynthetic analysis using one group C–X and C–C disconnections, two group C–X and C–C disconnections, ring synthesis (saturated heterocycles), synthesis of heterocyclic compounds and complex molecules.
scope_objective: • understand use of synthetic reagents. • learn retrosynthesis of organic molecules. • design the synthesis of organic compounds using appropriate reagents.
learning_outcomes: At the end of the course, the student should be able to • Apply common reagents in particular oxidizing and reducing reagents in organic synthesis • Understand how organometallic reagents such as organoboranes, organosilanes, organotins, organoaluminums, Grignard and Gilman-type reagents are used to form C–C or C–heteroatom bonds and transform functional groups. • Design the synthesis of organic compounds using appropriate reagents.

title: Physical Chemistry IV
description_handout: Weak forces; surface chemistry: interphase region, thermodynamics, surface films on liquids, adsorption of gases on solids, colloids, micelles, and reverse micellar structures; transport processes: kinetics, thermal conductivity, viscosity, diffusion, sedimentation; electrical conductivity in metals and in solutions; reaction kinetics, measurement of rates; integrated rate laws; rate laws and equilibrium constants for elementary reactions; reaction mechanisms; temperature dependence of rate constants; rate constants and equilibrium constants; rate law in non-ideal systems; uni, bi and tri molecular reactions, chain reactions, free-radical polymerizations; fast reactions; reactions in solutions; heterogeneous and enzyme catalysis; introduction to statistical mechanics; theories of reaction rates; molecular reaction dynamics.
scope_objective: This is the last one of the four Physical Chemistry courses named for M.Sc. (Hons.) Chemistry Programme. The course mainly covers chemical changes in terms of chemical kinetics, surface and interfacial phenomena, and the associated theories. The objective is to understand the chemical changes and also to be able to connect these changes to structure and equilibrium properties learnt in the previous courses. 3. Text Book: T1: Peter Atkins and Julio de Paula, Atkins’ Physical Chemistry, 10th Ed.(South Asia Edition), Oxford University Press, Oxford, 2014. Reference Book : R1. Levine Ira N., Physical Chemistry, 6th ed., Tata McGraw-Hill, New Delhi, 2011.

title: Instrumental Methods of Analysis
description_handout: Principles and practice of modern instrumental methods of chemical analysis. Emphasis on spectroscopic techniques such as UV Visible, infrared, NMR (1H, 13C and other elements, NOE, correlation spectroscopies), ESR, atomic absorption and emission, photoelectron, Mössbauer, and fluorescence. Other topics will include mass spectrometry, separation techniques, light scattering, electroanalytical methods, thermal analysis, and diffraction methods. Scope and Objective of the Course: Chemists extensively use modern sophisticated electronic instruments in various areas such as chemical analysis, structure determination, identification of reaction pathways and rates etc. This course aims to introduce the basic theory and experimental details of such chemical instrumentation. Some of the popular absorption spectroscopic techniques such as UV-visible, IR, NMR, mass spectrometry etc. will be discussed in detail. Text Books: T1. Kemp W., 'Organic Spectroscopy', 3rd ed., Palgrave, New York (1991). Reference Books: R1. Willard H. H., Merritt Jr. L. L., Dean J. A., Settle F. A. S., “Instrumental Methods of Analysis”, 7th Ed., Wadsworth, 2009, Cengage Learning India Pvt. Ltd. Fifth Indian reprint by CBS Publishers & Distributors Pvt. Ltd. R2. Silverstein R. M., and Webster F. X., “Spectrometric Identification of Organic Compounds”, 6th ed., John Wiley & Sons, New York (1998). R3. Skoog D. A., Holler F. J., and Crouch S. R., “Principles of Instrumental Analysis”, 6th ed., Thomson Brooks/Cole, Cengage Learning, New Delhi (2007). Course Plan: A. title: Introductory Computational Chemistry Laboratory
description_handout: In this course the major focus is on practical computation of electronic structure of atoms and molecules using open source and proprietary software; specific computational experiments will be in the areas of potential energy surfaces, geometry optimization, molecular geometry from symmetry and trigonometric relations without visualization software, molecular orbitals and bonding patterns, Hartree-Fock calculations, correlation energy and size-consistency, DFT based calculations, computing excited states using CIS, EOM-CCSD jobs for computing energies of excited, ionized and electron-attached states; methods to estimate activation energy, solvent effects etc.; molecular dynamics simulation, molecular mechanics will also be explored; the actual experiments may vary and can have more specific learning outcomes so as to enhance the course with the latest developments in electronic structure theories of chemistry.
scope_objective: This is an elective laboratory course to gain introductory exposure to practical computational chemistry with major focus on computation of electronic structure of atoms and molecules. Other branches of computational chemistry such as molecular dynamics simulation, molecular mechanics will also be explored briefly.
learning_outcomes: • CLO1: Defining the computational problem and identifying the computational method to study the same • CLO2: Preparing the input files and setting up the computational jobs • CLO3: Analyzing the output file and the generated data and interpreting to understand the phenomena

title: Photophysical Chemistry
description_handout: Absorption of the electromagnetic radiation; photophysical processes such as fluorescence, phosphorescence, non-radiative transitions, and delayed luminescence, excimer and exciplex formation; triplet state: radiative and non-radiative transitions; energy transfer, fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET), quenching of fluorescence; fluorescence decay; protein and DNA fluorescence; time-resolved emission spectra (TRES); time-dependent anisotropy decays; application of photophysics for the characterization of biological and bio-mimicking systems. In addition to the theory, through simple experiments, laboratory training will be imparted.
scope_objective: The main objective of this course is to introduce the students to basic concept of physical processes induced by absorption of light, pathways for loss of electronic excitation such as fluorescence, quenching, and energy transfer.
learning_outcomes: Key concepts of photophysical processes, analysis of Jablonski diagrams and excited state dynamics Interpretation and applications of spectroscopic techniques Calculation of photophysical parameters

title: Chemistry of Materials
description_handout: Solid state structure : unit cells, metallic crystal structures, polymorphism and allotropy, crystallographic direction and planes, closed packed crystal structures, polycrystalline materials, anisotropy; meso and micro porous materials: zeolites, composites, synthesis, characterization (XRD, SEM, TEM, AFM, FTIR, NMR, TGA, and DTA) and applications; ceramics and glass materials: crystalline and non-crystalline nature, glass- ceramics, processing; polymers: synthesis, structure, properties, inorganic polymers; mechanical properties: stress and strain, elastic and tensile properties, hardness, phase transformations, microstructure, alteration of mechanical properties; magnetic properties: atomic magnetism in solids, the exchange interaction, classification of magnetic materials, diamagnetism, pauli paramagnetism, ferromagnetism, antiferromagnetism, ferrimagnetism, superparamagnetism, ferromagnetic domains, hysteresis loop, hard and soft ferrites, applications; electrical properties: conductivity, band theory, types of semiconductors, time dependence of conductivity, mobility of charge carriers, metal-metal junction, metal–semiconductor junction, n-type and p-type semiconductors; optical properties: refraction, reflection, absorption, transmission, luminescence, photoconductivity, opacity and translucency in insulators, optical fibers; thermal properties: heat capacity, thermal expansion, conductivity, thermal stresses; corrosion: electrochemistry of corrosion of metals, different forms, environmental effects, prevention.
scope_objective: • To provide a comprehensive understanding of crystalline structures, crystal systems, unit cells, crystallographic directions and planes, defects, and structure determination techniques. • To develop knowledge of diffusion mechanisms, phase diagrams, phase equilibria, phase transformations, and their influence on microstructural evolution in materials. • To establish the relationship between processing, microstructure, and mechanical properties of metals, including stress–strain behavior, elasticity, tensile properties, hardness, and deformation mechanisms. • To introduce the structure and properties of ceramics, polymers, and other engineering materials, along with concepts of degradation, corrosion, electrical, and magnetic behavior. • To enable students to analyze material structures, interpret phase and microstructural information, and correlate structure–property relationships for engineering material design and applications. 3. Text Books T1. Materials Science and Engineering - An Introduction by William D. Callister, 10th Edition 4. Reference books: R1. Solid State Chemistry by Lesley E. Smart and Elaine A. Moore R2. Materials Science and Engineering by Donald R. Askeland and Pradeep P. Fulay R3. Materials Science for Engineers by James F. Shackelford and Madanapalli K. title: Organic Chemistry and Drug Design
description_handout: An introduction to organic chemistry principles and reactivities vital to drug design, drug development and drug action; the role of molecular size, shape, and charge, and in drug action; proteins and nucleic acids as drug targets; bioisosterism; ADME, QSAR and drug design; applied molecular modeling and combinatorial synthesis; Synthesis of some selected chemotherapeutic agents (antibacterial, antiviral agents, antimalarial, anticancer etc.)
scope_objective: To familiarize the students with basic aspects of drug discovery and more importantly, the applications of organic chemistry in drug design, important drug targets, marketed drugs, synthesis of drugs; the overall objective is to have a reflective teaching and learning environment
learning_outcomes: The student should be able to accomplish the following: CL01. Understanding about structure & function of receptors, enzymes, and nucleic acids CL02. Able to identify and list at least five biological targets for drugs CL03. For the above targets be able to identify ten important available drugs with molecular mechanism CL04. Be able to use computational software/tools to determine given properties of the drug target of his choice CL05. At the end, be able to rationally design and propose simple synthesis of a drug for a disease.

title: Green Chemistry and Catalysis
description_handout: Definition and overview of the twelve principles of Green Chemistry, alternative starting materials; alternative synthesis and reagents; E-factor and the concept of atom economy; the role of catalysis, alternate energy sources (microwave & ultrasound), catalysis by solid acids and bases, bio-catalysis, catalytic reduction, catalytic oxidation, catalytic C–C bond formation, cascade catalysis, enantioselective catalysis, alternative reaction media, renewable raw materials, industrial applications of catalysis.
scope_objective: The objectives of this course are to provide the students with a fundamental understanding of Green Chemistry with an emphasis on the design, prepare and use of chemicals and protocols that have little or no pollution potential or environmental risk. Catalysis being considered as the prime tool to efficiently inculcate the ‘green’ aspects, will be discussed at length including its types, guiding principles and milestone applications. The students will get exposed to the latest development trends to obtain a comprehensive understanding. 3. description: Environmental Chemistry 5 BITS G540 Research Practice 4 EE G501 Environmental Sampling and Analytical Methods 5 Elective 2 5 Elective 1 5 Elective 3 5 20 19 II BIO G525 Environmental Biotechnology and Waste Management 5 BITS G562T Dissertation 16 CHE G552 Advanced Transport Phenomena 5 or Or Elective 4 3 BITS G639 Practice School 20 Elective 5 3 16 16/20
description_handout: Energy-flows and supplies, fossil fuels, nuclear energy, nuclear waste disposal, renewable energy, industrial ecology, green chemistry, ozone chemistry, effect of SOx, NOx as pollutants, reformulated gasoline, water pollution and treatment, organochlorine and organophosphate pesticides, eco-system effects, Toxic chemicals – Effect of dioxins, polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) and species of metals such as lead, mercury, cadmium etc.
scope_objective: This course aims to provide students with a comprehensive understanding of the scientific principles underlying environmental issues and the strategies needed to achieve sustainable development. It introduces the relationship between human activities, industrial growth, energy consumption, and environmental quality, enabling students to understand both the causes of environmental degradation and the methods available to prevent or reduce it.
learning_outcomes: CLO 1: Explain the principles of energy flow and evaluate conventional and renewable energy resources, including fossil fuels, nuclear energy, and their environmental impacts. CLO 2: Analyze the concepts of industrial ecology and green chemistry for sustainable resource utilization and pollution prevention. CLO 3: Describe ozone chemistry and assess the environmental and health effects of air pollutants such as SOₓ, NOₓ, and reformulated gasoline. CLO 4: Evaluate the sources, effects, and treatment methods of water pollution for effective water quality management. CLO 5: Compare the characteristics, environmental fate, and ecological impacts of organochlorine and organophosphate pesticides. CLO 6: Assess the toxicity and environmental impacts of hazardous chemicals, including dioxins, polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), and heavy metals such as lead, mercury, and cadmium, and recommend appropriate pollution control measures.

title: Advanced Organic Chemistry
description_handout: The latest development in the area of organic chemistry will be taught in this course.
scope_objective: The course aims to cover topics in advanced areas of organic chemistry. The focus will be on the application of structure and theory to the study of organic reactions: nucleophilic aromatic substitution, organometallic reagents in organic synthesis, reaction dynamics, isotope effects, and molecular orbital theory applied to pericyclic and photochemical reactions; reactive intermediates including carbenes, carbanions, and benzyne; and asymmetric synthesis and multistep synthesis using the disconnection approach. Starting with fundamental principles and their application, the ultimate purpose of this course will be to understand the recent developments in organic chemistry. 3. title: Computational Thinking & Programming
description_handout: Basic model of computation, input, processing, output, and storage; problem decomposition, abstraction, and representation of solutions using flowcharts and pseudocode. Algorithmic thinking, formulation of algorithms, tracing and verification of correctness, and comparison of efficiency at a conceptual level. Programming fundamentals, expressions, variables, primitive and composite data types, type conversion, and operator precedence; conditional statements and structured decision making; bounded and unbounded iteration. Modular program design, functions, parameter passing, scope, and structured program development. Recursion, recursive problem solving, base and recursive cases, call stack behaviour, and comparison with iterative approaches. Data structures, arrays, strings, and structured data representations; pointers, dynamic memory allocation, and memory management. File handling, basic input/output operations and sequential data processing. AI-assisted programming, responsible use of AI tools for code generation, including prompt formulation, critical evaluation, debugging, and verification of generated code. Laboratory: Algorithm design and tracing; implementation of programs involving conditionals, iteration, functions, recursion, arrays, strings, structured data, pointers, and dynamic memory; file handling; and integrated problem-solving exercises with critical evaluation of AI-assisted code. 1. Scope and Objective: This course establishes computational problem solving as a discipline before it establishes programming as a skill. Students first learn to decompose a problem, abstract away detail, express a solution as an algorithm, and reason about its correctness and cost. They then learn to realise those solutions as working programs, progressing from control structures and modular design to recursion, structured data, pointers, and explicit memory management. The course is anchored in C so that students build an accurate mental model of storage, addressing, and program execution, which is the model assumed by subsequent courses in data structures, operating systems, computer architecture, and networks. This subject aims to achieve the following goals: ● To develop the ability to decompose problems, abstract essential detail, and express solutions as algorithms independent of any programming language. ● To build fluency in structured programming, covering data types, expressions, control constructs, and modular function design. ● To establish an accurate mental model of program execution and memory through recursion, pointers, and dynamic memory management. ● To develop competence in representing and processing structured and linked data, and in persisting data through file operations. ● To build the judgement required to evaluate, test, and verify AI-generated code, and to use AI programming tools responsibly and with due attribution. 2. Course Learning Outcomes: Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to: CLO1: Express computational problems using abstraction, algorithmic thinking, and structured representations including flowcharts and pseudocode. CLO2: Implement programs using fundamental constructs including variables, data types, conditionals, iteration, and modular function design. CLO3: Apply recursion and dynamic memory management to solve problems involving structured and linked data representations. CLO4: Implement file handling operations for sequential data processing and structured input/output. 3. Textbooks and References: T1. Jeri R. Hanly and Elliot B. Koffman, Problem Solving and Program Design in C, 8th Edition, Pearson, 2015. T2. Brian W. Kernighan and Dennis M. Ritchie, The C Programming Language, 2nd Edition, Prentice Hall, 1988. R1. Stephen G. Kochan, Programming in C, 4th Edition, Addison-Wesley Professional, 2014. R2. Tom Taulli, AI-Assisted Programming: Better Planning, Coding, Testing, and Deployment, O’Reilly Media, 2024. R3. Peter J. Denning and Matti Tedre, Computational Thinking, MIT Press Essential Knowledge Series, 2019. R4. Behrouz A. Forouzan and Richard F. Gilberg, Computer Science: A Structured Programming Approach Using C, 3rd Edition, Cengage Learning, 2007. R5. B. S. Gottfried and Jitender Chhabra, Programming with C, Schaum’s Outlines Series, 3rd Edition, McGraw Hill Education, 2017. R6. description_handout: Object orientation concepts, theories and principles; fundamental concepts of the object model: classes, objects, methods and messages, encapsulation and inheritance, interface and implementation, reuse and extension of classes, inheritance and polymorphism; overloading and overriding; static and dynamic binding; multithreaded programming; event handling and exception handling; process of object oriented requirements specification, analysis and design; notations for object-oriented analysis and design; case studies and applications using some object oriented programming languages. Object Oriented Design Patterns: Behavioural, Structural and Creational.
scope_objective: a) Gives an in-depth understanding of object-oriented programming using the java programming language, object- oriented analysis and design, and design patterns. b) In the classroom, the course will be taught with live demonstrations, running and debugging several examples on tools like Eclipse. c) The latter part of the course focuses on designing object-oriented software.
learning_outcomes: (CLOs) On successful completion of this course, students will be able to: CLO1. Explain the principles of object-oriented programming and apply core concepts such as abstraction, encapsulation, inheritance, and polymorphism in software development. CLO2. Design, implement, test, and debug medium-sized Java programs using classes, objects, interfaces, collections, generics, exception handling, file I/O, and multithreading. CLO3. Analyse object-oriented software requirements and represent software designs using appropriate UML diagrams and object-oriented design principles. CLO4. Apply commonly used object-oriented design patterns to develop software that is modular, reusable, extensible, and maintainable. CLO5. Evaluate alternative object-oriented design and implementation choices based on software quality attributes such as maintainability, flexibility, and reusability. title: Discrete Structures for Computer Science
description_handout: This course aims in providing mathematical foundations for many other computer science courses including data structures and algorithms, automata, compiler theory, databases, operating system etc. This course encompasses topics including sets & operation on sets; relations & equivalence relations; number theory; weak & strong form of mathematical induction; principle of inclusion & exclusion, pigeonhole principle; recurrence relations; digraphs & graphs, graph isomorphism & sub-graphs, spanning trees, Euler & Hamiltonian graphs, planar graphs, chromatic numbers & graph coloring; groups.
