title: Instructor-in-Charge
description_handout: The course covers features of programming languages and introduces the main programming paradigms. It covers, in detail, the semantics of the features of programming languages – Control Abstraction, Data Types, and Data Abstraction, Scope and Parameter passing, inheritance, polymorphism and Concurrency related features. It covers various aspects of runtime environments like global and local data, code, function call stacks, dynamically allocated data, runtime features for exceptions and threads. Different programming paradigms, namely imperative, functional, object oriented and logic programming will be discussed in detail. Students will be introduced to the significance of a construct and how different languages implement that. The Lambda calculus will follow an introduction to functional programming languages. Formal elements of logic programming and programming tasks that explore the logic paradigm will be discussed.
scope_objective: • Develop familiarity with the different paradigms of languages (imperative, functional, object oriented and logic) in programming and understanding the features of programming languages like abstraction, data types, etc. • Understand the aspects of run-time environments like global and local data, function call stacks, and static and dynamic allocation of data. • Introduction to the syntax and semantics of common functional programming languages. • Students will be encouraged to learn the design aspects of languages belonging to different paradigms rather than learning a new language. • Understand the basis of logic programming and basic elements of prolog. • Understand synchronization features in concurrent programming. 3. Textbooks: TB1. Programming Languages: Concepts and Constructs, Ravi Sethi, 2nd Edition, Addison Wesley, 1996. References: Ref1. Concepts of Programming Languages, Robert W. Sebesta, 10th Edition, Pearson Publishers, 2012. Ref2. An Introduction to Functional Programming Through Lambda Calculus, Greg Michaelson, Dover Publication, New York, 2011. Ref3. Types and Programming Languages, Benjamin C. Pierce, The MIT Press, 2002.

title: Reinforcement Learning
description_handout: Reinforcement Learning (RL) is based on the idea where we learn by interacting with our environment. It is a collection of machine learning techniques where agent(s) learn how to behave in an environment by performing actions and assessing the results. RL approach is building programs that learn how to predict and act in stochastic environment, based on experience. This course will provide an overview to students on some of the fundamental ideas on which modern RL is built including Markov decision processes, Mult-armed bandits value functions, Monte Carlo estimation, dynamic programming, TD methods, approximation methods, Actor-Critic methods, etc. This course will help students to understand and apply RL in several systems including video distribution systems, game development, IOT devices, robotics, clinical decision making, industrial process control, finance portfolio balancing, etc.
scope_objective: This course aims to achieve the following goals: • To provide students with the knowledge to structure a reinforcement learning problem. • To introduce students to learn and apply basic RL algorithms for simple sequential decision-making problems in uncertain conditions • To introduce students research and development work in reinforcement learning by interpreting state-of-the-art RL research and communicating their results. • To provide knowledge to students to build a RL system that knows how to make automated decisions. • To give students opportunities to understand the space of RL algorithms including Temporal Difference Learning, Monte Carlo, Q-Learning, approximation solution methods, A2C, A3C, etc. 3. Text Books: 1. Sutton, Richard S., and Andrew G. Barto. Reinforcement learning: An introduction. Second Edition, MIT press, 2018. 4. Reference Books: 1. Wiering, Marco A., and Martijn Van Otterlo. "Reinforcement learning." Adaptation, learning, and optimization 12.3 (2012). BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 2 5. scope_objective: s: This course develops a comprehensive understanding of computer architecture and organization, from quantifying processor performance to designing a working processor and its supporting memory system. It begins with performance measurement and comparison using key metrics, benchmarking tools, and Amdahl's law. Building on this, it covers the MIPS architecture and instruction set. The course then examines the design of single-cycle and multi-cycle processor. It further explores pipelined processor design, the handling of structural, data, and control hazards through forwarding, stalling, reordering, and branch prediction techniques. The memory hierarchy is studied to exploit locality of reference, covering memory technologies, cache mapping functions, cache controller design, cache performance metrics, and multi-level caches. Finally, the course introduces advanced techniques for increasing instruction-level parallelism, including multiple issue, loop unrolling, speculation, and dynamic scheduling. TEXT BOOKS (T1) Patterson, David A & J L Hennenssy, Computer Organisation & Design, Elsevier, 6th Ed., 2021. (T2) Samir Palnitkar, Verilog HDL: A Guide to Digital Design and Synthesis, Pearson Education Asia, 2nd Ed. 2006. REFERENCE BOOK (R1) J.L. Hennessy & D.A. Patterson, Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach, Morgan Kauffmann, 6th Ed, 2019. description_handout: Finite automata and regular languages, equivalence, closure properties, context free languages and push down automata – equivalence, closures properties, concepts in parsing; Turing machines; computability :decidability and semi- decidability, recursive and mu-recursive functions, Church-Turing hypothesis, undecidable problems – the halting problem, reductions between languages, complexity classes – P, NP, and NP-completeness 2. Objective To provide a theoretical foundation for the process of computation and to impart an understanding of the notions of automata, formal languages, computability and complexity classes. 3. Scope This course covers basic concepts of formal models of computation and computability. It introduces a hierarchy of machines and languages to capture classes of computable sets. It concludes with a generic notion of computability, and complexity classes of computable functions. 4. Textbook 1. title: Data Mining
description_handout: Introduction to Data Mining, fundamental concepts; motivation and applications; role of data warehousing in data mining; challenges and issues in data mining; Knowledge Discovery in Databases (KDD); role of data mining in KDD; algorithms for data mining; tasks like decision-tree construction, finding association rules, sequencing, classification, and clustering; applications of neural networks and machine learning for tasks of classification and clustering. 2. Objective and Scope The course explores the concepts and techniques of data mining, a promising and flourishing frontier in database systems. Data Mining is automated extraction of patterns representing knowledge implicitly stored in large databases, data warehouses, and other massive information repositories. It is a decision support tool that addresses unique decision support problems that cannot be solved by other data analysis tools such as Online Analytical Processing (OLAP). title: Natural Language Processing
scope_objective: s The intent of the course is to present a broad undergraduate/post-graduate level introduction to Natural Language Processing (NLP, a.k.a. computational linguistics), the study of computing systems that can process, understand, or communicate in human language. title: Information Retrieval
description_handout: This course studies the theory, design, and implementation of text-based information systems. The Information Retrieval core components of the course include statistical characteristics of text, representation of information needs and documents, several important retrieval models (Boolean, vector space, probabilistic, inference net, language modeling, link analysis), clustering algorithms, collaborative filtering, automatic text categorization, and experimental evaluation. The software architecture components include design and implementation of high-capacity text and multimedia retrieval and filtering systems.
scope_objective: The course is designed to provide students with a broad understanding in the design and use of information retrieval techniques. The course also aims at providing a holistic view of information retrieval, which includes several retrieval concepts and techniques such as representation and indexing of data, text mining, websearch: basics and advances, multimedia retrieval, etc. 3. Text Books: T1. C. D. Manning, P. Raghavan and H. Schutze. Introduction to Information Retrieval, Cambridge University Press, 2008. https://nlp.stanford.edu/IR-book/pdf/irbookonlinereading.pdf 4. title: Advanced Computer Networks
description_handout: This is a graduate level course on computer networking and assumes a student has a basic understanding of computer network concepts. This course is a topic-based course which primarily covers topics from Internet Architecture, Internet Congestion Control, Software Defined Networking, Delay Tolerant Networks, Wireless Networking, Quality of Service & Traffic Engineering, Network Performance & Management, Overlay Networks and Network Applications. Several research papers/articles/case studies will be discussed on different aspects of computer networking. This course will introduce students to the basic design principles on which today's Internet is based upon along with the current and emerging research topics in the computer networking area. In addition, this course will cover some recent proposals to improve network performance, functionality and scalability. This course will provide plenty of opportunity for learning by doing through projects, assignments and laboratory exercises.
scope_objective: a. To understand the state of the art in network protocols, network architectures, and networked systems. b. To develop a strong understanding of the core concepts of computer networks. c. To get practice of reading the research papers and critically understanding the research of others. d. To engage ourselves in networking research.
learning_outcomes: CLO1. Analyze the design principles, architectures, protocols, and performance trade-offs of modern computer networks. CLO2. Critically evaluate networking research by identifying key contributions, assumptions, limitations, and alternative design choices. CLO3. Design, implement, and experimentally evaluate solutions to networking problems using appropriate tools and methodologies.

title: Cloud Computing

title: Reconfigurable Computing
description_handout: Overview of Programmable Logics. FPGA fabric architectures. Logic Elements and Switch Networks. Design and Synthesis of Combinational and Sequential Elements. Placement and Routing. Pipelining and other Design Methodologies. Fine-grained and Coarse-Grained FPGAs. Static and Dynamic Reconfiguration. Partitioning. Hardware/Software Partitioning and Partial Evaluation; Systolic Architectures. Users perspective of reconfigurability – implementation and use cases on modern FPGAs.
scope_objective: Reconfigurable (adaptive) computing is a novel yet important research field investigating the capability of hardware to adapt to changing computational requirements such as emerging standards, late design changes, and even to changing processing requirements arising at run-time. Reconfigurable computing thus benefits from a) the programmability of software similar to the Von Neumann computer and b) the speed and efficiency of parallel hardware execution.The purpose of the course reconfigurable computing is to instruct students about the possibilities and rapidly growing interest in adaptive hardware and corresponding design techniques by providing them the necessary knowledge for understanding and designing reconfigurable hardware systems and studying applications benefiting from dynamic hardware reconfiguration. 3. Course outcomes: CO1: Identify the role and advantages of reconfigurable computing compared to other computing paradigms. CO2: Understand FPGA design flow, placement, routing, and configuration aspects in reconfigurable systems. CO3: Understand reconfiguration techniques such as partial and run-time reconfiguration in adaptive hardware systems. CO4: Apply Verilog to model and implement digital designs on FPGA platforms.

title: Agentic AI
description_handout: Introduction to Transformers; advanced architectures beyond Transformers (state space mod- els/Mamba, mixture-of-experts, diffusion-based language models); Parameter Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) Basics (LoRA), advanced PEFT (QLoRA, DoRA, AdaLoRA, ReLoRA, quantization-aware adapters); inference and decoding (top-k, top-p, beam, contrastive; vLLM, KV-cache, PagedAt- tention, AWQ); Model quantization, pruning, distillation, on-device edge optimization; test-time compute (self-consistency, Tree, Graph-of-Thought); post-training & alignment (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) pipeline, PPO, REINFORCE, GRPO; direct alignment: DPO, SimPO, KTO, IPO; rejection sampling, instruction tuning, distillation, tool & function calling, Model Context Protocol (MCP)); Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) Basics, Advanced RAG (IR foundations, HyDE, RAPTOR, CRAG, DSPy); Agent Security (threat models, attack mecha- nisms and defense strategies, red teaming, blue teaming);evolutionary/genetic methods (prompt & agent evolution); multimodal LLMs & agents (Flamingo, BLIP-2, LLaVA; MM-ReAct, ViperGPT).
scope_objective: s of the Course: • Compare and justify LLM/agent architecture choices for long-context, latency, and reasoning. • Implement and evaluate PEFT methods under memory/compute constraints. • Design decoding and test-time compute strategies within fixed latency/cost budgets. • Build and align models/agents using RLHF and direct-alignment methods; diagnose reward hacking and length bias. • Construct robust, programmable RAG agent pipelines with provenance and corrective feed- back. • Analyze and mitigate AI agent security threats, conduct red & blue teaming. • Apply evolutionary search to improve prompts, tools, MCP usage and agent policies. • Fine-tune and evaluate multimodal LLMs/agents; integrate perception with tool-use plans safely. 1
learning_outcomes: At the end of the course, the students will be able to: • Explain and compare advanced LLM/agent architectures (Transformers, SSMs, Mamba, MoE, diffusion etc.). • Apply parameter–efficient fine-tuning (LoRA, QLoRA, DoRA, AdaLoRA, ReLoRA) under memory and compute constraints. • Configure decoding and serving (top-k, top-p, beam; vLLM, KV-cache, PagedAttention) to meet latency and cost targets. • Implement test-time compute strategies (self-consistency, Tree/Graph-of-Thought) and eval- uate accuracy–cost trade-offs. • Build post-training model/agent pipelines (SFT →reward modeling →RLHF or direct align- ment) and mitigate reward hacking/length bias. • Use direct-alignment methods (DPO, SimPO, KTO, IPO) and rejection sampling to improve helpfulness and safety. • Design robust RAG agentic systems (IR foundations, HyDE, RAPTOR, CRAG, DSPy) with provenance and corrective feedback. • Evaluate and defend AI agents against adversarial threats (prompt injection, data poisoning, tool misuse); perform red & blue teaming. • Employ evolutionary methods to optimize prompts, tools, MCP usage and agent policies against defined fitness metrics. • Fine-tune and assess multimodal LLMs/agents (e.g., LLaVA, MM-ReAct) with appropriate safety guardrails.

title: Introduction to Python
description_handout: Introduction to Python, analysis of the problem, design, implementation, and testing, Python pro- gramming fundamentals: program structure, data types, variables, expressions, assignment; Pro- gram control statements: if, else, logical operators, assignment operators, conditional operators, blocks. Program repetition statements: while, for; Data Structures: Lists, tuples, sets and dictio- naries; Using functions: writing functions enhance program modularity; String handling, File han- dling, Exception handling, Object-oriented fundamentals: classes, objects, methods, abstraction, predefined classes; Writing classes: programmer-defined classes, instance data and methods, parameters, overloading, encapsulation.
scope_objective: Python programming is an essential skill that is increasingly relevant in today’s technology- driven world. This course is designed to introduce students to the core concepts of Python programming, guiding them through essential topics such as problem analysis, design, implementation, and testing. Students will gain hands-on experience with Python programming fundamentals, including program structure, data types, variables, and expressions. The course will cover key programming concepts such as control statements (if, else, logi- cal and conditional operators), repetition statements (while, for loops), and data structures (lists, tuples, sets, and dictionaries). By the end of the course, students will have the knowledge and skills to write Python programs from scratch, design custom classes, and apply core programming techniques to real-world problems.
learning_outcomes: CLO1. Explain Python fundamentals including variables, data types, operators, and control structures. CLO2. Develop Python programs using conditional statements, loops, functions, and built-in data structures CLO3. Apply Python to solve basic business problems through calculations, decision logic, and simple automation. 1 CLO4. Analyze and debug Python programs to identify errors and improve code efficiency and readability.

title: Computational Thinking & Programming
description_handout: Basic model of computation, input, processing, output, and storage; problem decomposition, abstraction, and representation of solutions using flowcharts and pseudocode. Algorithmic thinking, formulation of algorithms, tracing and verification of correctness, and comparison of efficiency at a conceptual level. Programming fundamentals, expressions, variables, primitive and composite data types, type conversion, and operator precedence; conditional statements and structured decision making; bounded and unbounded iteration. Modular program design, functions, parameter passing, scope, and structured program development. Recursion, recursive problem solving, base and recursive cases, call stack behaviour, and comparison with iterative approaches. Data structures, arrays, strings, and structured data representations; pointers, dynamic memory allocation, and memory management. File handling, basic input/output operations and sequential data processing. AI-assisted programming, responsible use of AI tools for code generation, including prompt formulation, critical evaluation, debugging, and verification of generated code. Laboratory: Algorithm design and tracing; implementation of programs involving conditionals, iteration, functions, recursion, arrays, strings, structured data, pointers, and dynamic memory; file handling; and integrated problem-solving exercises with critical evaluation of AI-assisted code. 1. Scope and Objective: This course establishes computational problem solving as a discipline before it establishes programming as a skill. Students first learn to decompose a problem, abstract away detail, express a solution as an algorithm, and reason about its correctness and cost. They then learn to realise those solutions as working programs, progressing from control structures and modular design to recursion, structured data, pointers, and explicit memory management. The course is anchored in C so that students build an accurate mental model of storage, addressing, and program execution, which is the model assumed by subsequent courses in data structures, operating systems, computer architecture, and networks. This subject aims to achieve the following goals: ● To develop the ability to decompose problems, abstract essential detail, and express solutions as algorithms independent of any programming language. ● To build fluency in structured programming, covering data types, expressions, control constructs, and modular function design. ● To establish an accurate mental model of program execution and memory through recursion, pointers, and dynamic memory management. ● To develop competence in representing and processing structured and linked data, and in persisting data through file operations. ● To build the judgement required to evaluate, test, and verify AI-generated code, and to use AI programming tools responsibly and with due attribution. 2. Course Learning Outcomes: Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to: CLO1: Express computational problems using abstraction, algorithmic thinking, and structured representations including flowcharts and pseudocode. CLO2: Implement programs using fundamental constructs including variables, data types, conditionals, iteration, and modular function design. CLO3: Apply recursion and dynamic memory management to solve problems involving structured and linked data representations. CLO4: Implement file handling operations for sequential data processing and structured input/output. 3. Textbooks and References: T1. Jeri R. Hanly and Elliot B. title: Natural Language Processing
scope_objective: s The intent of the course is to present a broad undergraduate/post-graduate level introduction to Natural Language Processing (NLP, a.k.a. computational linguistics), the study of computing systems that can process, understand, or communicate in human language. The primary focus of the course will be on understanding various NLP tasks as listed on the course syllabus, algorithms for effectively solving these problems, and methods for evaluating their performance. This subject aims to achieve the following goals: • To introduce students, the challenges of empirical methods for natural language processing (NLP) applications. • To introduce basic mathematical models and methods used in NLP applications to formulate computational solutions. • To provide students with the knowledge on designing procedures for natural language resource annotation and the use of related tools for text analysis and hands-on experience of using such tools. • To introduce students research and development work in information retrieval, information extraction, and knowledge discovery using different natural language resources. • To give students opportunities to sharpen their programming skills in neural networks (and deep learning) for computational linguistics applications. 2. title: Information Retrieval
description_handout: This course studies the theory, design, and implementation of text-based information systems. The Information Retrieval core components of the course include statistical characteristics of text, representation of information needs and documents, several important retrieval models (Boolean, vector space, probabilistic, inference net, language modeling, link analysis), clustering algorithms, collaborative filtering, automatic text categorization, and experimental evaluation. The software architecture components include design and implementation of high-capacity text and multimedia retrieval and filtering systems.
scope_objective: The course is designed to provide students with a broad understanding in the design and use of information retrieval techniques. The course also aims at providing a holistic view of information retrieval, which includes several retrieval concepts and techniques such as representation and indexing of data, text mining, websearch: basics and advances, multimedia retrieval, etc. 3. title: Product Design
description_handout: The course covers various approaches to designing and developing a successful product. User research, requirements analysis, problem-specific creative solution-finding, costing, synthesis and analysis of design are included. Modularization necessary for administering large design exercises and design decision-making processes, is deliberated. Concepts of value engineering, Engineering ethics, and Design for X, along with case studies, are also incorporated.
scope_objective: This course is designed to impart the knowledge required to develop a new product – understand the opportunity, develop a concept, and implement a concept. After the successful completion of this course, students shall be able to understand and use the various processes, tools and techniques required for designing a product: product specification development; concept generation, concept selection, concept testing and embodiment; product architecture; industrial design; design for X; analytical and numerical models; physical prototypes, models and experimentation; environmental, economic and social issues in product development; patents and intellectual properties. 3. title: Electrical Machines
description_handout: Transformer: Constructional features, equivalent circuit and phasor diagram - regulation and efficiency, parallel operation. Three phase transformer connections; Harmonic in transformers; Testing; Phase conversion; Autotransformer. D.C Machines: Construction, armature windings, armature voltage and torque equations, classification. D.C generators, performance characteristics; D.C motors - torque/speed characteristics, speed control and braking. Testing and efficiency. Induction machines: Constructional features and rotating magnetic field. Circuit model and phasor diagram. Steady state characteristics. Testing, starting and speed control. Time harmonics and space harmonics. Wound rotor induction motors, Single phase induction motors - classification and equivalent circuit. Synchronous machines: Constructional features; synchronous generators and motors; equivalent circuit and phasor diagram; power and torque characteristics and capability curves. Parallel operation. Salient pole synchronous machine - phasor diagram and determination of synchronous reactances; starting and speed control of synchronous motors. Special machines- universal motors, Induction generators.
scope_objective: Electrical Machines are the work horse in almost all industries ranging from few watts’ power to several mega watt power applications. The scope of this course is to study of working principle & operating characteristics of Electrical Machines for the mode of Generation, and Utilization of Electrical Power. The specific objective of this course is to gain better understanding of various conventional electrical-magnetic devices such as Transformer, DC Machines and AC Machines. The course covers theory as well as detailed experimental component for better understanding of the concepts.
learning_outcomes: The students will learn about the operating principles, constructional features, equivalent circuit diagram, efficiency, testing & control and different type of performance characteristics of transformers, DC machines, induction and synchronous machines. The further details are given in the course plan.

title: ELECTRONIC DEVICES
description_handout: (as per the Bulletin): Crystal structure and growth of semiconductor, electrical conduction in solids, Elementary quantum physics (Photoelectric effect, uncertainty principle, Schrodinger wave equation and tunneling), energy bands in solids, charge carriers in semiconductors, excess carriers in semiconductors, Fabrication of p-n junctions, equilibrium conditions, forward and reverse biased junctions, metal-semiconductor junctions Bipolar junction transistors, field effect transistors (JFET, HEMT, MOSFET), Special diodes (varactor diode, solar cell, LEDs, Tunnel diode and HBT).
scope_objective: s: The course provides a comprehensive understanding of the characteristics, operation and limitations of semiconductor devices. This course starts with explanation on crystal structure, semiconductor materials, fundamentals of semiconductors. This course helps in developing the understanding about excess carriers in semiconductors and its application. In-depth study on ‘junctions’ prepares the students for even a detailed study on devices to be studied later like FET, BJT, MOSFET viz. commonly employed in Integrated Circuit (IC) technology. Concepts of optoelectronic diodes will also be discussed in this course.
learning_outcomes: At the end of this course, students will be able to:  CLO1: Explain the fundamentals of semiconductor materials, crystal structures, electrical conduction, quantum physics concepts, and energy band theory governing electronic devices.  CLO2: Analyze charge carrier transport, excess carrier behavior, and the electrical characteristics of semiconductor materials under equilibrium and non-equilibrium conditions.  CLO3: Evaluate the operation and characteristics of semiconductor junctions, including p-n junctions, metal-semiconductor junctions, and their behavior under forward and reverse bias conditions.  CLO4: Explain the operating principles, characteristics, and applications of major semiconductor devices, including BJTs, JFETs, HEMTs, MOSFETs, and special semiconductor diodes.  CLO5: Apply the fundamental principles of semiconductor device physics to analyze the performance and limitations of electronic and optoelectronic devices used in modern integrated circuits and electronic systems.

title: Communication Systems
description_handout: Analysis and design of communication systems; analog and digital modulation and demodulation, frequency conversion, multiplexing, noise and distortion; spectral and signal-to-noise ratio analysis, probability of error in digital systems, spread spectrum.Introduction to the basic principles of the design and analysis of modern digital communication systems. Topics include source coding, channel coding, baseband and passband modulation techniques, receiver design, and channel equalization 1. Scope and Objective of the Course: This course intends to cover the basic understanding of functionalities of various block-sets involved in communication system. Course starts with an overview of communication systems, communication process, generic model and block diagram description. The course also reviews important concepts of signal and systems, and random variables which are useful for understanding and analyzing communication systems. The course covers both analog and digital communication systems. The course also covers information theoretic approach to deal with the random additive noise. The course deals with analog and digital modulation schemes in a deterministic way as well as analyzes the effect of random noise on the performance of communication systems. The course introduces performance metrics such as SNR and BER and performance limits of communications for both analog (using Nyquist rate) and digital (using Shannon theorem). The course has a lab component which includes simulation experiments for analog and digital communication systems using MATLAB and Python software. The objective of the course is to equip students with fundamental understanding to model, design, and analyze analog and digital communication systems for various practical scenarios. This course will serve as a basis to learn advanced level courses on communications and develop physical layer algorithms. Students will be given assignments on communication system modeling using MATLAB and Python. Students are expected to have an understanding of Signals and Systems, Electronic Devices and Circuits, Mathematics, and basics of Electromagnetic Field Theory. 2. Text Books: T1: B.P. Lathi and Zhi Ding, “Modern Digital and Analog Communication Systems”, 4th Edition, Oxford University Press, 2017, South Asis Edition (Adapted by H.M. Gupta) T2: Simon Haykin & Michael Moher, “Communication Systems”, 5th Edition, WSE, John Wiley & Sons, 2010. 3. Reference Books:  R1: John G. Proakis, Masoud Salehi, “Communication Systems Engineering”, 2nd Edition, Pearson, 2002.  R2: Simon Haykin, “Communication Systems”, 4th Edition, John Willey & Sons, 2001. BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 2  R3: A. Papoulis, S. Unnikrishna Pillai, “Probability, random variables, and stochastic processes”, 4th Edition, TMH, 2002. 4. Course Plan: Module No. Lecture Session Reference Learning Objectives (I): Introduction to Communication Systems and Bandwidth (2 Lectures) Lectures 1–2: Overview of the course; taxonomy of communication systems; block- level description of an end-to-end communication system; baseband and passband transmission; brief review of the Fourier transform and signal spectrum; signal bandwidth, channel bandwidth and bandwidth requirements in communication systems. T1: chapters 1, 2 Describe the functional blocks of an end-to-end communication system; distinguish between baseband and passband transmission; interpret communication signals in the time and frequency domains; and relate signal bandwidth to channel bandwidth. (II): Analog modulation and Demodulation (12 Lectures) Lectures 3–10: Amplitude-modulation techniques: DSB-SC, AM with carrier, SSB-SC, VSB; angle-modulation techniques: frequency modulation and phase modulation; bandwidth and power requirements; generation of AM and FM signals; Armstrong method of FM generation; and frequency-division multiplexing. T1: chapters 3,4 Explain frequency translation and the principles of amplitude and angle modulation; compare analog modulation schemes in terms of bandwidth and power requirements; describe methods for generating AM, FM and PM signals; and explain frequency-division multiplexing. Lectures 11–14: Synchronous detection; envelope detection; FM and PM demodulation; phase-locked-loop-based demodulation; and superheterodyne receivers. T1: chapter 3,4 Explain synchronous and envelope detection; describe FM- and PM-demodulation techniques, including PLL- based
scope_objective: This course intends to cover the basic understanding of functionalities of various block-sets involved in communication system. Course starts with an overview of communication systems, communication process, generic model and block diagram description. The course also reviews important concepts of signal and systems, and random variables which are useful for understanding and analyzing communication systems. The course covers both analog and digital communication systems. The course also covers information theoretic approach to deal with the random additive noise. The course deals with analog and digital modulation schemes in a deterministic way as well as analyzes the effect of random noise on the performance of communication systems. The course introduces performance metrics such as SNR and BER and performance limits of communications for both analog (using Nyquist rate) and digital (using Shannon theorem). The course has a lab component which includes simulation experiments for analog and digital communication systems using MATLAB and Python software. The objective of the course is to equip students with fundamental understanding to model, design, and analyze analog and digital communication systems for various practical scenarios. This course will serve as a basis to learn advanced level courses on communications and develop physical layer algorithms. Students will be given assignments on communication system modeling using MATLAB and Python. Students are expected to have an understanding of Signals and Systems, Electronic Devices and Circuits, Mathematics, and basics of Electromagnetic Field Theory. 2. Text Books: T1: B.P. Lathi and Zhi Ding, “Modern Digital and Analog Communication Systems”, 4th Edition, Oxford University Press, 2017, South Asis Edition (Adapted by H.M. title: Electromagnetic Fields and Microwave Engineering
description_handout: Review of Maxwell's equations; Wave propagation: Normal & Oblique incidence; Transmission Lines & Smith Chart, Waveguide: Rectangular & Cylindrical waveguides; Dielectric Waveguides; Cavity resonator, equivalent Circuit Model, characteristics; Microwave devices (Waveguide based and planar); S parameters; Measurement & Impedance Matching; Microwave Generators & Amplifiers; Antennas and its characteristics and types. Scope and objective of the course: This course provides a comprehensive understanding of electromagnetic wave theory and microwave engineering, focusing on Maxwell’s equations, wave propagation, and transmission line theory. It covers the analysis and design of waveguides, cavity resonators, and dielectric structures. Students will explore microwave devices, S-parameters, impedance matching techniques, and measurement methods. The course also introduces microwave generators, amplifiers, and various types of antennas with their characteristics. The objective is to equip students with the theoretical foundation and practical skills needed to analyze, design, and apply high-frequency systems in modern communication, radar, and sensing applications. Learning Outcomes: Upon completion of this course, students will be able to analyze electromagnetic wave propagation using Maxwell’s equations, understand wave behavior at interfaces, and design transmission lines with impedance matching using the Smith Chart. They will gain proficiency in characterizing waveguides, cavity resonators, and microwave devices, as well as interpreting S- parameters for network analysis. Students will also learn measurement techniques, explore microwave sources and amplifiers, and evaluate various antenna types and their radiation characteristics for practical applications. 1. Textbook: 1) TB1: David Pozar, “Microwave Engineering”, 4th edition, John Wiley & Sons, 2012. 2) TB2: John D. Kraus and Daniel A. Fleisch, “Electromagnetics”, 5th ed., McGraw-Hill, New York, 1999. 2. Reference Books : i) RB1: David K. Cheng, “Field and Wave Electromagnetics,” 2nd ed. Pearson Education, New Delhi, 2009. ii) RB2: Samuel Y. Liao, “Microwave devices and circuits,” 3rd ed. , PHI 2008. iii) RB3: J. D. Krauss et al., “Antennas and Wave Propagation”, 4th edition, TMH 2010. 3. Course Plan: Lec. title: PRINCIPLES OF ECONOMICS
description: Principles of Economics 3 Humanities Electives 3 (min) or or AUE F211 Basic Design for Visualization 3
description_handout: This course is a foundation course for the students entering into the discipline of Economics & Finance. This introductory course teaches the basic concepts related to the economic system that are listed as follows: Introduction to Economics (Microeconomics) & Economic Problems; Demand, Supply, & Elasticity; Household Behavior and Consumer choice; The Production Process; Costs and Output Decisions; Demand for Production Inputs; Market Imperfections: Monopoly, Oligopoly, Monopolistic Competition; Introduction to Macroeconomics and the Problems; Measurement of National Income & Output; Money Supply and the Banking System
scope_objective: The main objective is to introduce the fundamental concepts and tools necessary to acquire an understanding of economic decision making of market participants such as Individual households, firms, and the government. title: [Fundamentals of Finance and Accounting]
description: Fundamentals of Finance & Accounts 3 ECON F242 Microeconomics 3
description_handout: Accounting is the language of business. Through this language, the business (i.e. the Company) not only maintain the records of transactions it undertakes during the course of its existence but also communicates with the outside world by publishing various financial reports that summarize transactions undertaken by the company. Therefore, it is important to note here that this course entails two important and interrelated aspects, i.e., a. Recording transactions, and b. Preparing financial statements such as balance sheet, income statement, etc. Since b. follows a., it is important to learn the recording of transactions first to learn preparing financial statements. The course will introduce you to the following key concepts: introduction, standards and basic rules of accounting, double-entry accounting system, identifying and recoding transactions, preparing trial balance, dealing with incomplete transactions, preparing the balance sheet, types of ownership, credibility and role of auditing, measuring income, adjustments to the accounts, preparing the statement of cash flows, recording sales revenue, reporting inventories and cost of goods sold, recording capital assets, liabilities and interest, stockholders' equity and valuation of financial assets. This course is specifically designed to meet the educational needs of second year Economics students and students pursing Finance minor program. To complete the program requirement, the students from Economics and Finance background require a basic understanding on accounting principles and financial statement analysis. This course serves that purpose, and it is prerequisite to other advanced courses that students from (MSc) Economics and Finance (minor) undertake in the subsequent semesters. Hence, being elementary in nature this course has got its relevance and importance. Besides, a few students also take this course as an elective to pursue their academic interests in the field of finance.
scope_objective: The scope of this course largely encapsulates an introduction to the reporting system used by businesses to record and convey financial information to investors, analysts, and regulators. This reporting system is referred to as financial accounting. The key learning objectives that this course accomplishes enables participants in learning: a. how companies identify and record transactions that have a financial impact and are critical to day-to-day functioning of the company. b. how using a systematic procedure, the recorded transactions are summarized into meaningful and standardized reports (financial statements) such as the balance sheet, statement of income etc. c. the key components that form part of these financial statements. d. how these financial statements are analyzed and what information do they convey about the financial well-being and prospects about the company.
learning_outcomes: Students who complete this course would be able to a. Understand the accounting methods for recording the business transactions. b. Evaluate various financial concepts and preparation of financial statements-balance sheet, income statement, and cash flow statement. c. Identify the financial position and performance of the companies. d. Make better economic decisions while undertaking investments in financial assets.

title: MATHEMATICAL AND STATISTICAL METHODS
description: Mathematical & Statistical Methods 3 ECON F243 Macroeconomics 3
description_handout: The course is designed to provide a basic understanding of various statistical and mathematical methods useful for decision-making and for understanding applications in other economics and finance courses. The course is divided into two parts: Statistical Methods and Mathematical Methods. Statistical Methods include methods of collecting and describing statistical data – types of data and data collection methodologies, sampling methods & design, data describing methods (graphical and numerical); Correlation and Regression analyses; Index numbers: Concepts, uses, and methods of construction; Analysis of Time-series: Components, data generating process, and stationarity; Statistical Inference: Introduction to Probability and its distributions, sampling distributions, theory of estimation, Tests of Hypotheses testing (Parametric & Non-Parametric); and Mathematical Methods include Concepts from Linear Algebra & their Applications (Matrices, Input-Output analysis, and Game Theory); Concepts from Calculus and their applications; Introduction to Optimization in Economics and its Applications.
scope_objective: The main objective is to learn how to use mathematical and statistical methods in economics. It involves a review of the fundamentals of mathematics and statistics, which can be used in applied economics. Knowledge of these fundamentals and their application in applied economics would help students better understand the entire economic system and the policymaking process. At the end of this course, students will be able to understand and solve graduate-level problems in economics and finance using the knowledge they have gained. Specifically, this course uses fundamentals from calculus, algebra, optimization, and basic statistics. This course would lay the foundation for students to understand related courses in economics and finance, such as econometrics and growth theory.
learning_outcomes: CLO1. Apply appropriate methods for data collection, sampling, organization, and descriptive analysis, using graphical and numerical techniques to summarize and interpret statistical data. CLO2. Analyze relationships among economic and business variables using correlation and regression techniques, and construct and interpret index numbers for relevant applications. CLO3. Analyze time-series data by identifying its components, understanding the underlying data-generating process, and assessing stationarity. CLO4. Apply probability concepts and statistical inference techniques, including probability and sampling distributions, estimation, and parametric and non-parametric hypothesis testing, to draw valid conclusions from data. CLO5. Apply mathematical methods to economic problems, using concepts from linear algebra, input-output analysis, game theory, calculus, and optimization to formulate and solve economic decision problems.

title: ECONOMIC ENVIRONMENT OF BUSINESS
description_handout: Businesses are the driving force behind a nation's economic activity since they enable its population to attain a higher quality of living. It is essential to understand that a business firm does not operate in a vacuum but in a given environment and must interact and transact its business within this environment. Business environment refers to the totality of all individuals, institutions, and other forces external to a business unit but potentially affecting its performance. Business enterprises are micro units within an economic environment that represents the macro. The economic environment is the “given” within which firms and their managements must operate. So, the business environment and the manner and effectiveness of the interaction of an enterprise with its environment would generally determine its success or failure.
scope_objective: The course aims to (1) Create familiarity with economic environment concepts and indicators, economic policies, and economic regulation (2) Develop the ability to analyze and anticipate changes in the economic environment and, (3) Enable students to take more effective business decisions by being responsive to the changing external economic environment. The objective of this course is to unravel all those economic factors that are external to and beyond the control of individual business enterprises and their management, with a focus on the Indian context.
learning_outcomes: of the Course: This course will educate students on the interdependencies and linkages between business and its environment, focusing on the Indian context. Moreover, it will improve comprehension of various external economic factors affecting the business environment. For instance, the business climate in India is influenced by variables such as GDP, inflation, fiscal policy, monetary policy, industrial policy, etc., which have both direct and indirect effects. Furthermore, it will thoroughly comprehend many economic elements in the business environment more pragmatically.

title: ISSUES IN ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT
description_handout: This course provides a comprehensive and contemporary examination of the major issues, challenges, and policy debates in economic development by integrating theoretical perspectives, empirical evidence, and real-world applications. It views development as a multidimensional process that extends beyond economic growth to encompass structural transformation, human development, institutional quality, technological progress, environmental sustainability, and social inclusion. The course explores why countries experience divergent development trajectories and examines the roles of markets, governments, institutions, globalization, and technological change in shaping long- run development outcomes. Drawing upon classical and contemporary development theories, with particular emphasis on India and other developing economies, the course examines a broad range of development issues, including poverty, inequality, unemployment, population dynamics, demographic transition, migration, urbanization, education, health, agriculture, industrialization, infrastructure, financial inclusion, foreign investment, governance, environmental degradation, climate change, artificial intelligence and development, digital transformation, and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Through analytical frameworks, empirical evidence, policy debates, and case studies, students will develop the ability to critically examine development challenges, interpret development indicators, and evaluate alternative policy interventions for achieving sustainable, inclusive, and equitable development.
scope_objective: The primary objective of this course is to equip students with a rigorous understanding of the theoretical, empirical, and policy dimensions of economic development while fostering the analytical skills required to evaluate contemporary development challenges. The course enables students to understand the economic, social, institutional, technological, and environmental factors that influence development outcomes across countries and regions. It emphasizes the interrelationships among economic growth, structural transformation, employment generation, poverty reduction, income distribution, human capital formation, institutional development, and environmental sustainability. Students will critically examine competing development theories and policy paradigms, evaluate the effectiveness of development strategies adopted by different countries, and analyze the role of public policy in promoting inclusive and sustainable development. The course also introduces emerging issues that are reshaping development discourse, including artificial intelligence and development, digital transformation, climate resilience, financial inclusion, gender equality, governance, and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Equal emphasis is placed on developing students' analytical, quantitative, and research competencies through the interpretation of development indicators, evaluation of empirical evidence, policy analysis, and application of contemporary development concepts to real- world economic issues. By the end of the course, students will be equipped to critically assess development policies and contribute to evidence-based decision-making in both academic and policy contexts. title: Financial Management
description_handout: Financial Management is a foundation course offered to finance minor students and as a disciplinary and open elective. The Financial Management course has several practical applications to financial decision-making and encompasses topics having a varying degree of complexity. It is usually taught at the graduate level such as MS/MBA or at the PhD. This course ECON/FIN F 315 is designed to suit the level of academic experience and exposure in finance for undergraduate students having just taken a first course on Fundamentals of Finance and Accounting. The course’s learning objectives focus on the primary financial decisions undertaken by the financial manager of an organisation to achieve the principal objective of the firm. In an increasingly competitive and globally integrated world marked by all-pervasive technological advancements, the roles and responsibilities of financial managers are expanding in response to the explosion in the number of firms striving for success. On the one hand, corporations are hungry to fulfil their financing needs, so on the other are the investors, looking for the best return on the buck they invest. The wide range of investment avenues available to investors explains the extent of innovations happening in the financial markets worldwide. However, with uncontrolled growth comes the risk of an uncontrolled collapse and the financial crisis of 2008 is a classic case of fault lines in the financial markets. To retain the confidence and faith of investors and forge robust and sustainable growth, the firms must impress suppliers of capital (investors) with adequate rewards to compensate them for the risks they undertake. More importantly, the modern viewpoint of the roles and responsibilities of the board of directors and the C-suite managers has departed from the traditional profitability perspective to the wealth maximisation principle. The firm must protect and strengthen the rights of its stakeholders, such as employees, suppliers, customers, the environment, investors, etc. Hence, the wealth maximisation principle influences the decisions firms make about their financing policy, investment policy, and dividend distribution policy. The role of the financial manager - which is central to the decision-making concerning finances (money, capital, investment etc.) – plays a critical role in ensuring seamless day-to-day operations, maintaining profitability and sustaining reliable long-term performance along with adherence to the company’s ESG (sustainability) policies. Primarily, the course objectives hover around key decisions made by financial managers, including financing, investing, capital structure, and shareholder rewarding policies. The contents of this course enable the participants to appreciate the interdependencies between these decisions and their impact on the firm's survivability. title: Derivatives & Risk Management
scope_objective: The objective of this course is to provide students an introductory level familiarity with a particular type of financial instruments known as DERIVATIVES. To achieve the stated objectives, the course provides a detailed description on the structure (read, design) and utility (read, relevance) of the most common and popular financial derivatives namely, Options, Futures, and Swaps. The scope of the course entails acquainting students with the mechanics of trading and settlement of derivative instruments in the financial markets and their function as insurance products for hedging financial risk. No understanding about financial instruments or their derivatives is complete without a thorough grasp over interest rate concepts and hence the course also includes discussion on topics such as time value of money, term structure of interest rates and their role in valuation of bonds, computation of yield and forward interest rates, estimating bond-price volatility, and the role of bond duration and convexity in mitigating interest rate risks. The topics covered in the course will, at an introductory level, enable participants to learn about common risks prevalent in the financial markets and how to manage its impact on investment exposure by using derivatives. Discussion on valuation of financial derivatives and a brief introduction to creating synthetic investment positions by combining derivatives prepares students for advanced level courses such as Financial Engineering and Financial Risk Analytics and Management. The course concludes with a survey of selective topics of contemporary interest to risk management industry such as forecasting volatility, estimating value-at-risk, etc. The topics covered in the course will also assist students in preparing for competitive professional international certifications such as Financial Risk Manager (FRM) and Chartered Financial Analyst (CFA). 2. Prerequisites: This is an elementary course on Derivatives and Risk Management and does not assume any prior knowledge of Financial Markets, Instruments and Derivatives. However, familiarity of basic economic theory such as law of supply and demand, utility maximization principle, compounding and discounting of cash flows, etc. are desirable. The course is not mathematically rigorous and a first-year course on elementary linear algebra, calculus, probability, and differential equations will be sufficient to grasp the contents of the course. It is expected that students have technical know-how of MS excel as it will be used to demonstrate required computations, wherever required, and for carrying out take-home assignments. title: BUSINESS ANALYSIS AND VALUATION
description_handout: This course focuses on the essential tools and frameworks for evaluating the value of companies through financial analysis. Students will explore key concepts such as internal growth, mergers and acquisitions, along with valuation methodologies like discounted cash flow and relative valuation. Designed for those with prior knowledge in finance and accounting, the course equips students with the skills to analyze financial statements, assess market conditions, and identify key performance drivers. Ideal for aspiring professionals in investment banking, corporate finance, and consulting, this course enhances analytical capabilities and strategic thinking in business valuation and decision-making.
scope_objective: The Process of measuring and managing the value of companies is a central aspect of financial analysis. Globally, managers are in pursuit of adding value to their firms via two important means. One, by enhancing the firm’s productive capacity through internal (or organic) growth, which has a simultaneous positive impact on its stock price. Second, through mergers and acquisitions (a decision involving factors external to the firm) that interlocks with corporation’s key strengths, and yield benefits in the long run. Hence, asking, “What is something worth?” is a vital question to business decision making, and the principal objective behind this course is to provide the learners with the conceptual basis, intuitive reasoning, and analytical framework to answer this question. The focus of this course is on valuing equity (or ownership) in a firm and estimating the value of the overall enterprise. The coverage relies on discounted cash flow, relative valuation, and contingent valuation approaches for extracting the value of a business. Since financial statements serve as the basis for all types of valuation methods, the course begins by providing brief framework on the principles governing the financial statements, and adjustments that are often required to capture the underlying business reality. Students who are either currently pursuing or would like to embark on a career in investment banking, corporate finance, venture capital, entrepreneurship, or business consulting will find the course material to be most useful. The course also carries a broader appeal to individuals who are interested in enhancing their understanding of financial analysis, and in learning how businesses measure and create value for their investors. BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 2 Important: This is not a beginning level course. The course presumes that you have a prior exposure on a variety of introductory concepts in finance, accounting, and statistics. For beginners, it is therefore highly recommended that they go through the introductory material in finance and accounting concepts at the earliest. Feel free to contact the I/C ASAP in case you are facing difficulty in following the classroom discussions. 3. Expected Learning Outcome of the Course: The course aims to provide students with a comprehensive understanding of financial analysis, advanced accounting practices, and valuation techniques. By the end of the program, learners will be able to effectively analyze financial statements, gaining insights into an organization's performance and financial health. A critical component of the curriculum focuses on valuation methods, where students will learn to assess the value of assets and investments using various approaches, such as discounted cash flow analysis and market comparables. This knowledge will empower them to evaluate investment opportunities critically and make informed decisions that can significantly impact an organization's financial strategy. Overall, these outcomes will prepare students for successful careers in finance and accounting, equipping them with both analytical and practical skills essential for navigating complex financial landscapes.

title: Security Analysis and Portfolio Management
description_handout: Security Analysis and Portfolio Management addresses two connected problems: what a financial asset is worth, and how much of it a particular investor should hold. The first half of the course develops valuation. Students examine the characteristics and risk-return profiles of the major asset classes – equity, fixed income, and derivatives – and the fundamental, quantitative and technical techniques used to estimate intrinsic worth. Analysis of economy, industry, and stock specific fundamentals are carried out for valuing stocks. Hence, asset valuation forms a major component of this course. Another important aspect of the course is on modern portfolio concepts, where the criterion changes: a holding is no longer judged on its own merits but by its contribution to the risk and return of the whole. This covers modern portfolio theory, diversification and correlation, asset allocation, and the construction of portfolios aligned to a stated investor's objectives, constraints and risk tolerance.
scope_objective: The objectives of the course are to provide an introduction to: • Types of financial securities and their salient characteristics. • Investment philosophy and its role in asset allocation and long-term personal finance management. • Modern portfolio theories and their applications in portfolio design and evaluation. • Equity and debt valuation using fundamental analysis and relative valuation techniques. • Technical analysis. • Financial derivative contracts and their applications.
learning_outcomes: • Distinguish the major classes of financial securities — equity, fixed income, derivatives and alternatives — by their claim structure, risk-return profile and role within a portfolio. • Value individual securities using techniques appropriate to the instrument, including discounted cash flow and relative valuation for equity and yield-based measures for fixed income, and state the assumptions on which each valuation rests. • Measure and decompose investment risk, separating systematic from unsystematic components, and evaluate investments on a risk-adjusted basis rather than on raw return. • Construct a diversified portfolio using correlation and modern portfolio theory, and justify the resulting asset allocation against a specified investor's objectives, time horizon and risk tolerance. • Apply derivative instruments to hedge or modify portfolio exposure, and explain the payoff profile and risk of each strategy employed. • Assess portfolio performance using risk-adjusted measures and attribution analysis, and determine when a portfolio requires rebalancing as market conditions change. 4. title: New Venture Creation
description_handout: The purpose of this course is to not only study entrepreneurship but also practice it. Student teams are expected to create a technology product-based or service/SaaS-based startup and complete the business model canvas, including all the building blocks of creating a venture. In order to create a successful startup, student entrepreneurs will be required to comprehend the five phases of startup creation: (1) idea and problem validation; (2) solution validation and product market fit (PMF); (3) go to market (GTM) and scalability; (4) operations and institutionalization; (5) Startup teams will work on customer discovery, product development, market research, technology viability, fundraising, competitive analysis, team formation, marketing & sales strategy, and storytelling. The course features workshops/guest- lectures from entrepreneurs, investors and academicians with strong experience in creating and running Startups. Participating teams will be assigned an experienced, dedicated entrepreneur mentor who will guide them through the semester and can choose to mentor after the course is concluded. The top teams may be invited to compete for seed funding in early 2027 to pursue their business idea for incubation after the completion of the NVC course and thereby launch the business.
scope_objective: NVC’s mission is to empower student founders with the choice and tools to become entrepreneurs Hence, the course aims to provide students with an opportunity to launch/ prepare to launch startups post-NVC. NVC helps them to think and act entrepreneurially. The central mystery of entrepreneurship is how to transform an idea into an organizational entity where people can channel their energy and creativity to produce a reliable output that creates economic value. Some of the questions that will be addressed are: Which specific market segment of customers should you focus on? How do you plan for a new venture? How do you build an effective venture team? How do you establish your venture’s identity and legitimacy? How do you win customers? How will your venture make money? How do you manage your venture’s dependence on key external partners? 3. title: RISK MANAGEMENT AND INSURANCE
description_handout: Introduction to risk; types of risk; risk measurement; risk management techniques; risk avoidance, loss control, loss financing, risk retention, risk transfer, internal risk reduction through diversification etc.; insurance business and operations; insurance pricing; insurance v/s hedging; life, health and income risk; property and liability risk – commercial and personal; social insurance; insurance regulation 2 Scope and Objective of the Course: This course will examine the way in which business and society make an assessment of, control and transfer risk. The scope of this course is to provide a broad understanding of risk and insurance as a means to manage it. This forms the foundation to facilitate the students in their further studies on insurance. The course introduces the concept of risk and techniques of identifying, measuring and managing it. In this context, insurance as a risk management tool is discussed with references to its role, functions and basic principles as applicable to different classes of insurance. title: Urban Water Management
description_handout: Urban Water Management is an advanced course focusing on the planning, design, operation, and assessment of urban water systems under increasing pressures of population growth, urbanization, and climate change. It explores the complete urban water cycle, including supply, sanitation, drainage, and environmental flows, with strong emphasis on sustainable and resilient urban development. The course addresses technical, social, economic, and regulatory challenges through a multidisciplinary lens. Students are exposed to contemporary topics such as stormwater management, water-sensitive urban design, and water quality monitoring. Practical software-based training modules on stormwater modelling, flood forecasting, and hydroinformatics are integrated to bridge theory and real-world applications. Students will also gain insights into advanced asset management systems, sustainability indicators, GIS tools, and the effect of urbanization on hydrological behavior. This industry-oriented course prepares students for professional roles in government, consulting, and research sectors concerned with smart, equitable, and sustainable urban water solutions.
scope_objective: The course aims to equip students with comprehensive knowledge and practical skills in managing urban water systems effectively and sustainably. The scope spans water supply, sanitation, stormwater, groundwater, and urban drainage management. It incorporates key concepts in water-sensitive urban design, reuse and recycling of wastewater, climate-resilient infrastructure planning, and integrated urban water modelling. Emphasis is placed on understanding emerging urban water challenges, regulatory frameworks, and digital tools for decision support. Through hands-on sessions, case studies, and software exposure, the course objectives are: (1) To understand the integrated urban water cycle and its components; (2) To develop competence in water quality and infrastructure assessment; (3) To analyze risks and sustainability indicators in urban water systems; (4) To apply hydroinformatics tools for modeling and performance evaluation; and (5) To foster decision-making skills relevant to urban water management, policies, and climate adaptation strategies.
learning_outcomes:  Understand and assess the urban water cycle and system interactions under climate change and urbanization.  Demonstrate practical knowledge in water quality, stormwater, and sanitation system design and management.  Use hydroinformatics and modeling tools for flood forecasting and system performance

title: Electrical Machines
description_handout: Transformer: Constructional features, equivalent circuit and phasor diagram - regulation and efficiency, parallel operation. Three phase transformer connections; Harmonic in transformers; Testing; Phase conversion; Autotransformer. D.C Machines: Construction, armature windings, armature voltage and torque equations, classification. D.C generators, performance characteristics; D.C motors - torque/speed characteristics, speed control and braking. Testing and efficiency. Induction machines: Constructional features and rotating magnetic field. Circuit model and phasor diagram. Steady state characteristics. Testing, starting and speed control. Time harmonics and space harmonics. Wound rotor induction motors, Single phase induction motors - classification and equivalent circuit. Synchronous machines: Constructional features; synchronous generators and motors; equivalent circuit and phasor diagram; power and torque characteristics and capability curves. Parallel operation. Salient pole synchronous machine - phasor diagram and determination of synchronous reactances; starting and speed control of synchronous motors. Special machines- universal motors, Induction generators.
scope_objective: Electrical Machines are the work horse in almost all industries ranging from few watts’ power to several mega watt power applications. The course covers theory as well as detailed experimental component for better understanding of the concepts.
learning_outcomes: The students will learn about the operating principles, constructional features, equivalent circuit diagram, efficiency, testing & control and different type of performance characteristics of transformers, DC machines, induction and synchronous machines. title: ELECTRONIC DEVICES
description_handout: (as per the Bulletin): Crystal structure and growth of semiconductor, electrical conduction in solids, Elementary quantum physics (Photoelectric effect, uncertainty principle, Schrodinger wave equation and tunneling), energy bands in solids, charge carriers in semiconductors, excess carriers in semiconductors, Fabrication of p-n junctions, equilibrium conditions, forward and reverse biased junctions, metal-semiconductor junctions Bipolar junction transistors, field effect transistors (JFET, HEMT, MOSFET), Special diodes (varactor diode, solar cell, LEDs, Tunnel diode and HBT).
scope_objective: s: The course provides a comprehensive understanding of the characteristics, operation and limitations of semiconductor devices. This course starts with explanation on crystal structure, semiconductor materials, fundamentals of semiconductors. This course helps in developing the understanding about excess carriers in semiconductors and its application. In-depth study on ‘junctions’ prepares the students for even a detailed study on devices to be studied later like FET, BJT, MOSFET viz. commonly employed in Integrated Circuit (IC) technology. Concepts of optoelectronic diodes will also be discussed in this course.
learning_outcomes: At the end of this course, students will be able to:  CLO1: Explain the fundamentals of semiconductor materials, crystal structures, electrical conduction, quantum physics concepts, and energy band theory governing electronic devices.  CLO2: Analyze charge carrier transport, excess carrier behavior, and the electrical characteristics of semiconductor materials under equilibrium and non-equilibrium conditions.  CLO3: Evaluate the operation and characteristics of semiconductor junctions, including p-n junctions, metal-semiconductor junctions, and their behavior under forward and reverse bias conditions.  CLO4: Explain the operating principles, characteristics, and applications of major semiconductor devices, including BJTs, JFETs, HEMTs, MOSFETs, and special semiconductor diodes.  CLO5: Apply the fundamental principles of semiconductor device physics to analyze the performance and limitations of electronic and optoelectronic devices used in modern integrated circuits and electronic systems.

title: Communication Systems
description_handout: Analysis and design of communication systems; analog and digital modulation and demodulation, frequency conversion, multiplexing, noise and distortion; spectral and signal-to-noise ratio analysis, probability of error in digital systems, spread spectrum.Introduction to the basic principles of the design and analysis of modern digital communication systems. Topics include source coding, channel coding, baseband and passband modulation techniques, receiver design, and channel equalization 1. Scope and Objective of the Course: This course intends to cover the basic understanding of functionalities of various block-sets involved in communication system. Course starts with an overview of communication systems, communication process, generic model and block diagram description. The course also reviews important concepts of signal and systems, and random variables which are useful for understanding and analyzing communication systems. The course covers both analog and digital communication systems. The course also covers information theoretic approach to deal with the random additive noise. The course deals with analog and digital modulation schemes in a deterministic way as well as analyzes the effect of random noise on the performance of communication systems. The course introduces performance metrics such as SNR and BER and performance limits of communications for both analog (using Nyquist rate) and digital (using Shannon theorem). The course has a lab component which includes simulation experiments for analog and digital communication systems using MATLAB and Python software. The objective of the course is to equip students with fundamental understanding to model, design, and analyze analog and digital communication systems for various practical scenarios. This course will serve as a basis to learn advanced level courses on communications and develop physical layer algorithms. Students will be given assignments on communication system modeling using MATLAB and Python. Students are expected to have an understanding of Signals and Systems, Electronic Devices and Circuits, Mathematics, and basics of Electromagnetic Field Theory. 2. Text Books: T1: B.P. Lathi and Zhi Ding, “Modern Digital and Analog Communication Systems”, 4th Edition, Oxford University Press, 2017, South Asis Edition (Adapted by H.M. Gupta) T2: Simon Haykin & Michael Moher, “Communication Systems”, 5th Edition, WSE, John Wiley & Sons, 2010. 3. Reference Books:  R1: John G. Proakis, Masoud Salehi, “Communication Systems Engineering”, 2nd Edition, Pearson, 2002.  R2: Simon Haykin, “Communication Systems”, 4th Edition, John Willey & Sons, 2001. BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 2  R3: A. Papoulis, S. Unnikrishna Pillai, “Probability, random variables, and stochastic processes”, 4th Edition, TMH, 2002. 4. T1: chapters 1, 2 Describe the functional blocks of an end-to-end communication system; distinguish between baseband and passband transmission; interpret communication signals in the time and frequency domains; and relate signal bandwidth to channel bandwidth. (II): Analog modulation and Demodulation (12 Lectures) Lectures 3–10: Amplitude-modulation techniques: DSB-SC, AM with carrier, SSB-SC, VSB; angle-modulation techniques: frequency modulation and phase modulation; bandwidth and power requirements; generation of AM and FM signals; Armstrong method of FM generation; and frequency-division multiplexing. T1: chapters 3,4 Explain frequency translation and the principles of amplitude and angle modulation; compare analog modulation schemes in terms of bandwidth and power requirements; describe methods for generating AM, FM and PM signals; and explain frequency-division multiplexing. Lectures 11–14: Synchronous detection; envelope detection; FM and PM demodulation; phase-locked-loop-based demodulation; and superheterodyne receivers. title: ANALOG AND DIGITAL VLSI DESIGN
description_handout: This course introduces students to the principles and practical aspects of designing integrated circuits using CMOS technology. It covers both analog and digital VLSI design methodologies, exploring circuit-level building blocks, layout considerations, and performance trade-offs. Emphasis is placed on low-power, area- efficient, and high-performance circuit techniques, along with exposure to modern CAD tools and fabrication-aware design strategies. Students will gain experience designing critical components, including logic gates, adders, amplifiers, and mixed-signal interfaces.
scope_objective: ⮚ The course is designed to familiarize students with different design principles used in the Design of Digital & Analog VLSI Circuits & Systems using CMOS logic. ⮚ Understanding of CMOS technology fundamentals and their impact on design. ⮚ Design and analysis of digital logic circuits: static, dynamic, sequential. ⮚ Design and analysis of analog CMOS circuits: Op-Amplifiers, Advance current mirrors, Reference Circuit. ⮚ Exploration of Technology scaling trends, noise, and power-performance trade-offs. ⮚ Exposure to EDA tools for schematic capture, simulation, and layout. ⮚ Bridging theory with practical insights via Lab/Design assignments. ⮚ VLSI design activity will be understood by Synthesis and then Analysis at several successive levels of design abstraction.
