title: Internet of Things
description_handout: Introduction to IoT, Sensors and Actuators for IoT, Programming IoT end points, Communications and networking in IoT, Data management in IoT, Security issues in IoT, Emerging technologies. This course is discipline elective (DEL) for: Undergraduate level: B.E. (EEE), B.E (ECE), B.E. (E&I)/ dualites in those disciplines. For other discipline, it will be considered as an open elective (OPEL).
scope_objective: This module is designed to provide students with solid technical knowledge and skills to build Internet of Things (IoT) systems. Internet of things has evolved due to convergence of multiple technologies - embedded systems, sensor technology, real-time data analytics, machine learning etc. Traditional fields of embedded systems, wireless sensor networks, control systems, automation (including home and building automation), and others all contribute to enabling the IoT. This course comprehensively covers various technologies and tools used for enabling IoT solutions. Knowledge of various topics required for building IoT prototypes like sensors and actuators/ Communications and networking and data management is also imparted in this course. This course would also help the students understand the various IoT security challenges and solution to address them. The course will also give the students exposure to how various real world problems are being solved by IoT based solutions (like in applications for smart city, smart farming etc.). There would also be some hands on sessions where students would learn how to build and program IoT systems and make end-to- end solutions for different applications. Furthermore, assignments and projects in this course would help students build IoT prototypes and apply what they have learnt in the course to solve real world problems. 3. Course learning Objectives: Upon completion of this course, students will be able to: a. Understand and explain the fundamental concepts, architectures, enabling technologies, communication protocols, data-management techniques, and security challenges associated with Internet of Things systems. b. Design and develop IoT-based solutions by integrating sensors, actuators, microcontrollers, communication networks, cloud platforms, and data-analytics tools. c. Apply practical programming and system-integration skills to build, test, and evaluate end-to-end IoT prototypes for addressing real-world applications such as smart cities, smart agriculture, healthcare, and industrial automation.

title: Modern Control Systems
description_handout: Feedback control is a central aiding tool in a wide range of engineering and even some non-engineering applications. This is a second UG level course on the subject, which takes the so- called Modern approach as opposed to the Classical approach taken in the previous compulsory course on the subject. This course discusses the basic analytical and design techniques using the concept of state variables; the techniques of optimal control and estimation theory and an introductory level treatment of nonlinear systems. The underlying mathematical concepts of these techniques will be emphasized and also some flavor of applications will be given through examples, exercises and take home assignments drawn from various engineering domains.

title: Fiber Optics and Optoelectronics
description_handout: Optical communication systems and components; optical sources and transmitters (basic concept, design and applications); modulators (electro- optic, acousto-optic and laser modulation techniques); beam forming; focusing and coupling schemes to optical repeaters; optical amplifiers; optical field reception; coherent and non-coherent light wave systems; fiber optic communication system design and performance; multichannel light wave systems; long haul communications; fiber optic networks.
scope_objective: In the recent past, tremendous advances have been achieved in fiber optics and associated optoelectronics. These developments have made fiber - optic communication synonymous with the current worldwide revolution in information technology. This course aims at providing the students with a firm grounding in the major aspects of this emerging technology. Thus the course deals with the study of various building blocks of fiber optic systems, e.g. optical fibers, sources, detectors, modulators, optical amplifiers, etc. together with overall system design and performance analysis for communication applications.
learning_outcomes: At the end of this course, students will be able to:  CLO1: Basic configuration of a fiber-optic system, Merits of Fiber Optic system, Ray propagation through different types of optical fibers and Estimation of different parameters of optical fibers.  CLO2: Familiarization with the background for learning of electromagnetic wave propagation in medium, Modal analysis of planar optical wave guides, Modal analysis of cylindrical optical waveguide and characterization of optical fibers.  CLO3: Concept of semi-conductor p-n junction towards design LED, LED designs characterization and ILD condition for laser action, Optical transmitter design and applications  CLO4: Basic principle of opto-electronic detection, Types of photodiodes, Structures of photodetectors and optical receivers, Operation of Optical Amplifiers, Optical modulators and demodulators.  CLO5: Optical Communication system design for single wavelength and multi wavelength systems. Design of fiber optic sensors, Extrinsic and Intrinsic Sensors Distinct Types of Sensors and their Industrial Applications

title: Digital Image Processing
description_handout: This is the first course on digital image processing. It begins with an introduction to the fundamentals of digital images and discusses the various discrete transformations, which are extensively used in image processing. It then goes on to discuss the different image processing techniques such as image enhancement, automatic image classification, and recognition.
scope_objective: Digital Image Processing (DIP) involves the use of computer algorithms to perform operations on digital images to improve their quality, extract useful information, or prepare them for further analysis. The main objectives of DIP include enhancing image details for better visual interpretation, restoring corrupted images, compressing image data for efficient storage and transmission, and analyzing images for applications like medical diagnosis, satellite imaging, and object recognition. Its scope spans various fields such as healthcare, agriculture, surveillance, remote sensing, and artificial intelligence, making it a vital tool in both scientific research and everyday technology. 3. title: Semiconductor Fabrication Technology
description_handout: The course describes both theoretical and practical aspects of semiconductor fabrication technology. This course will take you on the journey of silica sand to silicon integrated circuit (IC), i.e., “making a chip”. Converting a single crystal of silicon into an IC requires several fabrication steps, such as epitaxy, oxidation, chemical vapor deposition, metallization, ion implantation, diffusion, etching, and lithography. All these process steps will be discussed. Further, the modeling of each processing step would be discussed in detail.
scope_objective: This course is designed to provide an introduction to the basic principles of semiconductor fabrication and to discuss various processing technologies. Fabrication of semiconductor chips is a joint venture by electrical engineers, chemical engineers, materials scientists, and physicists. This interdisciplinary course builds bridges across various disciplines. 3. Textbooks: TB: J. Plummer, M. D. Deal, and P. B. Griffin, Silicon VLSI Technology: Fundamentals, Practice and Modeling, Pearson Education. 4. Reference Books: R1: S. M. Sze, VLSI Technology, TATA McGraw-Hill. R2: S.A. Campbell, The Science and Engineering of Microelectronic Fabrication, Oxford. 5. Course Plan: Section Lecture # Topic Brief Reference I 1 - 2 Introduction to the Course A brief overview of the course and history, status, and future direction of IC fabrication. Ch. 1 TB II 3-5 Semiconductor Fabrication: Complete Process Flow Fundamentals, Requirements, Perspectives, and Prospects Ch. 2 TB III 6- 8 Crystal structures, defects, directions, planes Structural properties of Silicon Ch. 3, TB IV 9-11 Bulk single crystal growth to Wafer preparation, dopant distribution To learn the art of wafer preparation and some of the basic properties of these wafers. Ch. 6, TB VII 17-21 Lithography Different lithography techniques (Photolithography, Electron beam, X-ray, etc.), learn how to print the patterns on the wafer using optical exposure systems. Basics of Optical Systems Ch. 5, TB VIII 22-25 Dopant Diffusion (Doping process) Understand the doping concept by the diffusion method. Ch. 7, TB IX 26-29 Ion Implantation (Doping process) Understand the doping concept by the Ion Implantation method Ch. 8, TB X 30 Annealing of damages and masking during implantation How annealing helps recover damage, and how the thickness of the masking layer improves masking efficiency. Learning outcome of the course: Students will understand the fundamental principles of semiconductor materials, crystal growth techniques, and wafer preparation used in IC fabrication. They will be able to describe and compare major semiconductor fabrication processes, including oxidation, diffusion, ion implantation, lithography, etching, and thin-film deposition. Students will be able to apply cleanroom practices, safety protocols, and contamination control methods relevant to semiconductor manufacturing. Finally, they will be able to correlate fabrication steps with the electrical characteristics of semiconductor devices. title: Satellite Communications
description_handout: Review of microwave communications and LOS systems; the various satellite orbits like GEO, MEO, LEO; the satellite link analysis and design; the communication transponder system like INSAT, INELSAT etc; the earth segment and earth station engineering; the transmission of analog and digital signals through satellite and various modulation techniques employed; the multiple access techniques like FDMA, TDMA, CDMA, DAMA, etc; the INSAT program; salient features of INSAT – systems and services offered; satellite services offered by INTELSAT, INMARSAT and future satellites like IRIDIUM etc; future trends in satellite communications.
scope_objective: s of the Course: This course introduces satellite communication systems, combining radio-wave propagation, or- bital mechanics, satellite subsystems, modulation, and coding. Satellite link analysis and link- budget design form the core, applied hands-on component of the course, reinforced through in-class problem-solving sessions and selected simulation tasks. Students then study fixed- assignment multiple-access techniques (FDMA/TDMA/CDMA) and briefly explore random-access schemes, followed by applications in VSAT, mobile satellite, and GPS/DGPS. By the end of the course, students will be able to analyze satellite communication systems, able to design satellite links and evaluate their performance, develop and defend a link-budget analysis, and determine satellite position/coverage for a given orbit.
learning_outcomes: Some of the key learning outcomes are stated below. CLO1. Explain the fundamental concepts, historical evolution, segments, and subsystems of satellite communication systems. CLO2. Analyze radio-wave propagation effects and orbital mechanics (LEO/MEO/GEO) and their influence on system and link design. CLO3. Design and evaluate satellite RF uplink/downlink link budgets, including noise and intermodulation considerations, using hand calculations and simulation tools. 1 CLO4. Apply and compare digital modulation, coding, and multiple-access techniques (FDMA/TDMA/CDMA) for satellite systems. CLO5. Identify and evaluate VSAT, mobile satellite links, understand GPS/GNSS system ar- chitectures and their performance limitations CLO6. To understand, appreciate and analyze recent trends in satellite communications such as next generation non-terrestrial network/space-air-ground integrated network.

title: RF AND MICROWAVE CIRCUIT DESIGN
description_handout: Introduction to radio frequency engineering; advantages; various frequency bands; applications; Microwave passive components and high frequency modeling; Microwave network analysis: scattering parameters and Signal flow graph; vector network analyzer-dynamic range and IF bandwidth; Transmission lines; microstrip lines; impedance matching techniques-transmission line based and lumped circuit approach and layout generation. Power dividers and couplers, RF filter design; Filter scaling and transformation; Filter implementation using microstrip lines and lumped components; Amplifier design; noise, harmonic distortion, and intercept point analysis, amplifier design for gain and noise figure; oscillator design, one-port and two- port oscillator design, phase noise of oscillator, introduction to EMI and EMC, recent trends.

title: Real-Time Embedded Systems
description_handout: This course will introduce the general concepts related to real-time systems from introduction, to designing a real-time system (RTS). It will deal will a reference model of an RTS which can be applied to any RTS. It will also teach the scheduling algorithms, resource management techniques, issues in hardware and software design, Real-Time Operating System (RTOS), advanced concepts of software design and validation techniques for these systems. 1. Scope and Objectives: Real-time systems are those systems that require a deterministic upper time-bound for the execution of a job. With the proliferation of the embedded system, which is the heart of items ranging from common every day appliances to life-critical systems, a great deal of work has gone into the characterization and design issues of Real-time systems. The course focuses on the basics of Hardware design, advanced concepts of software design and validation techniques for these systems. Specifically we discuss the Operating system, Scheduling, Software techniques, Run-time environment, failure management algorithms, Reliability and Fault-tolerance of real-time systems etc. 2. Text Book: 1. Liu Jane W. S.: Real-Time Systems, Pearson Education, India 2003. 3. Reference Books: 1. Krishna C.M. & Shin K.G.: Real-Time Systems, McGraw-Hill 1997 2. Raj Kamal, Embedded Systems Architecture, programming and Design, Tata McGraw Hill 5. IEEE or related journal papers on some of the course topics. title: Signal Theory and Optimization
description_handout: Probability theory and random variables; joint, conditional, and marginal distributions; functions of random variables; moments, expectation, and statistical inequalities; introduction to random processes; stationarity, autocorrelation, ergodicity, and power spectral density; basic concepts of linear algebra: vector spaces, inner product spaces, linear operators and transformations, spectral decomposition; matrix factorizations including SVD, LU, and QR; positive definite matrices; orthogonal projections in Hilbert spaces; introduction to optimization: convex sets and convex functions; unconstrained and constrained optimization; Lagrange multipliers, Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions, duality, and numerical optimization techniques.
scope_objective: s: The instructor presents the content of the course "Signal Theory and Optimization" in five modules. The first module (module-0) comprises preliminaries covering signals classification, definitions, properties, limitations, and applications. The subsequent module (module-1) consists of axiomatic probability theory and random variables, joint, conditional, and marginal distributions of random variables, first and second order statistics, Moment generating function, characteristic function, functions of random variables, and statistical inequalities, generation and simulation of random variables. The third module (module-2) mainly introduces stochastic processes, specifications, concepts such as stationarity, autocorrelation, crosscorrelation, ergodicity, energy, and power spectral densities. The fourth module (module-3) consists of basic concepts of linear algebra, namely, vector spaces, linear independence and dependence, inner product spaces, linear operators and transformations (matrices), standard matrices (for example, positive definite and semidefinite matrices), matrix decompositions (for example, LU, and QR, Eigen BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus Instruction Division _ Please Do Not Print Unless Necessary value decomposition (EVD), singular value decomposition (SVD)) and their uses, Hilbert spaces and norms, projections, inequalities, orthogonalization. The fifth and final module (module-4) consists of an introduction to optimization: convex sets and convex functions; unconstrained and constrained optimization, Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions, duality, and optimization techniques such as Lagrange multipliers, numerical optimization (non-convex) techniques. The objectives of the foundational course are to lay strong foundations for i) probability and random signals and related theory, ii) linear algebra, matrices iii) optimization techniques and their uses in communications and signal processing. 3. Course Outcomes: At the end of the course Signal theory and optimization, students learn useful mathematical and probability concepts, tools (transforms, matrices, optimization), and techniques to model several phenomena that occur in communication systems and networks, and analyze and design them better. Specifically, they learn the significance of signal theory, fundamental laws of probability, finding moments of random variables, modeling using random variables, and random processes and their applications. Furthermore, generation and simulation of random variables using software tools like MATLAB/Python are also one of the essential practical outcomes of this course. In addition to strong random signal theory foundations, students learn useful techniques of linear algebra and matrices, optimization, which are useful in understanding and analyzing machine learning-aided next generation communication networks.

title: Modelling and Analysis of Electrical Machines
description_handout: Review of Rotating Electrical Machines, Element of Generalized Theory of Rotating Electrical Machines, Linear transformation and Reference-frame Theory, DC Machines, Three-phase Synchronous Machines, Three-phase Induction Machines, Special Machines, Introduction to motor parameters estimation and model generation using MATLAB
scope_objective: The objective of the course is to comprehend and analyse the steady-state, transient and dynamic behaviour of electrical machines using mathematical models, and also to familiarize the students about advanced modelling. The course will develop students’ understanding on modelling of electrical machines from conventional methods to advanced methods through generalized theory of electrical machines. Furthermore, the students will appreciate the scope and applicability of course with the help of hands-on practice using simulation tools and hardware setup, encouraging and strengthening their ability to approach and investigate important challenges of automation and e-mobility associated to research interests of industries and academia, for example, digital-twin, model predictive modelling and control, fault analysis, predictive maintenance, and advanced control. The prerequisite of this course is, to have a basic understanding of electrical circuits, electrical machines and control systems; mainly modelling of physical systems.
learning_outcomes: Students will be able to, a. Develop the model of electrical machines using actual machine variables and parameters. b. Develop generalized theory (unified approach) based model of electrical machines. c. Apply different transformations using reference frame theory to simplify machine modelling. d. Develop the block-diagram of electrical machines using their dynamic model. e. Develop and visualize machine-model using software such as MATLAB-Simulink, and use the model for analysis and control-loop design for hardware testing and implementation using real-time simulators such as TMS320F28379d.

title: Fundamentals of Optoelectronics
description_handout: This course introduces the principles, design, and applications of optoelectronic devices. The course begins with a description of the interaction of light with semiconductor materials in a p-n junction configuration. This includes the phenomena of absorption, electroluminescence, and stimulated emission. The distinction between direct and indirect semiconductor materials is noted. Basic devices are then described: photodiodes, light-emitting diodes (LEDs), semiconductor optical amplifiers, and laser diodes. Array detectors, including complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) and charge-coupled devices (CCD) arrays, and array LEDs are then introduced. Basic specifications and applications of each of these devices are described, including solar cells, imaging with array detectors, and LED displays. II. Textbooks and References: TB1: Optoelectronics and Photonics: Principles and Practices (2nd Edition) by S.O. Kasap. R1: Solid State Electronic Devices by Ben Streetman & Sanjay Banerjee. R2: Semiconductor Optoelectronic Devices by Pallab Bhattacharya. III. Course Objectives: • Understand the fundamental solid-state physics governing light-matter interactions in semiconductor materials. • Analyze the operation, design parameters, and performance metrics of modern optoelectronic emitters (LEDs, Lasers) and detectors (Photodiodes, Solar Cells). • Evaluate the engineering principles behind advanced display architectures, flexible electronics, and matrix-based image sensors. • Apply theoretical knowledge through hands-on computational modeling and simulation of optoelectronic device behavior. BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/AGSR Division _ Please Do Not Print Unless Necessary IV. Course Contents SI. No. Module Topic Outcome(s) 1 Physics of semiconductors (6 hours) Review of semiconductor concepts, carrier transport, and energy bands. Direct vs. Indirect bandgap semiconductors E-k diagrams). P-n junction principles, heterojunctions, and energy band diagrams under bias. Map energy band diagrams for direct and indirect bandgap semiconductors using E-k diagrams to predict radiative efficiency. 2. Light-Emitting Diodes (LEDs) (8 hours) Core principles of electroluminescence, efficiencies, and output spectrum. High-intensity quantum well LEDs and modern materials. White LEDs, phosphors, and driver electronics, Organic LEDs (OLEDs), Quantum Dot LEDs (QLEDs) Explain the role of quantum wells and modern semiconductor materials in high-brightness LED configurations. Evaluate the operating mechanisms of phosphor-converted white LEDs, OLEDs, and QLEDs for display and lighting applications. 3 Laser Diodes & Optical Amplifiers (6 hours) Laser oscillations: threshold gain coefficient and gain bandwidth. Steady-state semiconductor rate equations. Single-frequency lasers and Vertical Cavity Surface Emitting Lasers (VCSELs). Semiconductor Optical Amplifiers (SOAs). Formulate and solve steady-state rate equations to determine photon and carrier densities. Critique the design and structural benefits of single- frequency lasers, VCSELs, and Semiconductor Optical Amplifiers (SOAs). 4 Flexible substrates and display devices (6 hours) Flexible silicon and SoI wafers, Techniques for fabricating flexible Si- substrates, Thin Film Transistors (TFTs), TFT-LCD Displays Identify engineering constraints and candidate materials for flexible, stretchable, and wearable substrates. Assess the mechanical and electrical reliability of optoelectronic materials under mechanical stress. 5 Photodetectors & Photovoltaics (6 hours) Principles of the p-n junction, p-i-n, and Avalanche Photodiodes (APDs). Schottky junction and photoconductive detectors. Photovoltaic devices and solar cell efficiencies. Noise parameters in photodetection. Assess noise contributions (shot noise, thermal noise) to determine the Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) and Noise Equivalent Power (NEP) of a detector. Analyze the photovoltaic effect and extraction efficiency parameters that dictate solar cell performance. Active Matrix Arrays and Complementary Metal-Oxide- Semiconductor (CMOS) image sensors. description: Soft Switching Converter 3 Environmental Engineering Core Courses
description_handout: This course covers analysis of series and parallel resonant converters, load dependent properties of resonant converters with ZVS/ZCS boundary. Operation of these converters for Zero-current Switching and Zero-Voltage switching is discussed in detail. The concept of resonance is extended to analyze the soft switching mechanism of semiconductor devices Diode, MOSFET and IGBT to reduce the switching loss and possible mitigation of EMI. The zero-current- switching and the zero-voltage-switching quasi resonant switch cell is discussed for full bridge converter. Design example of zero-current-switching and zero-voltage switching class E-inverter is also covered in this course.

title: Power Quality
description_handout: This ME course is meant for equipping students with knowledge of prevalent power quality issues in the modern power distribution system, their causes and classifications covering voltage and current based power quality problems such as sag, swell, unbalance, harmonics and poor power factor. Various standards on power quality and their monitoring techniques are also covered. The course also majorly deals with power quality compensation techniques including both passive and active compensation, their design, analysis and modeling. The control techniques for active power compensators and active filters are also discussed. The lab component is designed to enrich students’ knowledge of power quality with practical hands on and simulation exercises.
scope_objective: A ME course focusing on electric power quality typically covers the analysis, mitigation, and improvement of power quality issues, including voltage variations, harmonics, and other disturbances, preparing graduates for careers in power utilities and industries. The objectives of this course are designed to help students to: a. Understand various power quality issues and their impact. b. Learn about power and power factor in single-phase and three-phase systems. c. Study conventional and active compensation techniques for power factor correction and load voltage regulation d. Gain knowledge of active filter techniques for harmonics elimination. e. Understand power quality improvement in power supplies, drive systems, and renewable energy systems. Learning outcomes of the course have been incorporated in the course plan on next page. 3. Text Books: a. T1: B. Singh, A. Chandra, K.A. title: NANO-ELECTRONICS AND NANO-PHOTONICS TECHNOLOGY
description_handout: Semiconductor fundamentals for Nanotechnology, Introduction to low dimensional nano-structures and Quantum Mechanics ,Scaling and nanoelectronics, Nano electronic device materials and circuits, Strain engineering and high speed quantum electronic devices, Optical properties of nano-structures, Linear and non linear effects of optical materials and structures, Nano photonic devices, Electronic Devices based on nano structures in evolution of Silicon Base Devices, Integrated photo electronic devices and systems and its applications, New Trends in Nano devices and technology.
scope_objective: This course provides a blend of electronic and photonic fundamentals and their applications to the fast moving technology involved in high-speed electronics, optical electronics and optical communication systems in terms of nano structures. Electronics and Photonics are becoming increasingly important as limitations of speed, size and bandwidth affect many electronic devices and systems. Moreover, integration of electronics and photonics becomes an important issue related to modern technical aspects like optical interconnects, integrated optical circuits etc. Here the fundamentals of semiconductors, quantum structures and transport properties related to quantum structures will be first discussed. That will be followed by electronic and optical properties and details of strain engineering. Finally all these basic concepts will be applied in understanding modern and photonic and electronic devices useful for engineering applications. Students will also be encouraged to learn hands-on-training in analysis/ simulation of some electronic-photonic devices using MATLAB/ SILVACO TCAD software. 3. Text Books: T1: “Modern V L S I Devices” Yuan Taur and Tak H Ning, Cambridge University Press, Fifth South Asia Edition 2017Reprinted 2020. T2: “Physics of Photonic Devices”, S. L. Chuang, Wiley Series in Pure and Applied Optics, 2009. 4. Reference Books: R1: “Solid State Electronic Devices”, Streetman and Banerjee, PHI Learning Ltd., 2009. R2: “Nanophotonics”, Paras N Prasad, Wiley Interscience,2004.. R3: “Semiconductor Devices Physics and Technology”, S. M. Sze, John Wiley and Sons, INC Second Edition. 5. title: Advanced Wireless Communications
description_handout: Evolution of wireless cellular technologies to 5G and beyond, review of matrix and signal theory for communication applications, introduction to stochastic geometry for performance analysis of wireless networks, D2D communications- modeling and analysis, cooperative communications-buffer-aided relaying and performance analysis, modulation and multiple access techniques-NOMA, OTFS, OAM. Introduction to potential technologies for beyond 5G/6G communications: IRS, molecular communications, and AI in wireless communications.
scope_objective: a) This course aims to introduce the students to the advances in wireless communications and expose them to the research options available for applications in the real-world implementation of the next- generation wireless networks. b) The course will introduce the students to current trends in the wireless industry with a specific focus on the 5G and beyond 5G communication networks. c) The course aims to equip students with tools for designing the engineering aspects of wireless communications. d) New techniques envisaged to be a part of the next-generation wireless networks, like D2D communications, NOMA, OTFS, and stochastic geometry applied to wireless communications, to name a few, will be covered to make the student industry and research-ready.
learning_outcomes: a) Evaluate the trade-offs in system design parameters (e.g., power, bandwidth, latency, mobility) in the context of modern wireless networks. b) Design and evaluate advanced modulation, coding, and diversity techniques for improving link reliability and spectral efficiency in various wireless environments. c) Analyze complex wireless channel models (e.g., time-varying fading, spatially correlated MIMO channels) and assess their implications on communication system performance.

title: Hardware and Software Codesign
description: Hardware Software Co-Design 4 ELECTRONICS AND COMMUNICATION ENGINEERING CORE COURSES L P U
scope_objective: This course deals with the system-level design of embedded systems comprised of both hardware and software. It investigates topics ranging from system modeling to hardware-software implementation. This course also teaches analysis and optimization processes for supporting algorithmic and architectural design decisions. It also helps the student gain design experience through different case studies. The course emphasizes a top-down design methodology driven by bottom-up constraints. The topics covered will include co-design of hardware and software involving key aspects like partitioning, mapping and optimization. 2. Course Learning Objectives (CLOs) are as follows a. Analyze embedded system requirements and develop suitable hardware–software co-design solutions by applying system-level modeling, partitioning, and synthesis techniques. b. Evaluate and optimize hardware–software architectures using partitioning algorithms, mapping strategies, and performance estimation methods to satisfy design constraints such as speed, area, power, and cost. c. Design and implement hardware–software co-designed embedded applications using contemporary design methodologies and FPGA-based platforms to address real-world engineering problems. 2. Introduction of BJTs, Introduction to operational amplifiers and applications. description_handout: Feedback control is a central aiding tool in a wide range of engineering and even some non-engineering applications. This is a second UG level course on the subject, which takes the so- called Modern approach as opposed to the Classical approach taken in the previous compulsory course on the subject. This course discusses the basic analytical and design techniques using the concept of state variables; the techniques of optimal control and estimation theory and an introductory level treatment of nonlinear systems. The underlying mathematical concepts of these techniques will be emphasized and also some flavor of applications will be given through examples, exercises and take home assignments drawn from various engineering domains.

title: Hydraulic and Fluid Mechanics
description_handout: Dimensions, units, dimensionless ratios, hydraulic similarity and the testing of models, Continuity and Bernoulli's equations, fluid properties, Reynolds experiment, laminar and turbulent flow in pipes, major and minor losses in flow through pipes, Flow in pipelines between reservoirs, open channel flow, Pumps, flow and velocity measurement devices.
scope_objective: This course introduces the foundational principles of fluid mechanics and their practical applications in hydraulic systems used in water and wastewater treatment plants and sewerage networks. It covers the behavior of fluids in motion and at rest, emphasizing both theoretical frameworks and engineering applications. Topics include flow regimes, pressure losses, open channel flow, pump performance, and hydraulic modeling. Students will develop analytical skills to solve real-world fluid flow problems and design efficient hydraulic systems.
learning_outcomes: (CLOs): Upon the completion of this course, students will be able to perform the following: 1. Fundamentals of Fluid Mechanics: Understand physical dimensions, units, and dimensionless analysis using Rayleigh and Buckingham π methods; Grasp the concept of hydraulic similarity and model testing 2. Fluid Properties and Flow Regimes: Analyze dynamic and kinematic viscosity; Distinguish between laminar and turbulent flow using Reynolds experiment and Reynolds number. 3. Flow in Pipes: Apply Poiseuille’s law for laminar flow pressure drop; Analyze velocity profiles and pressure loss in laminar and turbulent pipe flow; Use Moody diagram and Darcy’s law to determine friction factors. 4. Complex Pipe Flow Systems: Evaluate flow in non-horizontal and variable diameter pipes; Estimate minor losses due to expansions, contractions, and fittings. 5. Pipeline Flow Between Reservoirs: Assess head losses and solve problems involving series and parallel pipelines. 6. Open Channel Flow: Define hydraulic parameters like wetted perimeter and hydraulic mean depth; Use Chezy’s and Manning’s equations to calculate discharge and flow depth. BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 2 7. Pumps and Hydraulic Machinery: Understand types of rotodynamic pumps and their applications; Analyze pump performance, derive affinity laws, and interpret characteristic curves; Evaluate system losses and pump operation in series and parallel configurations.

title: Environmental Chemistry and Environmental Biotechnology
description_handout: The course will provide an overview of the different aspects of the environment and the chemistry integrally involved in it. Broad description of the constituents of the environment namely the hydrosphere, the atmosphere, the geosphere and the anthrosphere (tangible human interaction space) will be provided with emphasis on the chemical interactions involved in each of them in their respective formation, balanced existence, deterioration (pollution and degradation/ depletion) and remediation processes etc. The course will be essential to gaining an understanding of our environment and the chemistry behind the processes occurring within, with relevance to the current industrialized ecology. The course will also provide an overview of environmental biotechnology, emphasising biotechnological tools, such as microbial, genetic, and biochemical mechanisms involved in ecosystem function, pollution, and remediation. The course will cover sustainable biotechnological interventions in waste treatment, bioenergy production, and pollution control. It is designed to build a foundational understanding of how biotechnology integrates with environmental systems, enabling learners to address environmental degradation in the context of modern industrialized ecology. title: [Fundamentals of Finance and Accounting]
description_handout: Accounting is the language of business. Through this language, the business (i.e. the Company) not only maintain the records of transactions it undertakes during the course of its existence but also communicates with the outside world by publishing various financial reports that summarize transactions undertaken by the company. Therefore, it is important to note here that this course entails two important and interrelated aspects, i.e., a. Recording transactions, and b. Preparing financial statements such as balance sheet, income statement, etc. Since b. follows a., it is important to learn the recording of transactions first to learn preparing financial statements. The course will introduce you to the following key concepts: introduction, standards and basic rules of accounting, double-entry accounting system, identifying and recoding transactions, preparing trial balance, dealing with incomplete transactions, preparing the balance sheet, types of ownership, credibility and role of auditing, measuring income, adjustments to the accounts, preparing the statement of cash flows, recording sales revenue, reporting inventories and cost of goods sold, recording capital assets, liabilities and interest, stockholders' equity and valuation of financial assets. This course is specifically designed to meet the educational needs of second year Economics students and students pursing Finance minor program. To complete the program requirement, the students from Economics and Finance background require a basic understanding on accounting principles and financial statement analysis. This course serves that purpose, and it is prerequisite to other advanced courses that students from (MSc) Economics and Finance (minor) undertake in the subsequent semesters. Hence, being elementary in nature this course has got its relevance and importance. Besides, a few students also take this course as an elective to pursue their academic interests in the field of finance.
scope_objective: The scope of this course largely encapsulates an introduction to the reporting system used by businesses to record and convey financial information to investors, analysts, and regulators. This reporting system is referred to as financial accounting. The key learning objectives that this course accomplishes enables participants in learning: a. how companies identify and record transactions that have a financial impact and are critical to day-to-day functioning of the company. b. how using a systematic procedure, the recorded transactions are summarized into meaningful and standardized reports (financial statements) such as the balance sheet, statement of income etc. c. the key components that form part of these financial statements. d. how these financial statements are analyzed and what information do they convey about the financial well-being and prospects about the company.
learning_outcomes: Students who complete this course would be able to a. Understand the accounting methods for recording the business transactions. b. Evaluate various financial concepts and preparation of financial statements-balance sheet, income statement, and cash flow statement. c. Identify the financial position and performance of the companies. d. Make better economic decisions while undertaking investments in financial assets.

title: Security Analysis and Portfolio Management
description_handout: Security Analysis and Portfolio Management addresses two connected problems: what a financial asset is worth, and how much of it a particular investor should hold. The first half of the course develops valuation. Students examine the characteristics and risk-return profiles of the major asset classes – equity, fixed income, and derivatives – and the fundamental, quantitative and technical techniques used to estimate intrinsic worth. Analysis of economy, industry, and stock specific fundamentals are carried out for valuing stocks. Hence, asset valuation forms a major component of this course. Another important aspect of the course is on modern portfolio concepts, where the criterion changes: a holding is no longer judged on its own merits but by its contribution to the risk and return of the whole. This covers modern portfolio theory, diversification and correlation, asset allocation, and the construction of portfolios aligned to a stated investor's objectives, constraints and risk tolerance.
scope_objective: The objectives of the course are to provide an introduction to: • Types of financial securities and their salient characteristics. • Investment philosophy and its role in asset allocation and long-term personal finance management. • Modern portfolio theories and their applications in portfolio design and evaluation. • Equity and debt valuation using fundamental analysis and relative valuation techniques. • Technical analysis. • Financial derivative contracts and their applications.
learning_outcomes: • Distinguish the major classes of financial securities — equity, fixed income, derivatives and alternatives — by their claim structure, risk-return profile and role within a portfolio. • Value individual securities using techniques appropriate to the instrument, including discounted cash flow and relative valuation for equity and yield-based measures for fixed income, and state the assumptions on which each valuation rests. • Measure and decompose investment risk, separating systematic from unsystematic components, and evaluate investments on a risk-adjusted basis rather than on raw return. • Construct a diversified portfolio using correlation and modern portfolio theory, and justify the resulting asset allocation against a specified investor's objectives, time horizon and risk tolerance. • Apply derivative instruments to hedge or modify portfolio exposure, and explain the payoff profile and risk of each strategy employed. • Assess portfolio performance using risk-adjusted measures and attribution analysis, and determine when a portfolio requires rebalancing as market conditions change. 4. title: Financial Management
description_handout: Financial Management is a foundation course offered to finance minor students and as a disciplinary and open elective. The Financial Management course has several practical applications to financial decision-making and encompasses topics having a varying degree of complexity. It is usually taught at the graduate level such as MS/MBA or at the PhD. This course ECON/FIN F 315 is designed to suit the level of academic experience and exposure in finance for undergraduate students having just taken a first course on Fundamentals of Finance and Accounting. The course’s learning objectives focus on the primary financial decisions undertaken by the financial manager of an organisation to achieve the principal objective of the firm. In an increasingly competitive and globally integrated world marked by all-pervasive technological advancements, the roles and responsibilities of financial managers are expanding in response to the explosion in the number of firms striving for success. On the one hand, corporations are hungry to fulfil their financing needs, so on the other are the investors, looking for the best return on the buck they invest. The wide range of investment avenues available to investors explains the extent of innovations happening in the financial markets worldwide. However, with uncontrolled growth comes the risk of an uncontrolled collapse and the financial crisis of 2008 is a classic case of fault lines in the financial markets. To retain the confidence and faith of investors and forge robust and sustainable growth, the firms must impress suppliers of capital (investors) with adequate rewards to compensate them for the risks they undertake. More importantly, the modern viewpoint of the roles and responsibilities of the board of directors and the C-suite managers has departed from the traditional profitability perspective to the wealth maximisation principle. The firm must protect and strengthen the rights of its stakeholders, such as employees, suppliers, customers, the environment, investors, etc. Hence, the wealth maximisation principle influences the decisions firms make about their financing policy, investment policy, and dividend distribution policy. The role of the financial manager - which is central to the decision-making concerning finances (money, capital, investment etc.) – plays a critical role in ensuring seamless day-to-day operations, maintaining profitability and sustaining reliable long-term performance along with adherence to the company’s ESG (sustainability) policies. BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 2

The structure of the course enables students to: a. Develop an understanding about the variety of financial instruments and their valuations, b. Primarily, the course objectives hover around key decisions made by financial managers, including financing, investing, capital structure, and shareholder rewarding policies. The contents of this course enable the participants to appreciate the interdependencies between these decisions and their impact on the firm's survivability. title: Financial Risk Analytics and Management
description: Financial Risk Analytics and Management 3 0 3 MATH F212 Optimization 3 0 3 MATH F242 Operations Research 3 0 3 MATH F424 Applied Stochastic Process 3 1 4 MATHEMATICS CORE COURSES L P U MATH F212 Optimization 3 0 3 MATH F213 Discrete Mathematics 3 0 3 MATH F214 Elementary Real Analysis 3 0 3 MATH F215 Algebra I 3 0 3 MATH F241 Mathematical Methods 3 0 3 MATH F242 Operations Research 3 0 3 MATH F243 Graphs and Networks 3 0 3 MATH F244 Measure & Integration 3 0 3 MATH F311 Introduction to Topology 3 0 3 MATH F312 Ordinary Differential Equations 3 0 3 MATH F313 Numerical Analysis 3 0 3 MATH F341 Introduction to Functional Analysis 3 0 3 MATH F342 Differential Geometry 3 0 3 MATH F343 Partial Differential Equations 3 0 3 DISCIPLINE ELECTIVE COURSES
description_handout: This course focuses on the concept of financial risk in modern finance. Despite market volatility and irrational exuberance, effective risk quantification and management remain crucial. Regulators have imposed safeguards to curb excessive risk-taking by financial institutions. As a result, risk management has become a core function in the finance industry. The course is designed to prepare students for the growing demand in financial risk management roles. Financial risk (which includes interest rate risk, credit risk, foreign exchange risk and portfolio risk), Application of Asset price Theory, CAPM and Modern Portfolio Theory, Multifactor models of risk and return, Capital adequacy, BASEL Norms; Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review, Basel Committee on Banking Supervision guidelines, Value at Risk (VaR), VaR from regulator perspective, Responsive VaR Model, Addressing VaR weakness, Back testing Concepts - Checking the Strength of VaR Model, Issues with the Standard VaR models, Risk Not in VaR (RNIV) to VaR migration of risk, Volatility Clustering, Quantifying and Modeling volatilities, Hedging techniques, Options Greeks, Managing Risk with Derivatives.
scope_objective: The three core focus areas dealt with in this course are (i) Risk Identification, (ii) Risk Measurement, and (iii) Risk Management, in the context of modern-day finance. The scope and objective of the course is to enable students learn essentials of financial risk management. The three core focus areas along with the functions and workings of financial institutions encompass the entire coverage of this course. To meet the stated objective of the course, a detailed course plan is designed which students can refer in section 6 of this document.
learning_outcomes: a. Understand and classify financial risks such as interest rate risk, credit risk, foreign exchange risk, and portfolio risk in modern financial markets. b. Analyze and implement risk measurement tools such as Value at Risk (VaR), Responsive VaR, and backtesting techniques. c. Interpret and evaluate regulatory frameworks like Basel norms and its guidelines for capital adequacy and systemic risk control. d. Develop risk mitigation strategies using derivatives, including hedging techniques and options Greeks, to manage exposure effectively. BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 2

title: Modern Political Concepts
description_handout:  Concepts of State, Nation, Rights and Duties, Civil Society, Democracy, Citizenship and Justice.  Ideologies of Modern Politics: Social Contractualism, Liberalism, Socialism, Communism, Maoism, Anarchism, Secularism.  Selected Readings from key texts of leading thinkers in the History of Modern Western Political Philosophy including Machiavelli’s Prince, Hobbes’ Leviathan, Locke’s Second Treatise of government, Rousseau’s Discourse on the origin of inequality, Marx and Engels’ Communist Manifesto.
scope_objective: This Course introduces certain select concepts of Politics that are relevant to the Modern/ Contemporary period. The course helps in unravelling the contexts from which these concepts emerged through a study of ideologies as well as first-hand reading of key texts in the history of political thought. This course prepares the students to be informed active citizens. The design and its execution emphasize the comprehension of political thinking, the application of communication and analytical skills, and the understanding of human diversity. Modern political concepts enhance the knowledge of the political science discipline by offering the conceptual vocabulary along with various methods of inquiry. This course not only increases students’ knowledge of the history of classical and modern political thought but also enlightens them with the fundamental values and ethical issues contested in politics over time. This course informs about the alternative moral and ethical frameworks for (re)interpreting and evaluating contemporary political discourses. Scope: As an introductory course in Politics, this is based on lectures and reading texts. However, the students are encouraged to move beyond the textbook and familiarize with the research studies by eminent scholars. This course encourages to use critical thinking and evidence to understand and evaluate rival theories and interpretations. Accordingly, Students are expected to participate in the classroom discussions as well as initiate and moderate discussions on political issues that may have captivated their interest. This practice enables students to develop a critical understanding of various political discourses and equip them to address political theories and questions of political life and BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 2 values. Most significantly, this Course facilitates students’ engagement with various political debates of contemporary India and the world. 3. title: Environment, Development and Climate Change (EDCC)
description_handout: This course focuses on the concepts of environment, development, and climate change in the contemporary world. The nature and causes of environmental problems in developing and developed countries will be explored. Attention is given to both the causes and solutions of environmental problems and the role of state and non-state actors interacting at local, national and global scales. The goal of this course is for the learners to appreciate the people-environment relations and to understand the anthropocentric dynamics of development and climate change.
scope_objective: The objective of the course is to make the students aware of the debates and issues relating to sustainable development and climate change, so as to sufficiently challenge them to come up with practical solutions. The course covers theory and practice at the global and local levels and examines the contemporary policy and practice regarding environment, development and climate change. 3. Text Books: Hempel, C. Lamont (1998), Environmental Governance: The Global Challenge, Affiliated East West Press Pvt Ltd, New Delhi. (Reading material will be given in pdf format). 4. Reference Books: Humphrey R. Craig, Tammy L. Lewis and Frederick H. Buttel (2002), Environment, Energy, and Society. Wadsworth Group, USA. 5. title: Development Theories
description_handout: This course focuses on the concept of development, development theories and practices in the modern world. Interplay between theory and practice and the outcome of this relationship are also explored in the syllabus. The course provides an overview of development thinking from ‘classical’ development ideas to alternative and post development theories. The course then attempts to critically review contemporary debates about development, including the link between the current world order and the Development goals of the developing countries.
scope_objective: The objective of the course is to make the students aware of the debates and issues relating to development and post development. title: Introductory Psychology
description_handout: Psychology as a science, Perception, its nature, determinants, and measurement; Biological bases of behaviour; Consciousness, Motivation, and Emotion; Learning and behaviour modification; Memory and forgetting; Thought processes, Problem- solving, and Creative thinking; Individual differences—Intelligence, Gender, Personality, Stress, and Coping; Social thought and Social Behaviour; with an emphasis on psychological assessment, behavioural data, research analytics, and evidence-based decision-making.
scope_objective: To develop a conceptual framework for understanding the human behaviour; relevance of psychology in daily life and its application in social, educational, industrial, personal and other spheres.

Apply psychological principles to analyse everyday individual and social behaviour, decision-making, learning, motivation, stress, and interpersonal interactions. CLO3. Compare and critically evaluate major psychological perspectives, theories, and empirical evidence to explain human thought, emotion, and behaviour. CLO4. Demonstrate an understanding of psychological research methods, ethical principles, basic research design, and the interpretation of psychological data. CLO5. Evaluate individual differences in perception, intelligence, personality, emotion, and behaviour using evidence-based psychological concepts and appropriate assessment approaches. CLO6. Integrate psychological knowledge to promote self-awareness, effective communication, well-being, problem-solving, and responsible decision-making in academic, professional, and social contexts.

title: Effective Public Speaking
description_handout: Goals of Public Speaking, differences and similarities between Public Speaking and General Purpose Speaking, Role of Critical Thinking in Successful Public Speaking, Speaker’s Credibility; Different phases of Nervousness, dealing with Nervousness; Non- Verbal Communication, Using Body and Voice for communication, paralinguistic features; Using visual aids; Speech Writing and delivering- Effective Introductions and Conclusions; Speeches for Special Occasions; Team Presentations; Group Discussion and Job Interviews
scope_objective: s of the Course The course aims to familiarize students with the art of public speaking and help them become confident, ethical, and effective speakers in academic and professional contexts. Students will learn to manage public speaking anxiety, construct logical arguments, organize speeches, and deliver presentations using appropriate content, structure, language, paralinguistic features, kinesics, and visual aids. The revised course also enables students to use AI-assisted tools in a limited and responsible manner for idea generation, outline development, rehearsal feedback, and slide improvement, without replacing independent thinking or original expression. Students will be encouraged to assess AI output critically for accuracy, audience suitability, bias, and ethical use. 3. Classroom Methodology The classroom methodology includes lectures, group and pair work, practical activities, guided rehearsal, and performance-based tasks. The course remains strongly practice-oriented and develops speaking skills through JAMs, extempore speaking, storytelling, parliamentary debates, group discussions, interviews, and presentation tasks. Video clips and model speeches will be used for illustration. In addition, selected classroom activities may include AI-supported speech brainstorming, AI-assisted audience adaptation tasks, and guided reflection on AI-generated feedback, while preserving the same teacher-led, practice-based format intact.

title: Introduction to Conflict Management
description_handout: Nature and dynamics of conflict; characteristics of conflict; theories of conflict; reasons and sources of conflict; value of conflict in social change; different approaches to addressing and managing conflict; conflict analysis through socio-economic class; class-based dimensions of conflict; culture and globalization perspectives; role of culture in propagating conflict; role of globalization in nation-state conflict; workplace and organizational conflict dynamics; conformity theories and conflict; power of communication; identity-based perspectives on conflict; AI, technology, and conflict resolution; algorithmic and digital dimensions of conflict; negotiation techniques; mitigation and resolution techniques; conflict management styles.
scope_objective: To develop the knowledge and professional skills necessary to facilitate resolution of conflicts. Emphasis would be laid on skills and specific techniques to resolve inter-personal, organizational and community-based conflicts. At the conclusion of the course, the student will understand the basic dynamics of conflict, most significant interventions used to manage conflict, benefits and costs of conflict, recognize his or her preferred style of conflict management and develop an understanding and appreciation of the conflict management styles of others.
learning_outcomes: • Focus and familiarity with the theories and theorists in the conflict school of thought. • Understanding of the basis of conflict in society from the lens of structures like socio- economic class. • Understanding the debates around conflict from the standpoint of gender. • Understanding conflict from the point of view of culture. • Evaluating shaping of conflict from systems of globalization and ethnocentric tensions. • Understanding conformity theories and their association with conflict. • Understanding the power of communication and the development of self. • Evaluating the power of communication with respect to conflict resolution. title: Marxian Thought
description_handout: This course aims to introduce undergraduate students to key concepts of Marxist theory. After beginning with a brief survey of the dominant narratives on inequality and exploitation, students will be introduced to the critique of bourgeois history developed by Marx and Engels, particularly in their writings on dialectical and historical materialism. In order to get a clearer view of how capitalism produces surplus value, Marx’s Labor Theory of Value and other related concepts will be read and discussed. At regular intervals, this conceptual framework will be applied to analyze cultural texts (films, advertisements, popular culture etc.) in order to develop analytical skills that surpass conventional wisdom in the study of social and economic structures.
scope_objective: Considering that Marxist theory and practice is a vast field, this course has limited itself to some of the central concepts and questions that are timely and relevant to students in these modern times [Refer to the Modules]. The primary objective is to understand the Marxist critique of capitalism, and based on that understanding, examine if it is possible to forge another kind of society, more egalitarian and without fundamentally exploitative structures. 3. Primary Text and Viewing Material: Selections from these books and viewing material will be used based on the requirements of the class. o A Reader’s Guide to Marx’s Capital - Joseph Choonara o Chapters from Yanis Varoufakis o Selected Readings from Ha-Joon Chang Film Clippings for Class Discussion: Mandi, Yashowardhan Mishra (2019); Rang de Basanti (2006); Bread and Roses, Ken Loach (2000); The Wind that Shakes the Barley, Ken Loach (2006); Nae Pasaran, Felipe Bustos Sierra (2018) 1 BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 5. title: TECHNIQUES IN SOCIAL RESEARCH
description_handout: Introduction to social research: nature, purpose, relevance, dimensions, and the research process. Quantitative, qualitative, mixed methods, and triangulation. Social theory, ideology, positivist, interpretivist, critical, feminist, and postmodern perspectives. Research ethics and research design. Measurement, reliability, validity, scales, and sampling. Experimental, survey, field, historical-comparative, and nonreactive research methods. Data collection techniques, questionnaire design, interviewing, content analysis, and secondary data analysis. Quantitative and qualitative data analysis, coding, concept formation, inferential statistics, and report writing. Research analytics and software applications: statistical analysis using SPSS and Jamovi; qualitative coding and thematic analysis using NVivo; bibliometric, scientometric, and science mapping using Graphica (e.g., knowledge network visualization and research analytics).
scope_objective: This course seeks to provide knowledge and skills relevant for conducting social science research. It will cover the entire research process from problem formulation, interpretation of data (both qualitative and quantitative) to evaluation of research study. The course will also address fundamental social science issues, reasoning and approaches that govern certain methodologies. This course would help students in acquiring skills to undertake social research studies based on primary and/or secondary data.
learning_outcomes: CLO1: Explain the philosophical foundations, paradigms, and methodological approaches of social research, and distinguish between qualitative, quantitative, and mixed-methods research designs. CLO2: Design ethically sound social research studies by formulating research problems, conducting literature reviews, selecting appropriate research designs, sampling strategies, and data collection methods. CLO3: Apply principles of measurement, reliability, validity, scale development, and sampling to develop rigorous research instruments for social science investigations. CLO4: Analyze quantitative and qualitative data using appropriate statistical and qualitative analysis techniques, including the use of software such as SPSS, Jamovi, and NVivo. CLO5: Evaluate and interpret findings from diverse research methodologies, including experimental, survey, field, historical-comparative, content analysis, and secondary data research, to draw evidence-based conclusions. CLO6: Prepare and communicate research reports that demonstrate ethical research practices, critical interpretation of findings, and effective use of research analytics and visualization tools for scholarly dissemination.

title: COPYWRITING
description_handout: Copywriting is the corner stone of ALL successful marketing. Copywriting empowers you with the ability to turn words into dollars. Effective copy can play an important role in shaping perceptions about products, services and brands. The course requires a sound knowledge of advertising communications and will explore all aspects of writing for print, radio, television and online. It extensively prepares the students to write and develop ad copy for various media while selecting tone(s), style(s) and approach(es) for ad copy.…It further equips the students to communicate the strategy and specific assignments to a team using a Creative Brief.

title: Readings from Drama
description_handout: Drama as a distinct genre; History of drama; Performance and stagecraft; Evolution of drama from a theocentric to a logocentric plane; Distinct characteristics of Western and non-Western dramas; Aristotle’s Poetics and the genre of tragedy; Bharat Muni’s Natyashastra and the idea of comedy; Adaptation of myths as Drama; Modern drama.
scope_objective: The objective of the course is to introduce students to different types and forms of drama. In doing so, this course will familiarize students with various dramatic forms spanning different geographical spaces and time, thereby helping them to have a deeper understanding of the same. It will also enable the students to connect various dramatic forms through the study of visuals, timelines, and biographical and contextual readings that allow them to delve further into the history and conventions of the time period when these dramatic works were produced.
learning_outcomes: 1) Understand and analyze various dramatic forms keeping in mind recent trends and theoretical underpinnings. 2) Apply acquired knowledge in critically appreciating dramatic texts and performances. 3) Exhibit methodological proficiency to formulate research problems and write research papers.

title: LINGUISTICS
description_handout: Linguistics as a field of study and its relationship with other disciplines; nature of language; its varieties and role in society; concepts of structure, system, unit and class; theories of linguistic analysis.
scope_objective: The objective of the course is to acquaint students with the nature and functioning of language and the role it plays in the society. The fundamental linguistic concepts will be exemplified through English. Reference to Indian languages will also be made whenever possible.
learning_outcomes: Having successfully completed all the modules of the course, students will be able to understand ✓ the properties and important characteristics of a human language ✓ the structure of a language ✓ how meaning is derived ✓the use of language in various contexts ✓ the role of human brain in language production and perception ✓ the differences in language acquisition and language learning ✓ how a language changes over a period of time ✓ the relationship between language, society and culture ✓ the types and use of sign languages

title: Cross Cultural Skills
scope_objective: 1. Providing insights into intercultural communication with powerful and deeply held views from multiple cultures. 2. Familiarizing the students how to undertake that critical self-reflection which may lead to better appreciation of the cultural diversity possessed by communities worldwide. 3. Bringing into the discussions, the experiences of intercultural communication, knowledge of the field of communication studies and mass communication, and perceptions of intercultural communication as a woman and as men from diverse ethnic, racial and cultural backgrounds. 4. Using AI to enhance cross-cultural understanding, communication, and adaptation through interactive learning and real-world simulations. Learning Outcomes After doing this course the students will be able to: 1. Understand cross-cultural communication and its different dimensions based on national cultures, as propounded by Geert Hofstede and Edward T. Hall, as well as comparative study of various theories developed later, by researchers like Trompenaars & Hampden-Turner. 2. Gain a comprehensive understanding of how and why cultural groups differ and the nuances of cross-cultural teams. 3. Develop sensitivity to cultural variations in thinking, feeling, and behaving and adapting the same for cross-cultural communication effectiveness. 4. Learn management and interpersonal skills to reckon, predict, and leverage cultural differences. 5. Develop an appreciation for the global mindset vis-à-vis Indian cultural identity. 6. Know more about diverse national cultures and countries from class projects and presentations. title: Introductory Philosophy
description_handout: An overview of major philosophical traditions from the Western and Indian worlds. The course traces the nature and purpose of philosophy from classical Greek thought through modern rationalism, empiricism, and existentialism before turning to the classical Indian schools.
scope_objective: A critical survey of major Western and Indian philosophical viewpoints, from antiquity to contemporary thought. The course aims to equip students with the tools to critically evaluate philosophical arguments and to appreciate their relevance to questions of knowledge, ethics, and selfhood in human life. 3. Course Learning Objectives Upon completion of the course students will have • An understanding of the various philosophical schools of Indian and Western traditions. • A critical and comparative grasp of the philosophical viewpoints & debates. • An ability to build theoretical constructions and extend philosophical thinking to other disciplines. • An ability to practice the habit of thinking rationally and critically in leading an ethical and meaningful life

title: Popular Literature and Culture of South Asia
description: Popular Literature and Culture of South Asia 3 0 3
description_handout: South Asia as a region; culture and its representation through literature and cinema; politics of representation, breaking the stereotypes; bringing in the marginalized voices; writings of women; identity formation; concept of majority and minority; commonality in spite of all the differences, violence, migration and dislocation.
scope_objective: The objective of the course is to introduce students to Literature and Popular Culture of South Asia. In doing so, it will familiarize students to perspectives and scenarios that differ from their own culture, thereby, helping them to have deeper understanding of other cultures. This course aims to bridge the gaps in our understanding of our neighbors and enable us to have broader perspectives.
learning_outcomes: After completing the course, the students would be able to: • Have basic concepts of South Asia as a region • Understand, analyze different productions from the region and ponder on the implications of such representations • Apply acquired knowledge in real life scenarios by acknowledging common history, heritage and culture, as well as, the diversity of the region 2. Text Book: We will pick and choose from the following texts: T-1 Katha Series: 20 Stories from South Asia. New Delhi, 2012. 1. Bitter Fruit: The Very Best of Saadat Hasan Manto: Edited and Translated by Khalid Hasan 2. Kunzang Choden's The Circle of Karma– A Novel 3. Aravind Adiga’s The White Tiger 4. Khaled Hosseini’s The Kite Runners 5. Shyam Selvadurai's Funny Boy 6. Taslima Nasrin's Lajja (The Shame) Films: We will pick and choose from the following films: 1. The Kite Runner (2007) 2. Osama (2003) 3. Slumdog Millionaire (2008) 4. Namesake (2006) 5. The Reluctant Fundamentalist (2013) Following class discussions and student input, alternative texts and movies will be added and announced in class. Relevant reference books and reading material will be circulated through Nalanda. 4. identifying the common traits, cultural nuances and literary productions of the region. 5-6 Characteristic Features of South Asian Culture, Society and Literature An Overview of Contemporary Literature Reading Material 7-12 Afghanistan Understanding Afghanistan through pop lit and films The Kite Runners: both text and film; title: Organizational Psychology
description_handout: This course is floated to provide a brief understanding of how humans behave the way they do in an organization. This will be a highly informative course for people who want to understand the psychology of organizations and gain an in-depth understanding of the management functions of an organization at an individual level. The course would be highly relevant and suitable for students who wish to pursue a master’s in business schools because it will give them a sound theoretical understanding.
scope_objective: To develop a conceptual framework for understanding organizations and their various functions from a psychological viewpoint. The course would help students understand the behavior of humans at different levels of hierarchy in an organization and the relevant issues and processes imbuing them.
learning_outcomes: (CLOs): a) Students will know about what happens after they join the world of work. b) Students get to know what all operates and how to tackle various issues at workplace. c) Students will get first hand practical information related to adjusting in their respective workplaces. 3. title: SCIENCE FICTION
description_handout: Key concepts and histories of science fiction; major theoretical frameworks in SF; utopias, dystopias, and speculative futures; science fiction in relation to technological and ecological change; feminist, postcolonial, and global interventions in SF; engagements with artificial intelligence, posthumanism, and the animal; and the reimagining of cultural and ecological futures through speculative storytelling.

title: Human Resource Development
description_handout: This course is floated to provide a brief understanding of the practical ramification (or better subfield) of human resource management and deals with the significant issues related to developing human resources with special reference to its tripartite foundations of human betterment, organizational enhancement, and societal development. The course will help clarify the subtle difference between HR Management & HR Development. This will also enable curious minds to learn more about how training programs are planned, conceived, constructed, and delivered to potential stakeholders. HRD focuses on this core idea as to how the capabilities and credentials (and ultimately productivity) of the employees can be enhanced. 2. Course Learning Outcomes (CLOs): a) To develop a conceptual framework for understanding human behavior in organizations and develop human capital (manpower) in various sectors and spheres of the world of work. b) The course would be very beneficial for students trying to understand the management functions of one very significant department of any organization. c) To get a superficial idea about various training/skill development exercises and processes encompassing such activities. 3. title: SRIMAD BHAGAVAD GITA
description_handout: This course introduces students the timeless wisdom spoken by Lord Krishna in the Bhagavad Gita and enables them to appreciate and apply those in daily life. Beginning with the fundamentals of the need to understand spirituality, the content includes science of soul, various types of yogic practices, viz., karma-yoga (action in God consciousness), jnana-yoga (philosophical research for truth), dhyana-yoga (meditative practice), astanga-yoga (eightfold yoga system) and culminates with bhakti- yoga (devotional service to God). Adopting a topical approach, the course also touches upon these subject matters: the most confidential knowledge, three modes of material nature, nature, enjoyer and the consciousness, divine and demoniac qualities, and the perfection of knowledge.
scope_objective: Meant for anyone who wants to make his or her life peaceful, blissful and perfect by aligning oneself to the principles set forth in Srimad Bhagavad Gita. The prime objectives of this course are to understand our relationship (sambhandha) with God, the process of reviving that relationship (abhidheya), and the goal of that process (prayojana). In this context, the 5 important subject matter isvara, jiva, prakriti, kala and karma are discussed in detail. 3. Course Learning Objectives Upon successful completion of the course, students will be able to: 1. Explain the principal philosophical concepts of the Srimad Bhagavad Gita, including isvara, jiva, prakriti, kala, and karma, and the relationship among them. 2. Differentiate and analyse the major paths of yoga—karma-yoga, jnana-yoga, dhyana-yoga, and bhakti-yoga—along with their purpose and practical significance. 3. Apply the teachings of the Bhagavad Gita to improve time management, stress management, concentration, emotional balance, self-discipline, decision-making, and overall well-being in academic and personal life. title: Professional Ethics
description_handout: An introduction to the ethical concepts, theories, and codes that govern professional life. The course traces the foundations of ethics and the profession, before applying this framework across business, management, education, engineering, and computing.
scope_objective: This course provides a formal acquaintance with the concepts and frameworks of ethics; recognize the codes of ethics relevant to the experience of being a professional and develops an understanding of the ethical issues relating to professions generally, and to business, management, education, engineering, and computing in particular. Through the analysis of real-time case studies, students learn to appreciate the role of moral reasoning in issues of professional life. 3. Course Learning Objectives: Upon completion of the course students will have ● An understanding of the core concepts of ethics, the profession, and professional ethics, and their specific application across business, management, education, engineering, and computing. ● A critical and comparative grasp of competing ethical theories and professional viewpoints such as rule- following versus professional judgment. ● An ability to apply ethical theories and frameworks to real, contested professional dilemmas, extending this reasoning across multiple professional domains rather than any single one. ● An ability to practice the habit of sound ethical judgment and professional responsibility in one's own future career and conduct.
