title: INTERNATIONALRELATIONS
description_handout:  Introduction-A survey of the international politics since the 20th century; Rise of Nationalism; World Wars, Emergence of IR as a discipline and the nature of its subject matter.  Key Defining Events in IR: Creation of United Nations, Cold War, Fall of USSR, September 11, China’s entry into WTO.  Key theoretical frameworks: Classical IR thinkers and their location within the existing IR canon that include realism, liberalism, constructivism, critical theory, and Asian theory of IR.  Key Agents of IR: State, Empire, International and sub-national agents, foreignpolicy.  Key Structures in IR: State-system, Eurocentrism, Post-colonialism, Globalization, Security and Global Governance  Key Institutions in IR: International Society, International Diplomacy, Great Powers, Balance of Power, War, International Law and Human Rights Regime and the Climate Change Regime.  Assorted Themes: Global Health Regime- Pandemic and IR  India’s Foreign Policy: Locating India’s space in the contemporary global order: identifying the opportunities and Challenges (India-Pakistan-China), India and China in South Asia; India and United States.
scope_objective: International Relations is the study of an international system that is constituted by territorial states who enjoy sovereignty over matters of vital interests to them. This course offers the history of the international system, its functioning, theoretical frameworks, and the nature of the changing relations between the states and non-state actors. This course offers a critical reflection and analytical understanding of key defining events and the topical issues that not only shaped but also confronted the existing international order. The course encourages students to engage in debates on the nature of international order as well as the responses to the challenges of the current international order. The course is designed to offer both the theoretical frameworks and critical reflections on the contemporary affairs. Moreover, the students will be able to make a clear perception of the relationship between the international relations as a discipline and the practice of world politics. Considerable sessions are devoted to understanding India’s role in the contemporary world too. 3. Textbooks: John Baylis, Steve Smith, and Patricia Owen (eds), The Globalization of World Politics 7th ed (OUP: 2017). The soft copy of the book would be made available. title: ECOCRITICISM
description_handout: Ecocriticism has found its place in the Indian academy only in the last twenty years or so. The course is intended to familiarize the learners with ecological, deep ecological and tinai critical principles and show them how these could be effective critical tools. The course gives a humanistic perspective on how ecology is a new paradigm in cultural and literary texts. The learners will be exposed to recent ecocritical concepts which will challenge conventional attitudes and values which are detrimental to the well- being of our planet.
scope_objective: 1. To introduce the learners to one of the major postmodern critical trends. 2. To familiarize the learners with some key ecocritical concepts. 3. Huggan, Graham, and Helen Tiffin. Postcolonial Ecocriticism: Literature, Animals, Environment. Routledge, 2010. 5. title: Academic Writing Lab
description_handout: AI-supported, process-oriented, portfolio-intensive academic writing practice; AI-assisted drafting support, editing and feedback evaluation with emphasis on originality and academic integrity; writing process stages including planning, drafting, feedback, revision and reflection; structured writing portfolio with drafts, feedback and revision evidence; idea generation with a focus on clarity of thought; paragraph construction with topic sentences; logical sequencing and paragraph linking; organizational patterns including cause–effect, comparison, problem–solution and process description; text interpretation and transformation through summarizing, paraphrasing and originality maintenance; academic vocabulary; genre-based writing: analytical paragraphs, short essays, reflective responses, structured reports, data commentaries and case studies; visual information integration into writing; revision strategies for accuracy improvement; disciplinary and real-world contextualization of writing; reflective writing practices. title: Electrical Machines
description_handout: Transformer: Constructional features, equivalent circuit and phasor diagram - regulation and efficiency, parallel operation. Three phase transformer connections; Harmonic in transformers; Testing; Phase conversion; Autotransformer. D.C Machines: Construction, armature windings, armature voltage and torque equations, classification. D.C generators, performance characteristics; D.C motors - torque/speed characteristics, speed control and braking. Testing and efficiency. Induction machines: Constructional features and rotating magnetic field. Circuit model and phasor diagram. Steady state characteristics. Testing, starting and speed control. Time harmonics and space harmonics. Wound rotor induction motors, Single phase induction motors - classification and equivalent circuit. Synchronous machines: Constructional features; synchronous generators and motors; equivalent circuit and phasor diagram; power and torque characteristics and capability curves. Parallel operation. Salient pole synchronous machine - phasor diagram and determination of synchronous reactances; starting and speed control of synchronous motors. Special machines- universal motors, Induction generators.
scope_objective: Electrical Machines are the work horse in almost all industries ranging from few watts’ power to several mega watt power applications. The scope of this course is to study of working principle & operating characteristics of Electrical Machines for the mode of Generation, and Utilization of Electrical Power. The specific objective of this course is to gain better understanding of various conventional electrical-magnetic devices such as Transformer, DC Machines and AC Machines. The course covers theory as well as detailed experimental component for better understanding of the concepts.
learning_outcomes: The students will learn about the operating principles, constructional features, equivalent circuit diagram, efficiency, testing & control and different type of performance characteristics of transformers, DC machines, induction and synchronous machines. title: ELECTRONIC DEVICES
description_handout: (as per the Bulletin): Crystal structure and growth of semiconductor, electrical conduction in solids, Elementary quantum physics (Photoelectric effect, uncertainty principle, Schrodinger wave equation and tunneling), energy bands in solids, charge carriers in semiconductors, excess carriers in semiconductors, Fabrication of p-n junctions, equilibrium conditions, forward and reverse biased junctions, metal-semiconductor junctions Bipolar junction transistors, field effect transistors (JFET, HEMT, MOSFET), Special diodes (varactor diode, solar cell, LEDs, Tunnel diode and HBT).
scope_objective: s: The course provides a comprehensive understanding of the characteristics, operation and limitations of semiconductor devices. This course starts with explanation on crystal structure, semiconductor materials, fundamentals of semiconductors. This course helps in developing the understanding about excess carriers in semiconductors and its application. In-depth study on ‘junctions’ prepares the students for even a detailed study on devices to be studied later like FET, BJT, MOSFET viz. commonly employed in Integrated Circuit (IC) technology. Concepts of optoelectronic diodes will also be discussed in this course.
learning_outcomes: At the end of this course, students will be able to:  CLO1: Explain the fundamentals of semiconductor materials, crystal structures, electrical conduction, quantum physics concepts, and energy band theory governing electronic devices.  CLO2: Analyze charge carrier transport, excess carrier behavior, and the electrical characteristics of semiconductor materials under equilibrium and non-equilibrium conditions.  CLO3: Evaluate the operation and characteristics of semiconductor junctions, including p-n junctions, metal-semiconductor junctions, and their behavior under forward and reverse bias conditions.  CLO4: Explain the operating principles, characteristics, and applications of major semiconductor devices, including BJTs, JFETs, HEMTs, MOSFETs, and special semiconductor diodes.  CLO5: Apply the fundamental principles of semiconductor device physics to analyze the performance and limitations of electronic and optoelectronic devices used in modern integrated circuits and electronic systems.

title: Digital Design
instructor_handout: CS F215 / ECE F215 / EEE F215 / INSTR F215
description_handout: Boolean Algebra & logic minimization; combinational logic circuits: arithmetic circuit design, Design using MSI components; Sequential Logic Circuits: flip flops & latches, registers and counters, Finite state machine; HDL Implementation of Digital circuits; Digital Integrated Circuits; Programmable logic devices; Memory organization; Algorithmic State machine; Introduction to computer organization; The course will also have laboratory component on digital design. 2. Textbook(s) T1: M. Moris Mano and Michael D. Ciletti “Digital Design,” PHI, 6th Edition, 2018. T2: G. Raghurama, S. Gurunarayanan, S. Mohan, Karthik, Pawan K. Ajmera, “Laboratory Manual”, 2022 3. Reference book(s) and online resources R1: Donald D. Givonne, “Digital Principles and Design” TMH, 2003 R2: W. Stallings, “Computer Organization and Architecture” PHE, 10th Edition, 2015 BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 4. Course Objectives 1. Understand ● Explain binary/BCD number representations and perform base conversions ● State the postulates of Boolean algebra and the meaning of minterms, maxterms, SOP/POS forms ● Describe the operation of standard combinational building blocks (adders, decoders, multiplexers, comparators, ALUs) and standard sequential elements (latches, flip-flops, registers, counters) ● Describe the characteristics of digital logic families (BJT, TTL, MOS) and PLD architectures ● Explain algorithms for signed multiplication (Booth's) and division 2. Apply ● Simplify Boolean functions using K-maps (including don't-cares, PI/EPI) and the Quine-McCluskey method ● Analyze and derive state tables/diagrams for a given sequential circuit ● Compare design tradeoffs between ripple-carry vs. carry-lookahead adders, and between different logic family implementations ● Trace/debug simple Verilog modules against their intended combinational or sequential behavior 3. Create ● Design combinational circuits (use of adders, decoders, mux/demux, PLDs) to meet given specifications ● Design sequential circuits (use of counters, registers, shift registers) from a given behavioral description ● Design a digital system from an algorithmic state machine (ASM) chart ● Implement and verify combinational/sequential designs in Verilog 5. Working in Binary ● Represent and convert numbers across binary/BCD systems, and apply Boolean algebra postulates to manipulate logic expressions ● Simplify Boolean functions using K-maps (minterms, maxterms, don't-cares, PI/EPI) into minimal SOP/POS forms ● Apply the Quine-McCluskey method as a tabular alternative to K-map simplification 2. title: ANALOG AND DIGITAL VLSI DESIGN
description_handout: This course introduces students to the principles and practical aspects of designing integrated circuits using CMOS technology. It covers both analog and digital VLSI design methodologies, exploring circuit-level building blocks, layout considerations, and performance trade-offs. Emphasis is placed on low-power, area- efficient, and high-performance circuit techniques, along with exposure to modern CAD tools and fabrication-aware design strategies. Students will gain experience designing critical components, including logic gates, adders, amplifiers, and mixed-signal interfaces.
scope_objective: ⮚ The course is designed to familiarize students with different design principles used in the Design of Digital & Analog VLSI Circuits & Systems using CMOS logic. ⮚ Understanding of CMOS technology fundamentals and their impact on design. ⮚ Design and analysis of digital logic circuits: static, dynamic, sequential. ⮚ Design and analysis of analog CMOS circuits: Op-Amplifiers, Advance current mirrors, Reference Circuit. ⮚ Exploration of Technology scaling trends, noise, and power-performance trade-offs. ⮚ Exposure to EDA tools for schematic capture, simulation, and layout. ⮚ Bridging theory with practical insights via Lab/Design assignments. ⮚ VLSI design activity will be understood by Synthesis and then Analysis at several successive levels of design abstraction. title: Linear Algebra and its Applications
description_handout: Quick review of Vector Spaces and Linear Transformations, Basis and Dimension, rank-nullity theorem, change of basis; Inner product spaces, Cauchy Schwarz's inequality, GramSchmidt orthonormalization, QR decomposition, Discrete Fourier Transform, and their applications, Spectral Theorem, Cayley-Hamilton Theorem, Decomposition theorem, and Jordan canonical forms, applications of SVD in Principal Component Analysis, use of SVD in low-rank approximations and to find least-squares solutions.
scope_objective: Linear algebra has applications in pure and applied mathematics, computer science, economics, engineering, mathematical biology, operation research, physics, and statistics. Linear algebra and matrix methods are also important for data analysis. Linear Algebra and its applications typically aim to equip students with a solid understanding of fundamental concepts in linear algebra and the ability to apply these concepts to the above fields.
learning_outcomes: After completion of thiscourse students should be able to CLO1.:Apply the Gram-Schmidt process toconstruct orthonormal bases in inner product spaces. CLO2.Utilize Cauchy-Schwarz inequalities to provegeometric boundaries and inner product behaviors. CLO3.Factor a matrix into orthogonal and upper triangular components for stable numerical computations. CLO4.Implement the Spectral Theorem and structuraldecomposition theorems CLO5.Formulate and compute optimal least-squaressolutions for linear models using pseudoinverses derived from SVD. CLO6.Apply Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to execute Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on high-dimensional datasets.

title: Object Oriented Programming
description_handout: Object orientation concepts, theories and principles; fundamental concepts of the object model: classes, objects, methods and messages, encapsulation and inheritance, interface and implementation, reuse and extension of classes, inheritance and polymorphism; overloading and overriding; static and dynamic binding; multithreaded programming; event handling and exception handling; process of object oriented requirements specification, analysis and design; notations for object-oriented analysis and design; case studies and applications using some object oriented programming languages. Object Oriented Design Patterns: Behavioural, Structural and Creational.
scope_objective: a) Gives an in-depth understanding of object-oriented programming using the java programming language, object- oriented analysis and design, and design patterns. b) In the classroom, the course will be taught with live demonstrations, running and debugging several examples on tools like Eclipse. c) The latter part of the course focuses on designing object-oriented software.
learning_outcomes: (CLOs) On successful completion of this course, students will be able to: CLO1. Explain the principles of object-oriented programming and apply core concepts such as abstraction, encapsulation, inheritance, and polymorphism in software development. CLO2. Design, implement, test, and debug medium-sized Java programs using classes, objects, interfaces, collections, generics, exception handling, file I/O, and multithreading. CLO3. Analyse object-oriented software requirements and represent software designs using appropriate UML diagrams and object-oriented design principles. CLO4. Apply commonly used object-oriented design patterns to develop software that is modular, reusable, extensible, and maintainable. CLO5. Evaluate alternative object-oriented design and implementation choices based on software quality attributes such as maintainability, flexibility, and reusability. BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 2

title: Discrete Mathematics
description_handout: Set theory: Sets, relations and functions, equivalence relations, partially ordered sets, countability of sets, lattices and Boolean algebras; Logic and methods of proof: Propositional logic, language of propositional logic, predicate logic and logical inference with quantifiers, introduction to different standard proof techniques; Combinatorics: Counting techniques, pigeonhole principle, inclusion-exclusion principle, recurrence relations, generating function, partitions; Graph theory: Graphs and digraphs, special types of graphs, trees, isomorphism, connectedness, Euler and Hamilton graphs.
scope_objective: Mathematics, described as a language of science, has acquired its unique position due to its precision and rigour. This makes essential the development of the sense for mathematical rigor as well as the habit of math- ematical thought process. The course will achieve this by introducing students to propositional and predicate logic. As an important follow-up, various methods of proof will be discussed. Several mathematical struc- tures like relations and orderings are studied due to their importance, not only in mathematics but also applied subjects like computer science. The course is also useful for the preparation for the study of computational concepts, techniques, and skills necessary to comprehend the structure of problems encountered in the design and analysis of algorithms.
learning_outcomes: Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to: CLO1. understand the basic process of mathematical reasoning CLO2. identify valid arguments and fallacies; CLO3. understand the structure of proofs of theorems in Mathematics; 1 CLO4. write valid mathematical proofs; CLO5. use powerful techniques for handling computing problems in Mathematics and Computation; CLO6. understand important structures having wide applications to sciences, computer programming and various classification problems.; CLO7. to create new relations with useful properties from a given relation; CLO8. to learn basic concepts of Graph theory.

title: Elementary Real Analysis
description_handout: Countable and uncountable sets, Real numbers and their properties, Sequence of real numbers, Continuous functions of real variable, Metric space, Compact set, Connected set, Completeness, Continuous function on a metric space, Riemann integration, Sequence and series of functions.
scope_objective: This course aims to discuss several properties of real numbers and functions of real variables. The notions of metric spaces will be introduced and a few concepts in analysis, such as continuity, the convergence of sequences, the convergence of sequences and series of functions, will be discussed. We will also discuss the rigorous theory of Riemann integration. Students will also learn to read and write rigorous proofs so that they can communicate mathematical ideas effectively. This course is also a basic course to build background for other advanced courses in mathematics.
learning_outcomes: CLO1. Students will learn about real numbers and their elementary properties, sequences of real numbers, and the generalization of distance to abstract sets. CLO2. Students will be introduced to the notion of convergence of series and sequence of functions. CLO3. Students will study the rigorous theory of integration.

title: ALGEBRA I
description_handout: Groups, subgroups, a counting principle, normal subgroups, and quotient groups, Cayley’s theorem, automorphisms, permutation groups, Sylow’s theorems, Rings, ring of real quaternions, ideals and quotient rings, homomorphisms, Euclidean rings, polynomial rings, and polynomials over the rational field.
scope_objective: The objective of this course is to provide an introduction to abstract algebraic structures, including groups and rings. The abstract setting allows for the study of disparate mathematical objects together. We can derive properties and structures that apply to concrete examples. We will see examples from number theory, linear algebra and geometry.
learning_outcomes: CLO1. Understand and apply the fundamental concepts of groups to solve algebraic problems CLO2. Analyze the structure of rings, integral domains and fields using algebraic theorems CLO3. Construct rigorous mathematical proofs to solve computational and theoretical problems

title: Foundations of Data Science
description_handout: This course introduces the mathematical foundations of data science with emphasis on probability, Gaussian models, statistical inference, nonparametric methods, optimization, dimensionality reduction, data preparation, and scalable data analytics. It develops core tools such as probability bounds, Bayesian inference, PCA and SVD, kernel density estimation, nearest-neighbor methods, and connects them to practical data-analysis problems. Pre-requisites: The course is self-contained. However, a basic understanding of probability theory, calculus, linear algebra, and elementary programming would be helpful. BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus Instruction Division _ Please Do Not Print Unless Necessary Course Objectives: Students will learn to  Model data using mathematically grounded ideas from probability, statistics, and linear algebra.  Bayesian updating, mixture models, nonparametric density and neighborhood methods.  Deal with high-dimensional data, PCA and SVD, and basic scalable analytics.  Support data preprocessing, visualization, and interpretation in modern data-science workflows. title: Mathematical Modelling
description_handout: Mathematical Modeling in Biology, Epidemiology, Model for Various Problems and Situation Using ODE and PDE, Classic Models in Ecology and Evolutionary Biology, Equilibria and Stability Analysis, Dynamics of Class-Structured Populations, Techniques for Analyzing Models.
scope_objective: The principal objective of this course is to familiarize students with the theory of population and a basic understanding of mathematical modelling of a real-world problem. Students will gain enough background to read theoretical population and evolutionary ecology literature, do simple modelling, and springboard to more complex theory if desired. Students will develop techniques for understanding and analysing simple, multivariate, and nonlinear models will be explored.
learning_outcomes: CLO1. Develop mathematical models of physical and biological systems using ODE. CLO2. Understanding the concept of qualitative analysis of the model equations. Particularly, equilibria analysis, linear stability analysis and bifurcation theory. CLO3. Analyze ecological and epidemiological models to interpret their dynamical behaviour and derive meaningful biological insights. CLO4. Implement and simulate mathematical models using MATLAB and interpret the computational results..

title: Multivariable Calculus
description: Multivariable Calculus 3 MATH F113 Probability and Statistics 3 PHY F101 Oscillations and Waves 3 MATH F102 Linear Algebra and Complex Variables 3 BITS F101 Social Conduct 1 EEE F111 Electrical Sciences 3 BITS K101 Physical Well-being and Creativity 1* BITS F102 Innovation and Design Thinking 1 18 19 II
description_handout: This course provides a foundational introduction to multivariable calculus and vector analysis, which are essential tools in engineering and the physical sciences. Students learn to analyze functions and geometric objects in two and three dimensional spaces, studying local behavior through differentiation and global properties through integration. Compared to single variable calculus, multivariable calculus introduces new ideas and describes behaviour in multiple directions and dimensions. These concepts play a central role in areas such as probability and statistics, fluid mechanics, electrical sciences and numerous other applications. The course develops mathematical techniques required to model real-world phenomena such as motion, flow, and fields. Key topics include polar coordinates, convergence of sequences and series, power series, Taylor and Maclaurin series, partial derivatives, and vector calculus, leading to fundamental integral theorems such as those of Green, Stokes, and Gauss.
scope_objective: s of the course:  To develop a solid conceptual understanding of functions of several variables.  Introduce partial derivatives and their applications in modelling and optimization.  To study multiple integrals and their use in computing areas, volume and mass.  Build geometric intuition via visualization of surfaces and vector fields.  To strengthen problem solving skills required for advanced engineering courses.
learning_outcomes: Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:  CLO1. Determine if an infinite series is convergent or divergent by selecting the appropriate tests.  CLO2. Apply techniques for plotting and analyzing curves in polar coordinates, including converting between polar and Cartesian forms, sketching polar graphs.  CLO3. Interpret parametric curves as trajectories described by position vectors, and compute associated velocity and acceleration vectors to analyze motion. BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division Please Do Not Print Unless Necessary  CLO4. Develop a deep understanding of the gradient vector, including its geometric meaning, its relationship to level curves and level surfaces, its role in directional derivatives, and its use in linear approximation and sensitivity analysis.  CLO5. Compute partial derivatives using the chain rule and total differentials, and apply these tools to model changes in multivariable systems.  CLO6. Formulate and solve optimization problems involving multiple variables, both unconstrained and constrained, using techniques such as Lagrange multipliers.  CLO7. Compute multiple integrals using appropriate coordinate systems, including rectangular, polar, cylindrical, and spherical coordinates.  CLO8. Perform change of variables in multiple integrals and understand the role of the Jacobian determinant.  CLO9. Set up and evaluate line integrals (for work and circulation), surface integrals (for flux), and volume integrals, and interpret their physical significance in applied problems. 4. Core concepts and mathematical derivations will be introduced through classroom lectures, while tutorial sessions will be devoted to reinforcing these ideas through guided problem-solving and application-based exercises. description_handout: This course presents the study of differential equations with the objective of introducing the classical methods for solving boundary value problems. It also serves as a basis for the applications of differential equations, Fourier series and Laplace transform in the various branches of engineering and sciences. Furthermore, it emphasizes on the role of orthogonal polynomials in dealing with Sturm-Liouville problems.
scope_objective: s • To understand the theory of first and second order ordinary differential equations and to learn methods to solve them. • To understand the series solution of second order ordinary differential equations and their interval of convergence. • To understand the Laplace transform, its properties, and applications for solving IVPs and BVPs. • To understand the Fourier series expansion of a function. • To understand the concept of eigenvalues and eigenfunctions and to use them in solving heat and wave equations.
learning_outcomes: After completing this course, the student will be able to 1) solve differential equations appearing in modeling of various processes in their respective engineering or science stream. 2) understand whether a given initial value problem is solvable or not. 3) understand the region in which the solution is valid (like in series solution approach). 4) solve the problems involving linear system of first order differential equations. 5) understand the eigenfunction expansion/Bessel series expansion of a function using respective orthogonality properties which can be further helpful in solving various problems in their engineering and science streams. title: OPTIMIZATION
description_handout: Introduction to optimization; linear programming; simplex methods; duality and sensitivity analysis; transportation model and its variants; integer linear programming nonlinear programming; multi-objective optimization; evolutionary computation techniques.
scope_objective: Engineers, scientists, analysts, and managers often face the challenge of making trade-offs between different factors to achieve desirable outcomes. Optimization is the process of making these trade-offs in the best possible way. Over the years, optimization problems have become well-established and are encountered in the physical sciences, engineering, economics, industry, planning, and many other areas of human activity. The objective of this course is to familiarize students with standard methods of solving optimization problems. This course covers various aspects of optimization, including a description of techniques such as Linear Programming and Nonlinear Programming, and their applications in various engineering and science disciplines, including economics and finance. Multi-objective optimization, which addresses optimization with more than one objective, is also discussed. Additionally, the course provides a brief and informative overview of the non- traditional optimization technique, Genetic Algorithms.

title: Discrete Mathematics

description_handout: Set theory: Sets, relations and functions, equivalence relations, partially ordered sets, countability of sets, lattices and Boolean algebras; Logic and methods of proof: Propositional logic, language of propositional logic, predicate logic and logical inference with quantifiers, introduction to different standard proof techniques; Combinatorics: Counting techniques, pigeonhole principle, inclusion-exclusion principle, recurrence relations, generating function, partitions; Graph theory: Graphs and digraphs, special types of graphs, trees, isomorphism, connectedness, Euler and Hamilton graphs.
scope_objective: Mathematics, described as a language of science, has acquired its unique position due to its precision and rigour. This makes essential the development of the sense for mathematical rigor as well as the habit of math- ematical thought process. The course will achieve this by introducing students to propositional and predicate logic. As an important follow-up, various methods of proof will be discussed. Several mathematical struc- tures like relations and orderings are studied due to their importance, not only in mathematics but also applied subjects like computer science. The course is also useful for the preparation for the study of computational concepts, techniques, and skills necessary to comprehend the structure of problems encountered in the design and analysis of algorithms.
learning_outcomes: Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to: CLO1. understand the basic process of mathematical reasoning CLO2. identify valid arguments and fallacies; CLO3. understand the structure of proofs of theorems in Mathematics; 1 CLO4. write valid mathematical proofs; CLO5. use powerful techniques for handling computing problems in Mathematics and Computation; CLO6. understand important structures having wide applications to sciences, computer programming and various classification problems.; CLO7. to create new relations with useful properties from a given relation; CLO8. to learn basic concepts of Graph theory.

description_handout: Topology and topological spaces, Metric spaces, Product and Quotient topology, Continuity and Homeomorphism, Connectedness, Compactness, Normal spaces, Classification of compact surfaces.
scope_objective: To introduce the students to the concepts of logical thinking in abstract terms using formal and axiomatic methods and to lay the foundations for further studies in abstract Mathematics.
learning_outcomes: Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to: CLO1. Define and analyze basic topological concepts, including topologies, bases, subspace topologies, product topologies, and quotient topologies, to construct and classify fundamental topological spaces. CLO2. Evaluate continuity and homeomorphisms to determine topologic equivalence between abstract spaces and investigate topological invariants. CLO3. Demonstrate a rigorous understanding of topological properties such as connectedness, compactness, countability, and separation axioms (including Hausdorff and Normal spaces). CLO4. Apply and construct formal mathematical proofs utilizing key structural theorems, including Urysohn's Lemma, Urysohn Metrization Theorem, and Tietze Extension Theorem.

title: Ordinary Differential Equations
description: Ordinary Differential Equations 3 Analysis 3 MATH F342 Differential Geometry 3
instructor_handout: BALRAM DUBEY, Email: bdubey@pilani.bits-pilani.ac.in, Chamber No: 6067-B
description_handout: Existence and uniqueness theorems; properties of linear systems; behavior of solutions of nth order equations; asymptotic behavior of linear systems; stability of linear and weakly nonlinear systems; conditions for boundedness and the number of zeros of the nontrivial solutions of second order equations; stability by Lyapunov's direct method; autonomous and non-autonomous systems.
scope_objective: Ordinary Differential Equations frequently occurs as mathematical models in many branches of science, engineering and economy. For a mathematician confronted with such a model there are a number of issues to address and various approaches to choose from: Is the problem well-posed? Do you expect the differential equation to have a solution? If so, is there a unique solution satisfying the given initial or boundary conditions? Can you find an explicit, analytical solution? This is only possible in rare circumstances. Geometric or qualitative methods: These methods give insights into general, qualitative features of solutions and do not require solving the differential equation. Stability and dependence on parameters: Having obtained a solution by any method, we would like to know how the solution changes if we change the initial data by a small amount (stability analysis) and if we change parameters in the differential equation (parameter dependence). Course helps deeper understanding of the complicated models that are there in the real life.

description_handout: Solution of non-linear algebraic equations; interpolation and approximation; numerical differentiation and quadrature; solution of ordinary differential equations; systems of linear equations; matrix inversion; eigenvalue and eigenvector problems; round off and conditioning.
scope_objective: s of the course: Enables one to devise algorithms for the numerical solutions of mathematical problems. Also discusses the error analysis of different algorithms.
learning_outcomes: Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to: • CLO1. Explain the fundamental concepts of numerical analysis, including sources of computational errors, floating-point arithmetic, error propagation, and conditioning. • CLO2. Apply appropriate numerical methods to determine the roots of nonlinear equations and evaluate the convergence, accuracy, and efficiency of different iterative algorithms. • CLO3. Solve systems of linear and nonlinear equations using direct and iterative numerical techniques and analyze the stability and conditioning of computational methods. • CLO4. Construct interpolation polynomials using standard interpolation techniques and estimate interpolation errors for function approximation. • CLO5. Compute numerical derivatives and definite integrals using finite difference and quadrature methods and assess the associated approximation errors. • CLO6. Obtain numerical solutions of ordinary differential equations arising from initial value problems using single-step and multistep numerical methods. • CLO7. Solve boundary value problems using finite difference methods and interpret the numerical solutions obtained. • CLO8. Determine dominant eigenvalues and eigenvectors of matrices using numerical algorithms such as the power and inverse power methods. • CLO9. Apply weighted residual techniques, including the Rayleigh–Ritz, Collocation, and Galerkin methods, to obtain approximate solutions of boundary value problems and compare their applicability and effectiveness. Classroom lectures will introduce the fundamental principles, mathematical formulations, and derivations of numerical methods. Tutorial sessions will reinforce these concepts through guided problem-solving, analytical exercises, and discussion of practical applications. Selected numerical methods will be implemented using MATLAB to provide hands-on computational experience, facilitate visualization, and enhance problem-solving skills. Student learning will be assessed continuously through quizzes, assignments, laboratory/computational exercises, and examinations to ensure the development of both conceptual understanding and practical proficiency. 5. title: Combinatorial Mathematics
description_handout: Combinatorics is often described briefly as being about counting, and indeed counting is a large part of combinatorics. As the name suggests, however, it is broader than this: it is about combining things. Questions that arise include counting problems: “How many ways can these elements be combined?” But there are other questions, such as whether a certain combination is possible, or what combination is the “best” in some sense. This course presents the different methods to solve the counting problems. We will mainly focus on combinatorial approach instead of algebraic approach. SCOPE and OBJECTIVES: Combinatorics is a fascinating and a broad subject. It’s hard to classify Combinatorics, but a common theme is that it deals with structures that are, in some sense, finite or discrete. What sets Combinatorics apart from other branches of Mathematics is that it focuses on techniques rather than results. The way a Theorem is proved is of bigger importance than the statement of the Theorem itself. Combinatorial reasoning underlies all analysis of Computer Systems. It plays a similar role in Discrete Operation Research Problems and in Finite Probability. It is very much useful in the analysis of the speed and logical structure of Operation Research Algorithms to optimize efficient manufacturing or garbage collections. It has been proven an efficient tool for Graph Counting. COURSE LEARNING OUTCOMES: The course focuses on different techniques related to counting problems. At the end of the course, student will be aware of many existing methods used to solve counting problems and when these methods are applicable. title: Applied Statistical Methods
description_handout: Applied Statistics is an exciting sub-area of Statistics. It has application in almost all science disciplines which deal with data and uncertainty. This course builds up fundamental concepts of various key statis- tical methods necessary to analyze/interpret a variety of practical business/engineering problems. This course emphasizes the role of statistics in one’s own field of study by making sense of data, developing self-ability to apply appropriate statistical methods, performing experimental designs and above all, re- alizing the limitations/inherent assumptions in a statistical test to avoid over interpretation or misinter- pretation. The thrust areas covered in this course include probability distributions, statistical inference, analysis of variance (ANOVA), regression and correlation, discriminant analysis, factor and cluster analysis, time series analysis and forecasting, nonparametric methods and statistical quality control. The theoretical learning will be complemented with various case studies and hands-on training in excel/R.

title: Multivariable Calculus
description_handout: This course provides a foundational introduction to multivariable calculus and vector analysis, which are essential tools in engineering and the physical sciences. Students learn to analyze functions and geometric objects in two and three dimensional spaces, studying local behavior through differentiation and global properties through integration. Compared to single variable calculus, multivariable calculus introduces new ideas and describes behaviour in multiple directions and dimensions. These concepts play a central role in areas such as probability and statistics, fluid mechanics, electrical sciences and numerous other applications. The course develops mathematical techniques required to model real-world phenomena such as motion, flow, and fields. Key topics include polar coordinates, convergence of sequences and series, power series, Taylor and Maclaurin series, partial derivatives, and vector calculus, leading to fundamental integral theorems such as those of Green, Stokes, and Gauss.
scope_objective: s of the course:  To develop a solid conceptual understanding of functions of several variables.  Introduce partial derivatives and their applications in modelling and optimization.  To study multiple integrals and their use in computing areas, volume and mass.  Build geometric intuition via visualization of surfaces and vector fields.  To strengthen problem solving skills required for advanced engineering courses.
learning_outcomes: Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:  CLO1. Determine if an infinite series is convergent or divergent by selecting the appropriate tests.  CLO2. Apply techniques for plotting and analyzing curves in polar coordinates, including converting between polar and Cartesian forms, sketching polar graphs. BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division Please Do Not Print Unless Necessary  CLO3. Interpret parametric curves as trajectories described by position vectors, and compute associated velocity and acceleration vectors to analyze motion.  CLO4. Develop a deep understanding of the gradient vector, including its geometric meaning, its relationship to level curves and level surfaces, its role in directional derivatives, and its use in linear approximation and sensitivity analysis.  CLO5. Compute partial derivatives using the chain rule and total differentials, and apply these tools to model changes in multivariable systems.  CLO6. Formulate and solve optimization problems involving multiple variables, both unconstrained and constrained, using techniques such as Lagrange multipliers.  CLO7. Compute multiple integrals using appropriate coordinate systems, including rectangular, polar, cylindrical, and spherical coordinates.  CLO8. Perform change of variables in multiple integrals and understand the role of the Jacobian determinant.  CLO9. Set up and evaluate line integrals (for work and circulation), surface integrals (for flux), and volume integrals, and interpret their physical significance in applied problems. 4. Method of conducting the course: The instructional approach for this course integrates theory, practice, and computational exposure. Core concepts and mathematical derivations will be introduced through classroom lectures, while tutorial sessions will be devoted to reinforcing these ideas through guided problem-solving and application-based exercises. To supplement in-class learning, three video lectures will be made available, showcasing the use of computational software (MATLAB) for visualization and problem-solving. Student learning will be evaluated on a continuous basis through quizzes, assignments, and examinations, ensuring both conceptual understanding and practical competence. 5. Textbook: TB. J. Hass, C. title: Fluid Mechanics
description_handout: This course covers the following topics: Mathematical preliminaries; Fluid statics and forces on submerged bodies; Integral relations for a control volume; Mass, Momentum and Energy Con- servation; Reynolds Transport Theorem; Differential relations for fluid flow, Analytical solution of Navier-Stokes equation; Dimensional analysis and similarity; Inviscid potential flows; Bernoulli’s Equation; Internal and external viscous flows; Basic compressible flows.
scope_objective: s of the Course: The objectives of the course are to learn about the following topics: • Introduction to fluid mechanics and establish its relevance in mechanical engineering. • Derivation of the equations governing mass, momentum and energy transport. • Application of the governing equation to solve simple fluid mechanics problems. • Non-dimensionalization of governing equations and identification of dimensionless numbers, Modeling and similarity concepts. • Two dimensional, inviscid, potential flows; Stream function, Velocity potential. • Analyze laminar and turbulent flows inside pipes, External flow past immersed bodies, Intro- duction to Boundary layer theory • One dimensional, compressible flow inside ducts of variable cross-section, normal and oblique shocks. 3. title: DESIGN OF MACHINE ELEMENTS
description_handout: The course introduces students to concepts and nuances of Mechanical Engineering Design. Content includes materials, standards and design of machine elements and application of scientific principles, technical knowledge, and imaginative skills to be developed in a student. The machine elements covered are Shafts, Screw fasteners, Welded joints, Springs, Brakes & Clutches, Bearings and Gears. The Tutorial classes of the course will be mainly used for assisted problem solving, consultation and evaluation.

title: [Advanced Manufacturing Processes]
description_handout: Unconventional manufacturing processes and analysis, micro-manufacturing technologies, introduction to computer-aided manufacturing, CNC machines, CNC Part programming, additive manufacturing, modelling and simulation of manufacturing processes, surface technologies, related laboratory exercise and fabrication project.
scope_objective: This course introduces students to advanced manufacturing technologies for fabricating components across multiple length scales. It focuses on the challenges of machining difficult- to-machine materials and transforming them into high-value products. The course emphasizes hands-on learning through CNC part programming, CNC machine operation, additive manufacturing, and digital-to-physical manufacturing workflows. Lectures complement laboratory sessions by covering the fundamentals, process capabilities, numerical methods, and optimization techniques required for the analysis and development of advanced manufacturing processes.
learning_outcomes: CLO1. Explain the principles, capabilities, limitations, and applications of advanced manufacturing processes, including CNC machining, additive manufacturing, and non- traditional machining. CLO2. Develop CNC part programs and implement digital manufacturing workflows to fabricate engineering components using advanced manufacturing systems. CLO3. Analyze the influence of process parameters, material properties, and machine characteristics on product quality, productivity, and process performance.

title: Engines, Motors, and Mobility
description_handout: The internal combustion engine (IC) is a heat engine that converts chemical energy in a fuel into mechanical energy, usually made available on a rotating output shaft. This is one of the dominating areas in prime movers. These engines are often used for the propulsion of a vehicle (i.e., automobile, truck, locomotive, marine vessel, or aeroplane), and other applications include stationary engines to drive generators or pumps and portable engines for things like chain saws and lawnmowers, etc. This course will introduce the students to system-level design concepts and the workings of internal combustion engines. Furthermore, electric mobility has become an essential part of the energy transition. This course focuses on the fundamentals of the technology behind electric vehicles. It will cover the contents such as the working principle of electric vehicles and delve into its key components, e.g. motors and power electronics, battery technology, charging technologies and future trends in the development of electric vehicles. title: Data Mining in Mechanical Sciences
description_handout: Introduction to data mining, clustering, classification & association, sequence analysis, regressions method, decision trees, machine learning, neural networks, SVM for engineering and manufacturing applications, data mining for product design, applications of data mining in production, planning and scheduling, data mining for defect identification, process and quality control, application of data mining in maintenance, data analysis for machine and manufacturing process monitoring, introduction to cyber physical systems, introduction to big data handling and big data analytics. II. Scope and Objective of the course: The primary focus of this course is on application of data mining methods in mechanical sciences and engineering. Following are the details objectives of this course: • Understanding the fundamental of data mining. • Building mathematical foundation for data mining. • Knowledge of data capturing to minimize the information losses. • Understanding of patterns in data, data classification and clustering. • Knowledge of application of identified patterns in data in fields like in-processing monitoring, machine monitoring, defect analysis, machine and maintenance scheduling etc. • Understanding of different prediction methods based on the data processing. • Understand the difference between artificial intelligence, machine learning and deep learning. • Knowledge of which data mining methods should be used for what type of data. • Understanding the concept of big data in mechanical and manufacturing domain and how to handle it. title: Energy Storage Technologies
description_handout: This course introduces the necessity, classification, operating principles, and applications of various energy storage technologies used in modern energy systems. Mechanical, thermal, electrochemical, electrical, and chemical energy storage systems will be discussed with emphasis on their design, operation, performance characteristics, advantages, limitations, and practical applications in electric vehicles, renewable energy integration. The course also covers emerging storage technologies including advanced battery systems, supercapacitors, hydrogen energy systems, and phase change material-based thermal storage systems.
scope_objective: The objective of this course is to provide students with a strong understanding of energy storage technologies and their role in sustainable energy systems. The course covers fundamental thermodynamic, electrochemical, and mechanical aspects of energy storage systems along with their design considerations, performance evaluation, safety issues, and practical applications. The course also aims to familiarize students with recent advancements, technical challenges, economic considerations, and future prospects of modern energy storage technologies. The course also introduces Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) as a simulation tool for the design, analysis, and performance evaluation of energy storage systems, with emphasis on thermal management and flow behavior. 3. title: Introduction to Sport Engineering
description_handout: The course essentially prepares engineering students to utilize their existing technical knowhow for sports applications. The specific topics will include, working with human and human movement patterns, qualitative and quantitative techniques for analysis of human movement. Sports performance measure and analysis. Anthropomorphy, Ergonomics and Task design. Computer application in sports, computerized performance measure. Sports surface and its impact on sports performance, surface testing methods. Sports and training equipment case study, business around sports
scope_objective: This is an introductory course to impart knowledge and skill set related to working with human in sports engineering application. Understanding human movement pattern and performance measurement. Understand, assess and analyze effect of equipment, sports surfaces and environment on sports performance. Use of ergonomic concepts, image processing, smart sensors and data analysis in sports engineering. Standard techniques of evaluation and testing of sports equipment and sports surfaces and appreciation of business around sports industry.
learning_outcomes: Course Learning Outcomes: By the end of this course, students will be able to: Understand the fundamentals of human movement and apply engineering principles to analyze sports performance. Appreciate the role of ethics, human factors, and design considerations in sports technology. Utilize modern computing tools for motion analysis and performance

title: Micro Fluidics And Its Applications
description_handout: This elective course introduces the fundamental principles and emerging applications of microfluidics. This is one of the dominating areas in prime movers. The course emphasizes both theoretical foundations and practical insights relevant to microscale fluid behavior, fabrication methods and devices. title: SMART MATERIALS
description_handout: The course introduces smart materials and smart structures through their physical mechanisms, characteristic responses and engineering use. Major topics include piezoelectric ceramics and polymers; one-way, two-way and magnetic shape-memory alloys; electro- and magnetorheological fluids; magnetostrictive and electrostrictive materials; and fibre-optic and FBG sensors. Basic modelling is embedded within the relevant material modules using physically interpretable equations and response curves. Applications include sensing, actuation, vibration control, damping, structural- health monitoring, energy harvesting and intelligent devices.
scope_objective: This undergraduate course develops a foundational understanding of stimulus- responsive materials and their use in smart structures. Emphasis is placed on physical mechanisms, observable behaviour, characteristic curves and straightforward engineering comparisons rather than advanced constitutive modelling. Guided demonstrations, basic experiments, case studies, paper reviews, assignments and project work will connect theory with practice. These activities are intended to develop scientific curiosity and encourage interested students to pursue further project- and research- oriented work in smart materials and structures.
learning_outcomes: CO1: Explain the terminology, operating principles, physical mechanisms and characteristic behaviour of major smart-material families and smart structural systems. CO2: Interpret basic characteristic curves, experimental observations and performance data to describe the sensing and actuation behaviour of smart materials. CO3: Compare major smart-material families and identify suitable materials for simple engineering applications based on their capabilities, limitations and operating requirements. CO4: Investigate smart-material behaviour through guided demonstrations, basic experiments, case studies, paper reviews or project work, and communicate the resulting observations and findings.

title: Mechanism and Robotics
scope_objective: This course is designed to provide an in-depth and holistic understanding of the technology and principles underlying modern robotics. Over the years, the demand for human-like machines capable of replacing or assisting humans in diverse and challenging work environments has grown significantly due to reasons such as efficiency, precision, safety, and the need to operate in hazardous conditions. In response to this need, the field of robotics has rapidly evolved and established itself as one of the most critical and promising areas of engineering for the future. The course aims to build a strong interdisciplinary foundation for students, focusing particularly on the mechanical aspects of robotic systems while integrating relevant knowledge from electronics, computer science, and control engineering. It will cover fundamental and advanced concepts related to mechanisms used in robotic systems, their unique characteristics, and detailed kinematic and dynamic analysis essential for design and development. Furthermore, students will gain insights into the design methodologies, practical implementation principles, and real-world industrial applications of robotics. The course will also explore current issues, trends, and innovations in robotics, enabling students to appreciate its impact across industries and prepare them for future technological advancements in this rapidly expanding domain. Text Book: (T1) Mittal R. K. & Nagrath, I. J., “Robotics and Control”, TMH, 2003 (Reprint 2010 or later). Reference Books: (R1) Groover, M. P., et al., “Industrial Robotics”, McGraw Hill ISE, 1986. (R2) Fu, K. S., et al., Robotic: Control, Sensing, Vision & Intelligence, McGraw Hill ISE, 1987 (R3) Robert J., Schilling, Fundamentals of Robotics: Analysis and Control, Prentice Hall, NJ, 2002. title: Finite Element Method
description_handout: Fundamental concepts, matrix algebra and gaussian elimination, one-dimensional problems, trusses, two-dimensional problems using constant strain triangles, axisymmetric solids subjected to ax- isymmetric loading, two-dimensional isoparametric elements and numerical integration, beams and frames, three-dimensional problems in stress analysis, scalar field problems, dynamic con- siderations, pre-processing and post processing.
scope_objective: The scope of the course is limited to an introduction to FEA as applied to elasticity problems in solid and structural mechanics. This course will train the students to analyze real-world structural mechanics problems using the finite element method. Students will be introduced to the mathe- matical basis of finite element analysis, on which nearly all structural analysis software are built. The objectives of the course are: CO1. Understand strong and weak formulations, methods of weighted residuals Rayleigh-Ritz method. CO2. Understand the finite element method procedure, which converts a given boundary value problem into a set of algebraic linear equations that can be solved using computer. CO3. Understand the implementation of FEM for linear analysis of 1D and 2D problems of solid mechanics and heat transfer. 3. Textbooks: TB1. Introduction to the Finite Element Method, J. N. title: Deep Neural Networks
description_handout: Introduction to neural networks, approximation properties, backpropagation, deep network training, regularization and optimization, convolution neural networks, recurrent neural networks, attention models, transformers, neural architecture search, federated learning, meta-learning, applications in time series modeling and forecasting, online (incremental) learning. II. Scope and Objective of the course: This course is designed to impart the knowledge to understand the basics of deep learning and their applications in mechanical engineering. title: Industrial Robotics and Controls
description_handout: This course provides a comprehensive foundation in industrial robotic systems and robot control. Topics include principles of robot kinematics, statics, dynamics, and control; rigid body motion and coordinate transformations; rotation matrices, Denavit-Hartenberg parameters forward and inverse kinematics; Jacobian analysis, workspace and singularity analysis; trajectory planning and motion optimization; robot statics and dynamics using Euler–Lagrange and Newton–Euler formulations; control system for robot, independent joint control, computed torque control, and force control; end-effector and gripper design for robotic manipulation and precision assembly; sensor-integrated robotic systems; collaborative robotics; robotic work-cell implementation; and case studies and applications of industrial robots in intelligent manufacturing environments.
scope_objective: This course provides fundamental, theoretical, and applied knowledge of industrial robotics and robot control with a strong emphasis on hands-on learning and industry-oriented applications. The course develops a rigorous foundation in robot kinematics, dynamics, motion planning, and control required for the modelling, analysis, and operation of industrial robotic manipulators. Students will gain practical exposure to industrial robotic systems used in modern manufacturing environments for robotic manipulation, precision assembly, collaborative robotics, and intelligent production systems. Laboratory sessions and project-based learning will focus on robotic manipulator programming, trajectory generation, end-effector design, sensor-integrated robotic systems, and robotic work-cell implementation using industrial-grade platforms. Course Outcome: Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to: CO1 Apply principles of robot kinematics, dynamics, and control to model and analyze industrial robotic manipulators. CO2 Design and implement motion planning and control strategies for industrial robotic tasks such as pick-and- place, assembly, and material handling. CO3 Design and deploy sensor-integrated robotic work cells for real-world manufacturing applications with closed-loop control. CO4 Demonstrate hands-on proficiency and industry readiness by solving practical robotics problems through labs, projects, and industry-led sessions. title: Moulding Methods for Electronic Components
description_handout: This course provides students with a comprehensive understanding of molding methods used for plastic components in the manufacturing of electronic components. It will introduce students to different molding techniques used for plastic components, and equipment, process considerations, and applications in the electronics industry. The second module provides an overview of the different materials, characterization and testing procedures, and environmental safety considerations in the electronic industry. In the third and fourth modules, students will be exposed to different plastic- moulding processes used in the fabrication of electronic components. The last module will provide basic design aspects related to injection mould, compression mould, transfer mould, and blow mould for fabricating electronic components. Through a strong focus on experimental exposure and industry case studies, students will develop practical insights into advanced manufacturing systems used in the electronics industry.
scope_objective: This course introduces theoretical, analytical, and practical knowledge of plastic materials used in the electronic industry, as well as the manufacturing methods for plastic components. It provides students with basic knowledge of advanced casting methods for fabricating plastic components for the electronics industry. It enables learners to understand the principles of various advanced casting methods, the casting machines used, the mechanisms of these processes, the parameters involved, and basic design aspects related to mould. Additionally, this course provides industrial/practical exposure to industrial component development and various application areas with case studies. 3. Course Outcomes CO No. Course Outcome CO1 Develop an understanding of the moulding processes and testing techniques involved in the fabrication of plastic components in the electronics industry. CO2 Selection of appropriate materials for the electronic industry. CO3 Design and fabricate different plastic components using moulding processes. CO4 Acquire basic design skills related to injection mould, compression mould, transfer mould, and blow mould. CO5 Demonstrate hands-on proficiency and industry readiness by solving practical electronic component fabrication problems through labs, projects, and industry-led sessions.

title: Computer Aided Design & Additive Manufacturing
description_handout: This course provides a comprehensive understanding of advanced computer-aided design (CAD) and digital product development techniques used in modern engineering design and manufacturing. It covers geometric modelling of parametric curves, surfaces, and Non-Uniform Rational B-Splines (NURBS), along with geometric transformations, mass property evaluation, and product data exchange standards for seamless CAD interoperability. The course intro- duces Design of Experiments (DoE) for design optimisation and provides extensive hands-on training in basic and advanced Geometric Dimensioning and Tolerancing (GD&T) based on the ASME Y14.5 standard using commercial CAD software. Students will also explore the fundamentals of generative design, topology optimisation through industrial case studies, and the principles and applications of additive manufacturing, enabling them to design innovative, lightweight, and manufacturable engineering products.
scope_objective: The course aims to develop knowledge and practical skills in advanced CAD, geometric mod- elling, topology optimisation, and additive manufacturing techniques. It enables students to apply geometric modelling, GD&T (ASME Y14.5), generative design, and modern engineering software to design, analyse, and validate innovative and manufacturable engineering products. description_handout: The course has wide-ranging application in Engineering structures, Machine tool structures, metal forming, and cold working. The studies deal with the determination of stresses and displacements in common structural forms beams, shafts, shells etc. subjected to external forces. The course covers basic theory of elasticity, 2-D and 3-D problems of elasticity, Theories of plastic flow, Flow of ideally plastic and strain hardening metals, and theory of metal forming processes. 2. Course Level Objectives: The course is for higher degree students to prepare them in applying the theory on some problems of practical and design interest. The students will be able to appreciate underlying meaning of material and structural behavior under complex loading conditions. Students are also encouraged to do assignments using the ANSYS/ABAQUS package to solve problems of elasticity and plasticity to compare the analytical solutions. CO1: Understand the concept of stress and strain in situations where large deformations are involved. CO2: Appreciate the governing differential equations that describe a general boundary value problem in elasticity. CO3: Solve the general elasticity boundary value problems with various boundary conditions using methods of complex variable techniques CO4: Appreciate the concept of yielding and yield criteria. title: Micro Fluidics And Its Applications
description_handout: This elective course introduces the fundamental principles and emerging applications of microfluidics. This is one of the dominating areas in prime movers. The course emphasizes both theoretical foundations and practical insights relevant to microscale fluid behavior, fabrication methods and devices. Scope and Objective of the Course: The scope of this course spans across fundamental science, device engineering, and emerging real-world applications at the micro- and nano-scale. This course provides a comprehensive understanding of microscale fluid dynamics, and control principles central to microfluidic systems. The course objectives are to understand the basics of microfluidics and the physics governing microfluidic flows and interfaces, to explore various microfabrication techniques suitable for fluidic devices and to analyze and understand the microfluidic systems applications in various engineering domains. title: ADVANCED VLSI DESIGN
description_handout: The field of Digital Very Large-Scale Integrated Circuits has gone through dramatic evolutions and changes. This course builds on the previous course MEL G621 VLSI DESIGN. It is intended to give a detailed knowledge and experience in the design of advanced VLSI circuits and chips in todays and future nano-scale CMOS technologies. Design of high-performance digital systems, failure issues, and remedies of problems. Topics will focus on current issues, including: wiring resistance and how to deal with it, power and Ground noise and regulation, clock (or asynchronous) system design and how to minimize clocking overhead, high-speed I/O design, energy minimization, including leakage control. Major VLSI design challenges are followed by careful treatment of several versatile digital and mixed analog-digital circuit building blocks frequently utilized in VLSI chips.
scope_objective: The development of digital technology over the past 50 years has revolutionized the design and performance of everything from mobile phones to cars and entertainment systems; and engineers continue to enhance the performance of these devices. Recent developments in nanotechnology promise further large increases in processing power with lower power requirements, and will open up a whole new world of applications for digital techniques. The course aims to learn new techniques to keep up-to-date with developments in an industrial and/or research setting, and will have hands-on experience of the different stages of the design of a modern digital system.
learning_outcomes: Students will develop an understanding of common design and timing issues/challenges in digital systems. They will be introduced to high-speed/low-power circuit logic/ power minimization techniques, as well as wiring models used in digital systems. Additionally, they will learn about the clock system design and various noise sources that can interfere with these systems.

title: Advanced VLSI Architectures
description_handout: The course explores advanced VLSI processor architectures, their implementation strategies (microarchitectures) and associated memory hierarchies and their microarchitectures for high-performance system design. It also covers the various techniques utilized to leverage parallelism at hardware, application and compiler levels. Students will gain an understanding of how (beyond instruction-level parallelism) data-level parallelism, thread-level parallelism and task-level parallelism can be exploited to architect and implement different processing cores e.g.: Vector Processors, SIMD processors and Multimedia processors, Graphical Processing Units (GPU) and Multi-core processors, Domain Specific Processors, and Memory hierarchy organizations for the above processors. The course also explores the emerging research directions in VLSI processor design and system architectures.
scope_objective: The objective of the course is to understand and gain an in-depth view of Advanced VLSI Architectures, specifically to study various processor architectures, associated microarchitectures, and memory organizations that have evolved to exploit different types of parallelism to increase processor performance. The scope of the course covers the following in detail: a. Study of advanced processor architectures and associated implementation techniques (microarchitectures) and memory organization techniques b. This includes the study of Vector, SIMD, GPU, and Domain Specific architectures and implementations c. Study of architectures and implementations that exploit thread-level parallelism and task-level parallelism via multi-processing (includes multicore processors) d. Study of memory hierarchy design for CPUs, vector processors, GPUs, and application domain-specific processors
learning_outcomes: a. Explain the advantages of CORDIC in hardware implementation, especially in terms of multiplier-less architecture, low power, and area efficiency. b. Analyze the design principles of advanced VLSI processor architectures and their microarchitectural implementation strategies for high-performance computing systems. c. Evaluate various memory hierarchy designs and optimizations, including their microarchitectural aspects, in the context of different processor types. d. Apply concepts of parallelism—such as instruction-level, data-level, thread-level, and task-level parallelism—to optimize system performance. e. Design architectural solutions using specialized processing units such as SIMD processors, vector processors, multimedia processors, GPUs, multi-core systems, and domain-specific accelerators. f. Explore contemporary research trends and emerging technologies in VLSI processor and memory system architecture to identify potential areas for innovation.
makeup_policy: implementation. Recent (and research) architectures and their implementations for machine learning. 7. title: Advance Analog and Mixed Signal Design
description_handout: Mixed signal blocks design issues,, design of high resolution, speed Comparators,, design of Active Mixers-balanced/ unbalanced,, Data Converters Architectures, CMOS multipliers , dividers and modulators , filters- active/ passive/ switched capacitor, Signal Conditioning and sensor associated circuits, Frequency Synthesizers, Phase Locked Loop, Power Management Circuits, Integrated Voltage Regulators, Energy Harvesting Circuits, Analog Testing, Analog layouts, noise issues, emerging trendshigh
scope_objective: This course is designed to provide in-depth knowledge and hands-on expertise in designing advanced analog and mixed-signal integrated circuits with a focus on modern CMOS technologies. The course aims to bridge the gap between analog fundamentals and practical design of performance-critical blocks such as Phase-Locked Loops (PLLs), oscillators, and Analog-to-Digital Converters (ADCs). It equips students to analyze, architect, and implement key mixed-signal blocks considering design trade-offs, non-idealities, and layout constraints. Emerging trends such as energy harvesting, sensor interface circuits, and digitally assisted analog systems are also discussed to build readiness for research and industrial innovation.
learning_outcomes: Upon successful completion of this course, the students will be able to: a. Analyse and Design high-resolution, high-speed comparators, mixers, and signal conditioning blocks for mixed-signal interfaces. b. Architect and Evaluate various ADC and DAC topologies based on speed, resolution, power, and area metrics. c. Design and Simulate PLLs and oscillator-based clock generation systems with attention to phase noise, jitter, and loop stability. d. Implement of Biasing Circuits and Optical/Wireline Receiver Transmitter circuits. AUGSD/AGSRD Division Pilani Campus e. Understand and Apply analog layout methodologies, matching principles, and noise-aware design techniques. f. Demonstrate Proficiency in using industry-grade tools (e.g., Cadence) to model, simulate, and layout mixed-signal circuits.

title: Verification, Test, and Testability of VLSI Circuits
description: Verification, Test and Testability of VLSI Circuits 5 M.E. Electronics and Control Core Courses
description_handout: VLSI design flow, Simulation based verification, Test bench tools and languages, System Verilog, Formal verification, Impact of scaling, wafer sort or probe test, DC and AC parametric test, Test economics and product quality, Fault models and types; Fault equivalence, Fault dominance, Automated test generation for combinational logic (fault simulation, ATPG, D-algorithm, PODEM, FAN); Test generation for sequential logic; Testability measures, Design for testability (Full-scan and partial scan, BIST, Boundary scan), Delay fault; Analog and mixed signal circuit testing, Memory test, IDDQ test
scope_objective: The objective of this course is to deal with the study of VLSI design flow, Functional verification, verification flow, need of electronic testing, fault modeling, test generation for combinational circuits, test generation for sequential circuits, fault simulation, Built-In Self-Test (BIST), Memory testing, Design for Testability (DFT), SoC test, fault diagnosis, Analog/RF test.
learning_outcomes: Students will learn the VLSI design flow, understand the importance of design verification during design flow and also understand the importance of post fabrication testing in VLSI design flow with exposure to the design tools.

title: AUTOMATION AND CONTROL
scope_objective: This course is intended to a comprehensive knowledge of the technology related to Mechatronics and Automation. The necessity of integrating and embedding electronics and microprocessor into mechanical systems have been long felt, due to rapid progress in microprocessor computer based technology, in domestic products to manufacturing systems. Mechatronics is a recently defined engineering field that builds on the traditional mechanical engineering studies, combines it with technologies from the electrical, electronics, computer and control fields, using techniques such as simultaneous engineering to provide solutions in manufacturing applications. Also, mechatronics has been applied to manufacturing and other industrial automation: robotic automation found in car automated production lines, such as welding, and assembly line in computer integrated manufacture etc. Thus, the manufacturing system is greatly enhanced by the application of mechatronics. This course will develop overall background of the student in interdisciplinary mechatronic technology and a broad introduction to the issues encountered and techniques required in developing mechatronic products and automation systems. 2.
