title: Lean Manufacturing
description_handout: Fundamentals of continuous improvement, value-added and waste elimination, elements of lean production: small lot production, setup time reduction, maintaining and improving equipment, pull production systems, focused factories and group technologies, work cells and cellular manufacturing, standard operations, quality of design, systems for eliminating defects, simplified production planning and control systems: scheduling for smooth flow, synchronizing and balancing process, planning and control in pull production, beyond the production systems: managing the supply chain, activity based costing, performance measurement.
scope_objective: In factories around the globe, Toyota consistently raises the bar for manufacturing, product development and process excellence. The result is an amazing business success story: steadily taking market share from price- cutting competitors, earning far more profit than any other automaker, and wining the praise of business leaders worldwide. With a market capitalization greater than the value of General Motors, Ford and Chrysler combined; Toyota is the world’s most profitable automaker. Toyota’s well known “secret weapon” is lean manufacturing – the revolutionary approach to business processes that it invented in the 1950’s and has spent decades for perfecting. Today business around the world is attempting to implement Toyota system to maintain competitive advantage. But are they? The course explains Toyota’s unique approach to Lean manufacturing, that drive Toyota’s quality and efficiency obsessed culture. You will valuable insights that can be applied to any organization and any business process, whether in services or manufacturing. You will discover how the right combination of long- term philosophy, processes, people and problem solving can transform your organization into a lean, learning enterprise – the Toyota way. At the end of this course, the students will be able to understand the importance of lean manufacturing / The Toyota Way as a strategic weapon, the students will be able to understand the World –Class power of the Toyota way 3. Text Books: TB1. Pascal Dennis, "Lean Production Simplified", 2nd Edition, Productivity Press, 2007. TB2. Jeffrey K. Liker, “The Toyota Way”, MaGraw-Hill Edition, New Delhi, 2004. 4. title: INNOVATION AND DESIGN THINKING
description_handout: Human-centered innovation, Design thinking (DT), consumer needs, creativity for new ideas/products (or re- design products) for solving problems, DT process’ stages– inspiration, ideation & implementation, DT tools – stakeholder map, user persona, Hook’s canvas, empathy map, AEIOU model, PoV, problem statement, stakeholder wish list, SCAMPER, prototyping & testing, MVP or minimum viable product, business model/canvas & business ecosystem. scope_objective: The objective is to develop knowhow and skills that promote human-centered approach to innovation through design thinking (DT). It will aim to develop understanding of consumer needs & using creativity for new ideas/products (or re-design products) for solving problems. Course will also help understand prototyping, testing of new ideas & see the context of the larger ecosystem. Focus will be on understanding design thinking concept and tools for effective innovations that can solve consumers’ needs holistically. Design Thinking process is laid across 3 stages- inspiration, ideation and implementation for new product development or re-design & concepts like MVP or minimum viable product, business model/canvas & business ecosystem will be also covered. title: Marketing
description_handout: This basic course in marketing is designed to familiarize students with the strategic and tactical decision making process in marketing that deals with the fundamental goal of creating, communicating and delivering value to the customer. This requires a professional knowledge of market drivers, competitors’ capabilities, technological trends and the market dynamics of value. The focus will be on the imbibing the skills of uncovering market opportunities by asking certain strategic questions.
scope_objective: On successful completion of this course, participants will be able to critically analyze and intelligently draw inference about the marketing strategies of organizations. Through an intensive assignment an effort will be made to develop the necessary skills for crafting a typical marketing plan grounded in real world data. Finally, awareness of tools available to marketing managers to facilitate planning and decision-making would be one of the gains from the course. Students are encouraged to bring some of the topical issues of contemporary concern in marketing to the classroom for discussion. Students will also be expected to imbibe path-breaking classic marketing literature in a group setting through group discussions for a sound academic base. A number of journal articles will be discussed in this course to give the course its academic rigor. The course pedagogy lays special emphasis on “learning by doing” through regular discussion of 6-7 Harvard Business Review cases as well as through a group marketing project assignment. 3. title: Managing People & Organization
description_handout: The course studies human behavior in organizations at three levels: individual, group, and organizational systems. It examines variables and key concepts related to individual attitudes, motivation, and leadership, along with group dynamics, organizational structure, and change management, while also covering the strategic role of HRM in attracting, developing, motivating, and retaining talent through recruitment and selection, training and development, performance management, employee engagement, compensation, and talent management.
scope_objective: In the contemporary time, organizations across the world are facing economic and social consequences of global economic pressures and globalization. Under such scenario, they encounter many challenges and get various opportunities as well. Moreover, management of these challenges and opportunities has become crucial which essentially relies on an understanding of human behavior. The success of any organization in today's dynamic and volatile business environment is dependent upon the motivation and commitment of its employees. It is in this context the significance of organizational behavior comes into play. As people from diverse backgrounds and with different cultural values have to work together in the global economy, the study of organizational behavior assumes greater importance and relevance. This course focuses on the fundamental theories of behavior in organizations and managing employees in organizations with the objective of equipping students with the necessary concepts, tools, and techniques for understanding behavior in organizations, this course attempts to unfold human behavior at three levels (the individual, the group, and the organization). This course involves active learning and develops students' foundation against which the competencies required to create a successful organization can be built and developed.
learning_outcomes: By the end of the course the students are expected to:  CLO1. Comprehend the fundamental concepts in organizational behavior and human resource management and the tight coupling between them  CLO2. Apply concepts of organization behavior to their everyday workplace context  CLO3. Apply frameworks for managing talent at their workplace  CLO4.Comprehend the pros and cons of different organizational structures and apply them, as needed at their workplace.  CLO5.Comprehend the importance of organizational culture and change management strategies

title: Statistics & Basic Econometrics
description_handout: Probability and Probability Distributions, Characteristics of Probability Distributions, Some Important Probability Distributions, statistical inference, estimation and hypothesis testing; ANOVA, MANOVA, MANCOVA, the linear regression model (two-variable model, multiple regression, functional forms, dummy variables); regression analysis in practice (model selection criteria and tests, multicollinearity, heteroskedasticity, autocorrelation), simultaneous-equations models. Statistical package 'R' will be used in this course.
scope_objective: This course serves as an introductory exploration of statistical analysis and fundamental econometrics, wherein the principles of economic theory, mathematics, and statistical inference are employed to examine business phenomena. The curriculum encompasses a review of probability distributions, statistical inference, estimation, and hypothesis testing. It also covers analysis of variance (ANOVA), analysis of covariance (ANCOVA), and introduces multiple regression analysis, which remains the most widely utilized statistical technique within the field of econometrics. The latter part of the course addresses various practical considerations related to linear regression models, including the use of dummy variables, alternative functional forms, and the implications of violating classical regression assumptions. Students will engage in the study and application of regression analysis to diverse data sets, thereby gaining familiarity with core concepts such as the estimation of economic parameters, forecasting business outcomes, and conducting statistical inference. A weekly two-hour laboratory session will be conducted, during which students will learn to explore and analyze different types of economic data using R programming. This component aims to develop proficiency in advanced statistical and econometric techniques through practical applications in R.
learning_outcomes: By the end of this course, students should be able to: CLO1:Apply statistical and econometric models to estimate relevant business parameters, predict economic outcomes, and test hypotheses using quantitative data. CLO2:Understand the fundamental assumptions underlying the classical linear regression model and identify and address potential violations, such as autocorrelation and heteroscedasticity. CLO3:Develop and sustain a foundational knowledge of econometrics that will serve as a basis for further study in business analytics and advanced statistical methodologies.

title: Data Management & Warehousing (DMW)
description_handout: This course introduces students to the practical usage of databases, emphasizing SQL. As big data problems become more prevalent for businesses, this module introduces the basics of databases. After successful completion of the course, students will be able to learn why database management is essential, analyze the data requirements of a business scenario and represent these requirements utilizing entity-relationship (ER) diagrams, translate an ER diagram into normalized tables for a relational database management system, and write simple and relatively complex data retrieval queries. Students will learn how to extract valuable insights from databases through data analytics powered by SQL.
scope_objective: s The course covers various Database Management and Data Warehousing concepts and enhances learning effectiveness through developing scripting skills. It aims to provide students with the necessary knowledge and skills to understand the data infrastructure underpinning business intelligence and analytics. Students undertaking this course should be able to appreciate the complexities involved in Database management and be prepared to solve the issues a business analyst faces.
learning_outcomes:  Understand the database environment and the complete development process, including requirements gathering, design, and implementation.  Model data using Entity-Relationship diagrams and design logical and physical relational databases.  Write effective SQL queries to manage and manipulate data within relational databases.  Explain the architecture of database applications, foundations of data warehousing, and principles of data quality and integration.  Explore the role of databases in Big Data analytics and understand essential tasks in database administration.

title: Deep Learning for Business
description_handout: This course offers an introduction to deep learning and its practical relevance in business contexts. It covers foundational concepts such as neural networks, linear and logistic regression using neural architectures, deep neural networks, hyperparameter tuning, and advanced models like CNNs, RNNs, LSTMs, GANs, and deep reinforcement learning. The course blends theoretical understanding with hands-on applications to solve real-world business problems. It also highlights the challenges and limitations of deep learning methods in practice.
scope_objective: The course aims to equip students with foundational and practical knowledge of deep learning algorithms and their applications in solving business challenges. The course emphasizes: a. Understanding core deep learning architectures and techniques b. Translating business problems into machine learning tasks c. Developing, training, and tuning deep learning models using appropriate tools d. Applying deep learning to solve business challenges e. Utilizing TensorFlow and Keras libraries on Google Colab to implement and explore deep learning algorithms f. Recognizing the limitations, ethical concerns, and interpretability issues of deep models in business decision-making g. title: PRESCRIPTIVE ANALYTICS WITH MATHEMATICAL
scope_objective: Prescriptive analytics is the third and final phase of business analytics, which also includes descriptive and predictive analytics. Referred to as the "final frontier of analytic capabilities", prescriptive analytics entails the application of mathematical and computational sciences and suggests decision options for how to take advantage of the results of descriptive and predictive phases. The first stage of business analytics is descriptive analytics, which still accounts for the majority of all business analytics today. Descriptive analytics looks at past performance and understands that performance by mining historical data to look for the reasons behind past success or failure. Most management reporting – such as sales, marketing, operations, and finance – uses this type of post- mortem analysis. The next phase is predictive analytics. Predictive analytics answers the question of what is likely to happen in the future. This is where historical data is combined with rules, algorithms, and occasionally external data to determine the probable future outcome of an event or the likelihood that a situation will occur. The final phase is prescriptive analytics, which goes beyond predicting future outcomes to suggest actions to benefit from those predictions and show the implications of each decision option. While the term prescriptive analytics was first coined by IBM and was later trademarked by Texas-based company Ayata, the underlying concepts have been around for hundreds of years in the form of Operations Research. Prescriptive Analytics has been considered the next step towards increasing data analytics maturity and leading to optimized, ahead-of-time decision-making for business performance improvement. New Information and Communication Technologies (ICT), such as the Internet of Things (IoT), real-time streaming, and sensor-driven business operations, have bolstered prescriptive analytics and provided businesses with accurate prescriptions, facilitating reliable and effective decision-making. BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHONOLOGY AND SCIENCE, PILANI Pilani Campus Please Consider Your Environmental Responsibilities Do Not Print Unless Necessary Prescriptive analytics assists the decision-maker in identifying the best action (optimal solution) given the problem context. The difference between decisions made using descriptive/predictive analytics and prescriptive analytics is that a prescriptive analytics algorithm seeks the best decision (optimal solution) based on an objective function (sometimes multiple objective functions) and a set of constraints. Prescriptive analytics models attempt to solve complex optimization problems of the modern era. Students will be exposed to a powerful optimization software package, Lingo, so they can formulate and solve real-life Prescriptive Analytics problems. Students can download a trial version (free) of Lingo from https://www.lindo.com/index.php/products/lingo-and-optimization-modeling Using Lingo, large-scale, complex Prescriptive Analytics problems can be solved. 2. title: MARKETING ANALYTICS
scope_objective: ): This course equips students with the analytical frameworks, methods, and tools needed to make evidence-based marketing decisions across the customer lifecycle. It introduces the role of marketing analytics in supporting strategic and operational decisions, distinguishing business intelligence, analytics, and data science, and communicating insights through dashboards and data-driven storytelling. Students will apply analytical techniques to core marketing problems including customer segmentation and positioning, product and pricing analytics, market mix modeling, customer journey analysis, customer experience, retention and lifetime value, digital marketing measurement, and attribution. The course covers methods such as cluster analysis, multidimensional scaling, conjoint analysis, regression, price elasticity modeling, forecasting and diffusion models, principal component analysis, logistic regression, A/B testing, ANOVA, Bayesian networks, and optimization. The course also examines the growing role of artificial intelligence, machine learning, text and image analytics, recommender systems, personalization, and responsible generative AI in marketing. Emphasis is placed on practical interpretation and managerial application of results using tools such as Microsoft Excel, Power BI, DAX, and Python/R. By the end of the course, students will be able to translate marketing data into actionable insights, evaluate marketing performance, and develop data-informed recommendations for products, customers, channels, and brands. title: Financial Modelling and Valuation
scope_objective: s of the Course: A key component of financial management is the act of calculating and managing a company's value. In essence, managers work to increase the value of their companies in two ways: by increasing the firm's productivity through internal (or organic) growth and by making wise acquisitions that play to the company's core competencies. It follows that practically every significant business choice is decided by asking, "What is it worth?" This course's main goal is to arm you with the conceptual foundation, logical framework, and intuitive reasoning needed to make thoughtful decisions on company value. This course's emphasis is on asses ing the value of the entire enterprise and valuing stock in a company. For our study, we'll depend on the income and market approaches of financial valuation. The course begins by presenting a brief framework on the rules regulating financial statements and changes that are frequently needed to capture the underlying company reality because financial statements serve as the foundation for all types of valuation methodologies. We will use spreadsheet for building the financial model of a company. This course will be most helpful to students who are either pursuing a career in investment banking, corporate finance, venture capital, entrepreneurship, or business consulting or who would like to do so. The course also has a broader appeal to people who want to improve their BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus Instruction Division Please Do Not Print Unless Necessary knowledge of financial analysis and discover how companies produce and quantify value for their investors. 2. Format: This is a fairly challenging and ambitious course by design. We will use case studies and problem-solving techniques because the course objectives are grounded on the practical application of academic ideas. There will be lectures and discussions throughout class time. The readings will be integrated into the lectures' analytic principles, which will provide a helpful framework for a deeper comprehension of the instances. Please keep in mind that the goal of a valuation exercise is to use a series of techniques and logical steps that represent the complexity of the situation, not to get it "precise." 3. Text Books: T1 Palepu & Healy, “Business Analysis & Valuation - Using Financial Statements, Text & Cases,” Cengage Learning Publisher, 3rd Edition or Later (For Theoretical Framework) T2 Damodaran, “Valuation: Security Analysis for Investment and Corporate Finance,” John Wiley, 2nd edition or Later (For Financial Modelling Problems)

title: People Analytics
description_handout: There will be three weekly classes. Class time will be devoted to lectures, role-plays, exercises, questionnaire, case discussions and videotapes. Lectures will provide analytical concepts that will integrate the readings and serve as useful framework for a richer understanding of cases and role-plays. Role-plays, cases and videotapes provide the "application" aspects of this course. These participative activities are further enhanced by rigorous self-review (through Journal, Follow-up Report and Critique). Tests and Project will provide an opportunity to test comprehension of the theory and readings.
scope_objective: People Analytics is the application of data science and information technology in the domain of Human resource management. The present course is designed to progress the understanding of the role of data-driven decisions about people's issues in an organization. This emerging discipline signifies the strategic role of HR function in the contemporary organizations. However, with the advent of analytics, it has evolved into a holistic function taking care of all people related aspects at the workplace, not only traditional HR operations. It serves as a key driver in pursuit of sustainable competitive advantage for organizations by leveraging data driven practices for an improved decision making. Grounded on 4Ts principle: Task, Theory, Technique, and Technology; the course integrates underlying theories and principles, and data analytical tools and techniques to drive business objectives. The course is structured to equip students with hands-on experience on analytical softwares to track, maintain, retrieve, analyze, and interpret HR data (e.g., staffing, skills, performance ratings and compensation information) to contribute to business outcomes. This will serve the twin purpose of elevating the students’ understanding on nuances of analytics in organizations, which will aid in students’ value addition and employability. The learning objectives of the course are as under:  This course introduces the student to the theory, concepts, and business application of human resources research, data, metrics, systems, analyses, and reporting. title: Pharmaceutical Analysis
description_handout: Basic techniques of pharmaceutical analysis, data handling and analysis, sources of error in analysis. The analytical methods would comprise various titrimetric methods, such as acid-base, complexometric, non-aqueous, oxidation-reduction, precipitation, conductometric; physical and instrumental analysis such as gravimetric, polarography, nephelometry, amperometry, turbidometry, potentiometry; chromatographic separations such as TLC, column, ion-exchange, extraction methods such as gel-filtration, fractionation processes, analysis of metallic and non-metallic elements; water content, as well as evaluation of drug constituents in various pharmaceutical preparation.

title: Biological Chemistry
description_handout: This course focuses upon the physiological and medical significance of important biomolecules along with their use as drug targets. The course also elaborates the role of vitamins as prosthetic groups of enzymes and enzyme kinetics and regulation. The course deals with the understanding of chemical structures, biochemical reactions metabolic pathways related to carbohydrates, lipids, nucleic acids and protein synthesis and diseases arising from defects in these pathways.
scope_objective: The aim of this course is to describe and explain all biochemical processes of living organisms and their interactions with their networking both in health and disease conditions.
learning_outcomes: Understanding of basic metabolic pathways, diseases associated with errors in the pathways and drug targeting.

description_handout: Pharmacology of important classes of drugs including their mechanisms of action, therapeutic uses, side effects, toxic manifestations, indications and contraindications.

title: PHARMACEUTICAL FORMULATIONS II
description_handout: Physical, chemical, and biopharmaceutical considerations in formulations, absorption, distribution, and elimination of drugs; pharmaceutical additives; formulation, manufacturing, packaging, quality control, and stability of solid dosage forms, semi-solid dosage forms, liquids dosage forms, and sterile preparations including parenteral suspensions, emulsions, depot formulations; microencapsulation and controlled release formulations; targeted drug delivery systems; multi-unit particulate systems; transdermal, gastroretentive, and nasopulmonary drug delivery systems; aerosol products and packaging.
scope_objective: It is a course intended to give students insight into the problems involved in making drug dosage forms. It brings together the various sciences involved in developing pharmaceutical product formulations and evaluating their quality. The laboratory component involves some fundamental exercises in the evolution of products such as tablets, ointments, solutions, parenteral products, sustained-action medications, etc. It also imparts knowledge of newer dosage forms.
learning_outcomes: CLO1. Explain the principles of preformulation, formulation, manufacturing, packaging, quality control, and stability of conventional pharmaceutical dosage forms, including solid, liquid, semi-solid, and sterile preparations. CLO2. Apply pharmaceutical formulation principles and standard manufacturing techniques to prepare and evaluate conventional and modified-release dosage forms, while adhering to Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP) and quality requirements. CLO3. Compare and evaluate the design, advantages, limitations, and pharmaceutical applications of novel drug delivery systems, including controlled-release, targeted, transdermal, gastroretentive, multiparticulate, nasopulmonary, and aerosol dosage forms.

title: QUALITY ASSURANCE & REGULATORY AFFAIRS
description_handout: Quality control, assurance and management, various parameters for achieving quality pharmaceutical products, application of statistics in quality assurance, reliability, cGMP for pharmaceutical manufacturing , pharmaceutical process validation, drug regulatory affairs, clinical research protocols, new drug applications. 1. Scope and Objective of the course: This course deals with the basic need of quality in the manufacturing of Pharmaceutical products and it's build up with the help of quality control and quality assurance management. Various current Good Manufacturing Practices (cGMP) to be followed in a pharmaceutical organization and its validation procedure are part of the course. title: Immunopharmacology
scope_objective: This course covers key immunologic concepts: how the components of the immune system are generated, organized, and function; the mechanisms that lead to beneficial immune responses, immune disorders, and immunodeficiencies; methods to identify immune reactions; and ways to manipulate the immune system and its components to benefit the patient. This course will give the students an advanced understanding of the principles and mechanisms of the immune system and immune responses in the context of infection, malignancy and immunological disorders. The course will also enable the students to describe the fundamental mechanisms underlying immunologic disease and associate these mechanisms with strategies for therapeutic modulation of the immune system. It will help the students to gain the necessary transferable and research skills in basic and clinical immunology to promote lifelong learning and career development. 2. Text Book : 1. Kuby Immunology by Owen et al., 7th Ed. Freeman press. 2013. 3. Reference Books : 1. Janeway's Immunobiology, Eighth Edition. 2. Cellular and Molecular Immunology, Abul K. Abbas, Eighth Edition.

Characterization of nanopharmaceutcials using Atomic Force Microscopy (AFM), Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM), Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM), Dynamic Light Scattering (DLS) techniques. 1H and 13C Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) spectroscopy in structural characterization, Mass Spectrometry and its applications, Elemental analysis, Optical, chiro-optical techniques in structure elucidation.
learning_outcomes: Handling of analytical instruments for performing qualitative and quantitative analyses of drugs. Design and development of suitable analytical methods for drugs based on their physico-chemical characters meeting the standard requirements. Ability to interpret the analytical graphs and spectra for drug identification, characterization

title: Advanced Physical Pharmaceutics
description_handout: Physicochemical principles involved in effective formulation development, including various aspects like, pharmaceutical preformulation including bulk characteristics, polymorphism, solubility analysis, solid and solution state stability, compatibility. This course also cover various ICH guidelines like stability study, specifications, impurities which are required during formulation development. This course also discussed details about mechanical properties of powders, principles of dissolution, in-vitro in-vivo correlation (IVIVC), polymer science, etc.

title: CLINICAL RESEARCH
description_handout: Overview of new drug research and development; Bioethics and institutional review board; regulatory control of clinical trials for NDA & ANDA application; Good Clinical Practice (GCP); related ICH guidelines; applied clinical epidemiology and biostatistics; clinical trial study design; trial development (protocol, case report form, and data management); clinical trial management- coordinating clinical trial at the site, documentation methodology, implementing monitoring plan and performing quality control; statistical analysis and data interpretation; monitoring obligations and methods; and Medical writing & report preparation for various submissions.
scope_objective: There is a growing need for clinical researchers in the health industries (pharmaceutical, biotechnology/medical device companies, research institutes, and hospitals) involved in the development of new drugs and therapies. This course is aimed at training students in conducting clinical trials on humans with new drugs/therapies before they are introduced to the market. Students completing the coursework will gain specialized knowledge and skills required to design, monitor, and manage clinical trials. Courses include the drug development process; regulations, guidelines, and standards; research methodology and biostatistics; clinical trial organization, monitoring, and documentation; and project management. 3. title: Pharmaceutical Biotechnology
scope_objective: The course deals with the principles and techniques of biotechnology with direct application in the field of pharmaceutical sciences. It aims at bringing together the principles of molecular biology, molecular genetics, biochemical engineering, protein engineering, enzymtechnology, bio- informatics required to develop a successful biotechnology based pharmaceutical product. The applications of genetic engineering, recombinant DNA technology, hybridoma technology, transgenic animals, gene therapy, drug delivery aspects of biotechnology products and their clinical evaluation are also dealt with in this course. 1. title: Pharmaceutical Administration & Management (PAM)
description_handout: This course introduces students to various organizational aspects, focusing on pharmaceutical management. Topics include technology innovation, drug planning, strategy, project execution, product development, production, scale-up, marketing, IPR, HR, industrial relations, documentation, R&D, and ethics.
scope_objective: The objective of the course is to help students understand new drug and product considerations and planning; strategic considerations; project implementation; product development; production management & scale-up; marketing strategy; human resources development; ethical issues; and R&D management.

CLO3: Analyze the roles of research and development (R&D) management, human resource development, industrial relations, and ethical practices in achieving sustainable and compliant pharmaceutical operations.

title: Retrosynthetic Analysis
description_handout: This course deals with the strategy and tactics involved in the synthesis of organic molecules. The idea is to identify key structural features in the target molecules and then go backward logically to identify appropriate starting materials and chemical reactions for their synthesis. Knowledge and understanding of common organic reagents and reaction mechanisms are required for this course.
scope_objective: Most life-saving drugs are organic molecules. This course aims to develop a logical understanding which can be used to propose the synthesis of an organic compound. This course teaches various strategies and tactics together with the common nomenclature used in Retrosynthetic Analysis. At the end of the course, students should be able to propose a synthetic scheme for various drug molecules with appropriate justification. 3. title: Pharmaceutical Applications of Polymers and Biopolymers
scope_objective: This course includes the analysis of polymers and biopolymers at a molecular scale, and design of devices used in contact with biological systems. Topics include molecular interactions between bio- and synthetic molecules and surfaces; design, synthesis, and processing approaches for materials that control cell functions; and application of state-of-the-art materials science to problems in tissue engineering, drug delivery, vaccines, and cell-guiding surfaces. This course covers the fundamental concepts (physical chemistry, chemistry, and materials physics, and biology) behind the design at a molecular scale of synthetic materials with biological functions. 2. title: Classical Mechanics
description_handout: This course introduces the principles of classical mechanics from Newtonian and analytical perspectives. It covers constrained motion, Lagrangian and Hamiltonian formulations, variational principles, central-force dynamics, canonical transformations, Poisson brackets, the kinematics and dynamics of rigid bodies in inertial, and rotating reference frames. Scope & Objectives: To provide a strong foundation in analytical mechanics and equip students with the mathematical and physical tools required to formulate, analyze, and solve problems in classical mechanics with elegance and rigor. Importantly, the course serves as a gateway to advanced topics in theoretical physics, including quantum mechanics, statistical mechanics, electrodynamics, and general relativity. Course learning outcomes:  Apply vector calculus, generalized coordinates, and analytical methods to formulate and solve problems involving the motion of particles and systems with constraints using Lagrangian and Hamiltonian formulations.  Analyze central-force motion and variational principles to derive equations of motion, identify conserved quantities, investigate orbital dynamics and stability, and explain the role of symmetries in classical mechanics.  Employ Hamiltonian mechanics, canonical transformations, generating functions, and Poisson brackets to transform, simplify, and solve dynamical systems while recognizing canonical invariants.  Evaluate the kinematics and dynamics of rigid bodies using orthogonal transformations, Euler angles, and rotating reference frames, including the analysis of Coriolis and related (non) inertial effects. Text Books: T1. H. Goldstein, C. Poole, and J. Safko, Classical Mechanics, Third Edition, Pearson Edu. Inc., 2002. T2. N. C. Rana and P. S. Joag, Classical Mechanics, McGraw Hill, First Edition, 2008. Reference Books:  L. D. Landau and E. M. Lifshitz, Mechanics, Third Edition, Butterworth-Heinemann, 2000.  L. N. Hand and J. D. Finch, Analytical Mechanics, Cambridge Univ. Press, 1998. 1 BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division Course Plan: T1 ==>Text Book-1, T2 ==> Text Book-2, CN ==> Class Notes Lecture Learning Objectives Topics Learning Outcome Ref. 0 A Few mathematical tools Vector Algebra: Basic Operations, Differential Operators (Gradient, divergence, curl, and Laplacian) in curvilinear coordinate systems, Multivariable Calculus (total derivatives and chain rule) Apply vector algebra, differential operators in curvilinear coordinate systems, and multivariable calculus to formulate and solve problems in classical mechanics. CN (Self revision) 1 Kinematics & dynamics of a mechanical system in Newtonian approach: A very brief overview Newtonian mechanics for a particle/system of particles: Conservation principles, etc. Recall the fundamental concepts of Newtonian kinematics and dynamics relevant to analytical mechanics. T1: 1.1 - 1.2 (Self revision), CN 2-3 Newtonian approach: A Critical analysis Constrained Motions: Classification of constraints. Degree of freedom (DOF), generalized coordinates. Determine the degrees of freedom of mechanical systems, and formulate their motion using generalized coordinates. title: OPTICS
description_handout: The course will cover Geometrical optics, wave optics, Diffraction, Laser theory, and the recent trends of research in the optical physics.
scope_objective: The objective of the course is to give an introduction to basic phenomena in optics and the techniques used to deal with them. The recent development of the subject and its application in the research level will be discussed. Course will assume a basic knowledge of optics at the level of the core Physics courses. The course will also provide theoretical background for the optics experiments done in Electromagnetism & Optics Lab. (PHYF214). 3. Text Books: Optics: Ajoy Ghatak, 8th Edition, Tata McGraw Hill 4. title: STATISTICAL MECHANICS
description_handout: This is a first course on Statistical mechanics aimed at students who have familiarity with classical mechanics, quantum mechanics, and classical thermodynamics. The stress is on developing the essential techniques of equilibrium statistical mechanics for non-interacting systems. Classical Thermodynamics, as a study of macroscopic properties of materials, is no doubt an incredibly elegant interface between us and nature. Historically born out of the remarkable power of empiricism in the nineteenth century, the laws of Thermodynamics have stood the test of time. In its breadth of generality and profundity, the subject has found applications in almost all areas of fundamental and applied sciences. Here, we must note that scientific pedagogy is not necessarily chronologically ordered. The fast development in our understanding of matter at the microscopic level through advances in the atomic theories in the twentieth century required classical thermodynamics to find reconciliation with physics at the microscopic level. The role of statistics in bridging the laws of mechanics with those of thermodynamics is probably as profound as the laws themselves. In a first course on statistical mechanics aimed towards a target audience comprising undergraduate students of basic sciences and engineering it is important to reveal the subject in its broad, multi-layered beauty. The course aims to look at Thermodynamics as an emergent phenomenon and emphasize the role of statistics in bridging the microscopic and macroscopic descriptions.
scope_objective: ❖ Develop familiarity with the basic techniques of equilibrium statistical mechanics. ❖ Understand the role of probability theory and statistics in relating microscopic and macroscopic descriptions of thermodynamic systems ❖ Learn key methods of ensemble theory ❖ Distinguish between quantum and classical statistical mechanics and compute essential properties of ideal Bosonic and Fermionic systems. 3. title: Computational Physics
description_handout: The course introduces elementary computational methods for obtaining approximate solutions to mathematical problems arising in physics. Topics include root finding, systems of linear equations, numerical quadrature, ordinary and partial differential equations, Monte Carlo simulation, and Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods. Emphasis will be placed on the hands-on implementation of basic algorithms and their application to representative physical systems.
scope_objective: The objective of the course is to develop a practical understanding of the basic numerical methods used to obtain approximate solutions of mathematical problems arising in physics. Emphasis will be placed on the hands-on construction of elementary algorithms, the translation of equations into finite computational procedures, and the interpretation and validation of numerical results. Students will also learn to use scientific programming and visualization tools, including Monte Carlo and Markov Chain Monte Carlo techniques, for studying relevant physical systems. 3. Textbooks: 1. title: Particle Physics
description_handout: (Just as every book has a preface, I will avail this space to elaborate about the course in great detail. It will be a synopsis of particle physics, providing context for the questions it addresses and a sense of the answers that will be discussed in the course. Hopefully, it will give you a fair idea of what particle physics is all about and what to expect from this course. The titles of paragraphs may seem out of place or even nonsensical in the first reading. Some things will fall in place as you read through the handout. For some other stuff, you may have to wait till the end of the course.) Bright blue sky: What are the most fundamental questions we can pose in Physics? 1. What are the most fundamental building blocks (called particles for the want of a better word) of the Universe? 2. What are the fundamental forces (interaction is a better word) that bind them to form the structural hierarchy we see at different levels? 3. What can we know about the particles and their dynamics if we know the answers to the above questions? 4. Are there fundamental principles that mandate the existence of different kinds of fundamental particles and different kinds of fundamental interactions? Is there an overarching theme in the answers we know? Particle Physics aims to offer concrete answers to the above questions, though some caveats remain. Our present understanding of these questions is summarised in the so-called Standard Model (SM) of Particle Physics. This course will offer some answers within the framework of the Standard Model of Particle Physics. Relativity + Quantum Mechanics = Quantum Field Theory: Before I give a glimpse of answers to the above questions, we must ask for the framework for particle physics. It turns out that the natural framework for particle physics is a quantum theory for a system of fields. Let us understand the reason behind this. We will be talking about the most fundamental particles and their interactions at the minutest length scales, so quantum mechanics is inescapable. To study smaller and smaller length scales, we need probes whose wavelengths are sufficiently small. Thus, we use extremely high-energy particles (relativistic velocities imply larger momentum and hence smaller wavelengths). Hence, special relativity is a must. How about the study of mesons (bound states of quarks-antiquarks) and BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 2 baryons (bound states of three quarks)? Here again, surprisingly, it is quantum mechanics that ensures relativistic conditions. Whenever you confine a quantum system to a tiny volume, uncertainties in the momenta become extremely large, implying relativistic conditions. Thus, quarks inside protons and neutrons are quite hot and hence relativistic. Now, under relativistic conditions, you can literally "cook" an arbitrarily large number of particles-antiparticle pairs, if you pump in a sufficient amount of energy. Thus, your underlying dynamical system must be inherently capable of describing situations involving an arbitrarily large number of particles. Thus, any framework with a fixed number of particles is doomed to fail. A system of fields with infinitely many degrees of freedom is the right dynamical system to describe relativistic interactions. Thus, relativity + quantum mechanics = Quantum Field Theory. Quantum Field Theory is demanding, and a typical graduate school has at least two courses in Quantum Field Theory before one can survey any literature in Particle Physics. However, the purpose of any undergraduate course in particle physics is essentially twofold: a) to provide a glimpse of the power of symmetry principles in the origin and classification of fundamental particles and their interactions, and b) to demonstrate the power of perturbative calculations of scattering cross-sections and decay rates via Feynman rules. To meet this end, we will follow an approach pioneered by Richard Feynman. This is the structure and approach of a first course in particle physics worldwide. It is just not possible to do squeeze in relativistic quantum field theory and particle physics in one semester, without any prior exposure to either of them. title: SOFT CONDENSED MATTER PHYSICS
description_handout: Soft matter or soft condensed matter is a subfield of condensed matter comprising a variety of physical systems that are deformed or structurally altered by thermal or mechanical stress of the magnitude of thermal fluctuations. They include liquids, colloids, polymers, foams, gels, granular materials, liquid crystals, and biomolecules. These materials share an essential characteristic feature in that predominant physical behaviors occur at an energy scale comparable with room temperature thermal energy. At these temperatures, quantum aspects are less significant. In this course, our aim would be to understand the structure, properties, and dynamics of the soft matter. What is the order of forces and times scales that affect the overall behaviour of this class of matter?
scope_objective: • Develop familiarity with the basics of soft condensed matter. • To develop an understanding about the forces and order of thermal fluctuations in soft matter. • Why some part of matter is classified as soft matter? 3. title: Group Theory and Applications
description_handout: This is an introductory course on Group Theory, designed for undergraduates and PhD scholars, with an emphasis on applications in physics. Many physical systems exhibit symmetry, which allows for a simplified analysis. The mathematical language of describing and studying a vast class of these symmetries is Group Theory. In each case, the symmetry operations are represented by individual group elements and their combinations. Discrete symmetries entail discrete groups, which may contain a finite or infinite number of elements. Continuous symmetries entail continuous groups (also called as ‘Lie groups’). In this course, we will cover the structure, classification, and representations of groups. We will see how group theory can help us understands some aspects of quantum mechanics, classical mechanics, and most importantly, particle interactions.
scope_objective: • Identify and classify discrete and continuous symmetries in physical systems using the foundational concepts of group theory. • Apply the principles of representation theory to decompose group representations into irreducible components and interpret their physical significance. • Demonstrate the application of group theory in quantum mechanics by analyzing the symmetry structure of the hydrogen atom and explaining the role of conserved quantities and degeneracies. • Analyze physical systems under spacetime symmetry transformations using continuous groups such as the Lorentz and Poincaré groups. • Analyze particle interactions and fundamental forces using the mathematical framework of Lie groups and Lie algebras. 3. title: Physics of Semiconductor Devices

The structure of any solid material plays an important role in their operation; the discussion will start with basic crystal structures and will cover the quantum theory of solids. In the later part of the course the discussion will be focused on the voltage current behavior of the devices. In the last part of the course, some special devices like solar cells, light emitting diodes etc. will be discussed.

title: Classical and Quantum Waves
description_handout: This course takes us from the study of oscillations to waves, and finally to the foundations of quantum mechanics, tracing a connected thread through classical and modern physics. We begin with an introduction to oscillations and the model of simple harmonic oscillations, damped and forced oscillations, leading to the phenomenon of resonance. We shall study coupled oscillators: normal modes and frequencies, and the continuum limit of a large number of coupled oscillators. We will study transverse vibrations of a stretched string, the one-dimensional wave equation, and traveling wave solutions to the wave equation. We shall study energy transport in waves and pulses on a string, and their interaction with a boundary: reflection and refraction. Wave phenomena, such as the interference of light waves from two coherent sources, will lead us to wave-particle duality, the concept of the photon, the de Broglie hypothesis, and matter waves. We shall study the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, the Schrödinger equation, and the wavefunction. We shall study the quantum problem of a particle in a one-dimensional box, energy quantization, barrier tunneling, the transmission coefficient, and introduce scanning tunneling microscopy as an application of quantum tunneling.
scope_objective: ● Understand oscillatory motion: Analyze simple harmonic motion, superposition of oscillations, and the effects of damping and external driving forces, including resonance and quality factor ● Master the physics of coupled systems and waves: Explain how coupled oscillators lead to normal modes, and how taking the continuum limit gives rise to wave phenomena, including the wave equation, traveling waves, and energy transport ● Analyze wave behavior and propagation: Distinguish between group and phase velocity, and describe how waves interact with boundaries and each other through reflection, refraction, and interference ● Grasp the foundations of quantum mechanics: Explain wave-particle duality, the de Broglie hypothesis, and the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, and apply the Schrödinger equation to determine wavefunctions and BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 2 energy quantization in simple systems ● Apply quantum tunneling to real-world technology: Calculate transmission coefficients for barrier tunneling and connect this phenomenon to practical applications such as scanning tunneling microscopy 3. Text Books: T1 Vibrations and Waves, A.P. French, CBS, 2003 T2 Concepts of Modern Physics by Arthur Beiser, Shobit Mahajan, and S. Rai Choudhury, Tata McGraw-Hill Companies, 2006 4. Reference Books: 1. R1: Physics Vol I & II, Halliday/Resnick/Krane 5th Edition, John Wiley, 2003 2. R2: Quantum Physics of Atoms, Molecules, Solids, Nuclei, and Particles, Eisberg & Resnick, John Wiley & Sons (2nd edition, 1985) 5. Course Learning Outcomes: 1. Develop the ability to analyze and understand oscillatory mechanical systems that are coupled 2. Ability to solve the wave equation for certain boundary conditions 3. To understand Interference and diffraction phenomena 4. To describe wave-particle duality and the photon concept, derive the de Broglie wavelength for matter waves, and articulate the physical meaning of the Heisenberg uncertainty principle 5. Solve the Schrödinger equation for a particle in a one-dimensional box, interpret the resulting wavefunctions, and calculate the quantized energy levels of the system 6. Calculate the transmission coefficient for a particle tunneling through a potential barrier, and explain how this phenomenon underlies the operation of a scanning tunneling microscope 6. title: Introduction to Classical and Quantum Waves
description_handout: Introduction to oscillations, simple harmonic motion, superposition of harmonic oscillations, damped and forced oscillations, resonance and quality factor: transverse and longitudinal waves, wave speed in a stretched string, wave equation in one dimension, traveling solutions to the wave equation, energy transport in waves, standing waves, travelling sound waves; Interference of light waves, introduction to diffraction; concept of photon, photoelectric effect, Compton scattering; wave-particle duality, de Broglie hypothesis and matter waves; 1D Quantum wave functions: properties and applications; Pauli’s exclusion principle and multielectrons atoms, introduction to X-rays and Lasers.
scope_objective: This course introduces the fundamental concepts of classical and quantum waves, beginning with simple harmonic motion as the basis of oscillatory phenomena and progressing through mechanical waves, sound, interference, and diffraction. It then explores the transition from classical to quantum physics by examining the wave-particle nature of light and matter, culminating in an elementary introduction to quantum wave functions and their applications to atomic systems, X-rays, and lasers. Designed for undergraduate students with a basic knowledge of calculus, the course emphasizes physical intuition, conceptual understanding, and qualitative reasoning over advanced mathematical formalism. Its objective is to provide a unified understanding of wave phenomena across classical and quantum physics, establish the conceptual foundations of modern physics, and prepare students for advanced courses in optics, quantum mechanics, condensed matter physics, and related disciplines. 3. Textbooks: (i) Principles of Physics (10th Edition) by Halliday, Resnick, and Walker, John Wiley & Sons. (T.B.) 4. Reference Books: (i) Physics, Vols. 1 & 2, by Halliday, Resnick, & Krane, 5th Ed., John Wiley & Sons. 2002. (ii) Berkeley Physics Course, Vol. 3, Waves, by Frank S. Crawford Jr, Special Indian Edition, McGraw-Hill, 2011. (iii) Fundamentals of Optics, Fourth International Edition, Jenkins & White, McGraw-Hill, 1981. (iv) Concepts of Modern Physics, 7th Edition, Arthur Beiser, McGraw-Hill, 2017 5. Course Learning Outcomes: (i) Explain the principles of simple harmonic motion and analyze damped and forced oscillations, resonance, and the superposition of oscillatory motion as the foundation of wave phenomena. 1 BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division (ii) Describe the behavior of classical waves, including wave propagation, wave equations, energy transport, sound waves, and the formation of standing waves in one-dimensional systems. (iii) Explain the wave nature of light through interference and diffraction and discuss the experimental observations that established the quantum nature of light, including the photoelectric effect and Compton scattering. (iv) Describe the concept of matter waves by explaining wave-particle duality, the de Broglie hypothesis, and the extension of wave concepts from light to material particles. (v) Interpret the physical meaning of quantum wave functions in one dimension and explain their role in describing quantum systems, including an introductory understanding of multi-electron atoms through Pauli's exclusion principle and the principles of X-rays and lasers. 6. title: Advanced Operations Management
description_handout: Types of Manufacturing, Manufacturing, maintenance, quality and service operations management concepts. Manufacturing Management measures, Factory/plant performance, Operations Improvement framework. Maintenance management, optimising maintenance costs; Improving asset lifecycle; Preventive maintenance; Total productive maintenance (TPM); Quality management - practices and processes; Total quality management (TQM); Service Operations Management definition; Customer loyalty and satisfaction.
scope_objective: This course details the various aspects and emerging concepts of operations management as they relate to the manufacturing/production function, maintenance, quality, and service operations. It provides a detailed view of each of the above functions, including their strategic importance, operational aspects, and roles in the supply chain. The objectives of the course are mentioned below: • This course will give students an overview of the various components of manufacturing and maintenance management as practised on the shop floor. The various kinds of manufacturing operations, the types of jobs performed, and the maintenance activities undertaken to ensure operational readiness and integration with other functions of the industry will be discussed. This will help one understand how the shop-floor execution and upkeep of resources (machines/equipment) are critical to the functioning of a coherent supply chain. • This will help the students to understand the importance of quality management. Explain the various quality management tools and techniques used in an organisation to ensure that quality products and services are produced. • This course will provide an overview of the service operations management. Customer service design, service operations and execution, and monitoring service delivery performance will be discussed. 3. Text Books: T1: Roberta S. Russell, Bernard W. title: Fundamentals of Nanoscience and Nanotechnology
description_handout: Nanotechnology is widely regarded as a transformative field with the potential to address critical challenges in energy, healthcare, electronics, and advanced manufacturing. This course is designed to introduce students to the fundamental concepts of nanoscience and nanotechnology, preparing them for further academic research or industrial careers in this rapidly evolving area. The course focuses on the fundamental science behind nanomaterials, their synthesis and properties, with emphasis on their size-dependent physical, chemical, electrical, optical, and thermal properties. Applications of nanomaterials in electronics, medicine, MEMS, photonics, catalysis, energy systems, and heat transfer will be discussed. The course also introduces essential quantum mechanical concepts relevant to nanoscale systems. In addition, emerging trends, large-scale manufacturing challenges, and future directions in nanoscience and nanotechnology are covered.
scope_objective: The course is structured to provide a comprehensive and interdisciplinary overview of nanoscience and nanotechnology. Students will learn common methods for the synthesis of nanoparticles and nanostructures. Special emphasis is placed on understanding the unique properties of nanomaterials and the scientific principles governing their behavior at the nanoscale. The course highlights real-world motivations and applications of nanomaterials across multiple technological domains. This course is well suited for students seeking foundational knowledge and practical exposure to nanoscience and nanotechnology, and serves as an effective entry point into advanced study or research in the field.
learning_outcomes: After successful completion of this course, the student will be able to: 2 BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus ACADEMIC— UNDER GRADUATE STUDIES DIVISION ◦Explain the fundamental principles of nanoscience, including size-dependent properties and quantum effects at the nanoscale. ◦Describe and compare common synthesis techniques used for nanomaterials. ◦Analyze the structure–property–application relationships of nanomaterials in areas such as electronics, energy, catalysis, and biomedical systems.

title: Fundamentals of Solid-State Physics
description_handout: This course provides a comprehensive introduction to the fundamental concepts of solid-state physics with a particular emphasis on semiconductor materials and their applications. It covers crystal structures and defects, the quantum and statistical principles governing electron behavior in solids, the origin of energy bands, and the electronic properties of metals, semiconductors, and insulators. The course further introduces carrier transport mechanisms, including drift, diffusion, and the Hall effect, before discussing the thermal, magnetic, and optical properties of solids. Throughout the course, the underlying physical principles are connected to modern semiconductor devices such as LEDs, solar cells, photodetectors, and sensors, providing students with the essential foundation required for advanced studies in materials science, condensed matter physics, and semiconductor technology.
scope_objective: This course introduces the fundamental principles of solid-state physics that underpin the behavior of crystalline materials and modern semiconductor devices. It encompasses crystal structures, basic quantum and statistical concepts, electronic band theory, semiconductor physics, and the thermal, magnetic, and optical properties of solids, while emphasizing their relevance to contemporary electronic and optoelectronic technologies. The primary objective is to develop a clear understanding of the relationship between the atomic structure of solids and their physical properties, explain the quantum mechanical origin of electronic behavior in materials, introduce the principles governing charge transport in semiconductors, and establish the scientific foundation necessary for the study, analysis, and application of semiconductor materials and devices in advanced engineering and physics courses.
learning_outcomes: (i) Describe crystal structures, Bravais lattices, crystal systems, common crystal structures, and Miller indices, and explain their significance in determining the physical properties of crystalline solids. (ii) Apply the fundamental principles of quantum mechanics to explain wave-particle duality, quantized energy levels, and the origin of electronic states in solids. (iii) Differentiate between Maxwell–Boltzmann, Bose–Einstein, and Fermi–Dirac statistics, and explain the statistical behavior of electrons and other particles in solids. (iv) Explain electrical conduction in solids using the Drude model and band theory, and relate density of states and effective mass to the electronic properties of materials. (v) Analyze the electrical properties of intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors and explain carrier transport through drift, diffusion, and the Hall effect. BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 2 (vi) Explain the thermal and magnetic properties of solids in terms of lattice vibrations, phonons, heat capacity, and magnetic ordering. (vii) Explain the optical properties of semiconductors and relate them to the operation of optoelectronic devices, including LEDs, solar cells, photodetectors, and semiconductor sensors.

title: ELECTRONIC DEVICES
description_handout: (as per the Bulletin): Crystal structure and growth of semiconductor, electrical conduction in solids, Elementary quantum physics (Photoelectric effect, uncertainty principle, Schrodinger wave equation and tunneling), energy bands in solids, charge carriers in semiconductors, excess carriers in semiconductors, Fabrication of p-n junctions, equilibrium conditions, forward and reverse biased junctions, metal-semiconductor junctions Bipolar junction transistors, field effect transistors (JFET, HEMT, MOSFET), Special diodes (varactor diode, solar cell, LEDs, Tunnel diode and HBT).
scope_objective: s: The course provides a comprehensive understanding of the characteristics, operation and limitations of semiconductor devices. This course starts with explanation on crystal structure, semiconductor materials, fundamentals of semiconductors. This course helps in developing the understanding about excess carriers in semiconductors and its application. In-depth study on ‘junctions’ prepares the students for even a detailed study on devices to be studied later like FET, BJT, MOSFET viz. commonly employed in Integrated Circuit (IC) technology. Concepts of optoelectronic diodes will also be discussed in this course.
learning_outcomes: At the end of this course, students will be able to:  CLO1: Explain the fundamentals of semiconductor materials, crystal structures, electrical conduction, quantum physics concepts, and energy band theory governing electronic devices.  CLO2: Analyze charge carrier transport, excess carrier behavior, and the electrical characteristics of semiconductor materials under equilibrium and non-equilibrium conditions.  CLO3: Evaluate the operation and characteristics of semiconductor junctions, including p-n junctions, metal-semiconductor junctions, and their behavior under forward and reverse bias conditions.  CLO4: Explain the operating principles, characteristics, and applications of major semiconductor devices, including BJTs, JFETs, HEMTs, MOSFETs, and special semiconductor diodes.  CLO5: Apply the fundamental principles of semiconductor device physics to analyze the performance and limitations of electronic and optoelectronic devices used in modern integrated circuits and electronic systems.

title: SOFTWARE ENGINEERING AND MANAGEMENT
description_handout: Software engineering is a discipline that allows us to apply engineering and computer science con- cepts in the development and maintenance of reliable, usable, and dependable software. There are several areas to focus on within software engineering, such as requirement specification, de- sign, development, testing, maintenance and project management. Software development outside of the classroom is a very complex process, mostly because real-world software is much larger and more complex. The purpose of this course is to present software engineering as a body of knowledge. The course is designed to present software engineering concepts and principles in parallel with the software development life cycle.
scope_objective: This course provides an ability to identify, formulate, and solve complex engineering problems by applying principles of engineering, science, and mathematics. This also develops an ability to function effectively in a team whose members together provide leadership, create a collaborative and inclusive environment, establish goals, plan tasks, and meet objectives. In addition, this course also facilitates an ability to develop and conduct appropriate experimentation, analyze and interpret data, and use engineering judgment to draw conclusions

title: Object Oriented Analysis and Design
description: The course covers the object oriented analysis and design methodology, requirements-analysis using a use case model, use interaction models to capture the requirements and the design of the solution, in sufficient detail. The course will also cover topics like design patterns, implementation, testing, and architecture with respect to object oriented systems. After completion of the course the students will have good understanding of object oriented analysis and design using the unified process and will be able to apply the methodology to typical cases. title: Derivatives & Risk Management
description: The objective of this course is to provide students an introductory level familiarity with a particular type of financial instruments known as DERIVATIVES. To achieve the stated objectives, the course provides a detailed description on the structure (read, design) and utility (read, relevance) of the most common and popular financial derivatives namely, Options, Futures, and Swaps. The scope of the course entails acquainting students with the mechanics of trading and settlement of derivative instruments in the financial markets and their function as insurance products for hedging financial risk. No understanding about financial instruments or their derivatives is complete without a thorough grasp over interest rate concepts and hence the course also includes discussion on topics such as time value of money, term structure of interest rates and their role in valuation of bonds, computation of yield and forward interest rates, estimating bond-price volatility, and the role of bond duration and convexity in mitigating interest rate risks. The topics covered in the course will, at an introductory level, enable participants to learn about common risks prevalent in the financial markets and how to manage its impact on investment exposure by using derivatives. Discussion on valuation of financial derivatives and a brief introduction to creating synthetic investment positions by combining derivatives prepares students for advanced level courses such as Financial Engineering and Financial Risk Analytics and Management. The course concludes with a survey of selective topics of contemporary interest to risk management industry such as forecasting volatility, estimating value-at-risk, etc. The topics covered in the course will also assist students in preparing for competitive professional international certifications such as Financial Risk Manager (FRM) and Chartered Financial Analyst (CFA). 2. Prerequisites: This is an elementary course on Derivatives and Risk Management and does not assume any prior knowledge of Financial Markets, Instruments and Derivatives. However, familiarity of basic economic theory such as law of supply and demand, utility maximization principle, compounding and discounting of cash flows, etc. are desirable. The course is not mathematically rigorous and a first-year course on elementary linear algebra, calculus, probability, and differential equations will be sufficient to grasp the contents of the course. It is expected that students have technical know-how of MS excel as it will be used to demonstrate required computations, wherever required, and for carrying out take-home assignments. title: RISK MANAGEMENT AND INSURANCE
description: Introduction to risk; types of risk; risk measurement; risk management techniques; risk avoidance, loss control, loss financing, risk retention, risk transfer, internal risk reduction through diversification etc.; insurance business and operations; insurance pricing; insurance v/s hedging; life, health and income risk; property and liability risk – commercial and personal; social insurance; insurance regulation 2 Scope and Objective of the Course: This course will examine the way in which business and society make an assessment of, control and transfer risk. The scope of this course is to provide a broad understanding of risk and insurance as a means to manage it. This forms the foundation to facilitate the students in their further studies on insurance. The course introduces the concept of risk and techniques of identifying, measuring and managing it. In this context, insurance as a risk management tool is discussed with references to its role, functions and basic principles as applicable to different classes of insurance. The objectives of the course are to provide students with  a comprehensive understanding for making risk management decisions to increase business value and individual welfare  a complete understanding of risk transfer through pooling and key features of insurance market  an understanding of the effects of and rationale for public policies that affect risk and its allocation  Knowledge about insurance markets and important details of an insurance contract as a risk management tool.  Assessing and evaluating insurance needs and implement effective solutions, involving and aligning the entire organization 3 Text Book: George Rejda and Michael McNamara ‘Principles of Risk Management and Insurance’ 14th edition, Pearson Education, 2022 (ISBN 9780134082578) 4 Reference Books:  John Teale, Insurance and Risk Management, CCH Australia Ltd, 2013  James Trieschmann, David Sommer, Robert Hoyt, Risk management and Insurance, Cengage Learning, 12 Edition, 2005  Harrington scott E.& Niehaus Gregory “Risk Management and Insurance” Tata McGraw-Hill, Second edition.2004 (or latest edition)  Scott E. Harrington & Gregory R. Niehaus, Risk Management and Insurance, McGraw Hill, 2nd edition.  Vaughan E.J & T. Vaughan : “Fundamentals of Risk & Insurance “John Wiley & Sons (Asia) Ninth edition.2003  Williams, Jr, M.L.Smith &Peter G. Young “Risk Management and Insurance” Mc Graw-Hill International, Eighth edition .1998  Dr.Gupta P.K, Insurance and Risk Management, Himalaya Publishing House, latest edition.  Against the Gods, The Remarkable Story of Risk, Bernstein, Peter L., New York, Wiley 1996  Websites: www.irdaindia.org ; www.tac.org.in ; www.rims.org 5 The Learning Outcomes By the end of the course, students should be able to:  Understand the fundamentals of risk management and insurance, practices, the methodology in the identification, analysis and management of risks.  Identify, interpret, and evaluate issues and implications associated with RMI in the global business environment.  The basic principles of insurance, as one possible risk financing tool, is also expected to be understood.  choose appropriate insurance policies related to – legal principles in insurance; life and health insurance; property and liabilities insurance; the role insurance intermediaries and functions of insurers and social insurance. 6 Course Plan: Please note that the actual topics/concepts to be covered in each head of lecture session will be provided separately. title: Digital Design
description: Boolean Algebra & logic minimization; combinational logic circuits: arithmetic circuit design, Design using MSI components; Sequential Logic Circuits: flip flops & latches, registers and counters, Finite state machine; HDL Implementation of Digital circuits; Digital Integrated Circuits; Programmable logic devices; Memory organization; Algorithmic State machine; Introduction to computer organization; The course will also have laboratory component on digital design. 2. Textbook(s) T1: M. Moris Mano and Michael D. Ciletti “Digital Design,” PHI, 6th Edition, 2018. T2: G. Raghurama, S. Gurunarayanan, S. Mohan, Karthik, Pawan K. Ajmera, “Laboratory Manual”, 2022 3. Reference book(s) and online resources R1: Donald D. Givonne, “Digital Principles and Design” TMH, 2003 R2: W. Stallings, “Computer Organization and Architecture” PHE, 10th Edition, 2015 BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 4. Course Objectives 1. Understand ● Explain binary/BCD number representations and perform base conversions ● State the postulates of Boolean algebra and the meaning of minterms, maxterms, SOP/POS forms ● Describe the operation of standard combinational building blocks (adders, decoders, multiplexers, comparators, ALUs) and standard sequential elements (latches, flip-flops, registers, counters) ● Describe the characteristics of digital logic families (BJT, TTL, MOS) and PLD architectures ● Explain algorithms for signed multiplication (Booth's) and division 2. Apply ● Simplify Boolean functions using K-maps (including don't-cares, PI/EPI) and the Quine-McCluskey method ● Analyze and derive state tables/diagrams for a given sequential circuit ● Compare design tradeoffs between ripple-carry vs. carry-lookahead adders, and between different logic family implementations ● Trace/debug simple Verilog modules against their intended combinational or sequential behavior 3. Create ● Design combinational circuits (use of adders, decoders, mux/demux, PLDs) to meet given specifications ● Design sequential circuits (use of counters, registers, shift registers) from a given behavioral description ● Design a digital system from an algorithmic state machine (ASM) chart ● Implement and verify combinational/sequential designs in Verilog 5. title: SMART MATERIALS
description: The course introduces smart materials and smart structures through their physical mechanisms, characteristic responses and engineering use. Major topics include piezoelectric ceramics and polymers; one-way, two-way and magnetic shape-memory alloys; electro- and magnetorheological fluids; magnetostrictive and electrostrictive materials; and fibre-optic and FBG sensors. Basic modelling is embedded within the relevant material modules using physically interpretable equations and response curves. Applications include sensing, actuation, vibration control, damping, structural- health monitoring, energy harvesting and intelligent devices.
description_handout: The course introduces smart materials and smart structures through their physical mechanisms, characteristic responses and engineering use. Major topics include piezoelectric ceramics and polymers; one-way, two-way and magnetic shape-memory alloys; electro- and magnetorheological fluids; magnetostrictive and electrostrictive materials; and fibre-optic and FBG sensors. Basic modelling is embedded within the relevant material modules using physically interpretable equations and response curves. Applications include sensing, actuation, vibration control, damping, structural- health monitoring, energy harvesting and intelligent devices.
scope_objective: This undergraduate course develops a foundational understanding of stimulus- responsive materials and their use in smart structures. Emphasis is placed on physical mechanisms, observable behaviour, characteristic curves and straightforward engineering comparisons rather than advanced constitutive modelling. Guided demonstrations, basic experiments, case studies, paper reviews, assignments and project work will connect theory with practice. These activities are intended to develop scientific curiosity and encourage interested students to pursue further project- and research- oriented work in smart materials and structures.
learning_outcomes: CO1: Explain the terminology, operating principles, physical mechanisms and characteristic behaviour of major smart-material families and smart structural systems. CO2: Interpret basic characteristic curves, experimental observations and performance data to describe the sensing and actuation behaviour of smart materials. CO3: Compare major smart-material families and identify suitable materials for simple engineering applications based on their capabilities, limitations and operating requirements. CO4: Investigate smart-material behaviour through guided demonstrations, basic experiments, case studies, paper reviews or project work, and communicate the resulting observations and findings.

title: Digital VLSI Design
description: We will study the fundamental structures of VLSI Systems at the lowest levels of system abstraction, namely those associated with the direct application of VLSI devices to particular problems of interest. The broad topics of coverage includes Principles of operations of CMOS transistors used as a digital switch and various other topologies used in Digital VLSI Design, Logic implementation strategies and performance characterization of the VLSI circuits, Low Power Design, different clocking strategies, symbolic layout systems, CMOS subsystems design and Memory modules.

title: Cloud Computing
description: The primary objective of the course is to introduce the student to cloud computing from architectural and design perspectives. As such, the emphasis of the course would be on the underlying infrastructure and architecture of clouds, techniques for enabling services and the quality of such services, as well as issues in designing clouds. Select research issues in performance, security, and management would also be addressed. Programming on the cloud would be encouraged but not taught in class. Students are expected to learn and understand tools and techniques for using, designing, and implementing clouds and services via assignments and a term project. 2. Text Book T1. None 3.
